Thus, dynamic stretching executed while one deliberately concentrates on progressively contracting and relaxing 
the muscle complex being stretched can prove invaluable in enhancing active flexibility. Although most fitness 
instructors believe stretching a relaxed muscle to be safer and more effective, the proven PNF techniques using 
phases o f contraction and relaxation can be both safe and very effective (see Ch 7). Application o f the PNF 
principles of spiral and diagonal patterns of movement can also produce superior three-dimensional functional 
ROM (range o f movement) to standard static stretches. In this respect, it is interesting to note that many 
conventional stretches are executed in only one plane at a time and very few rotational stretches about the 
longitudinal axes of the limbs are ever used. Thus, many of these stretches could be enhanced if they included 
elements of rotation and twisting, especially if they followed some of the patterns encountered in actual sport.
The use of quasi-isometric activity can be especially useful in developing active flexibility (see 1.9). This 
requires one to exercise a limb through a full range of movement against a resistance which is allowed to stretch a 
joint gently beyond its limit of static flexibility without producing any sudden movement which may recruit the 
myotatic reflex. Free weights, pulley and other functional training machines can be particularly versatile in 
allowing one to execute natural patterns of movement against resistance (see 4.2.7). In addition, longer periods of 
progressive isometric or quasi-isometric activity in full range movement produce greater gains in active flexibility.
Eccentric quasi-isometrics can be especially useful for enhancing functional range of movement, if one allows 
the load to force the joint to move slowly and eccentrically beyond its limit of static flexibility. Used as a method 
of improving flexibility, it does not have to be performed against very heavy loads; one should commcnce with 
small loads and use the progressive overload principle to gradually work up to near-maximal loads. In training 
with light or heavy loads, one should use multiple repetitions, gradually increasing the range of movement with 
each repetition. Both modes of quasi-isometrics may be used in conjunction with PNF techniques and patterns 
to improve fitness qualities such as static strength, static flexibility, dynamic flexibility, flcxibility-strength and 
flexibility-cndurance (see Ch 7).
Starting-strength is also extremely important to human muscular performance, so the use of injudicious 
stretching or part-range resistance training which can impair this quality should be discouraged. Conversely, 
resistance training of gradually increasing intensity in any zones of activc muscular inadequacy, particularly in the 
region of full extension, is to be encouraged. Unfortunately, most isokinetic machines display a small lag in their 
early phases and therefore are inadequate for developing starting-strength or functional flexibility in this critical 
joint zone. If the inertia of weights, machines or pulley systems renders them unsuitable for early rehabilitation, 
progressively sequenced isometric contractions at a variety of joint angles or work against elastic bands (with the 
fixed end moved to appropriate starting positions) can prove to be especially useful.
“Functional” stretching conditioning also has to cnhance the qualities of Jlexibility-speed. flexibility-strength 
(static and dynamic) and flexibility-endurance (static and dynamic) which are required for high level performance 
in sport. Flexibility-speed refers to the ability to produce efficient full ROM at speed; flexibility-strength to the 
ability to produce efficient, powerful static and dynamic movements over a full ROM; and flexibility-endurance to 
the ability to repetitively produce efficient full ROM under static and dynamic conditions. The importance of 
using a wide variety of carefully sequenced stretching methods of cyclically periodised intensity, duration and 
complexity then bccomes obvious.

could quite safely be included within the scope of PNF. If gentle bouncing forms of ballistic stretching are used 
over a gradually increasing range of movement, they will be seen to be a special type of contract-rclax or hold-relax 
PNF activity and therefore may be applied safely and effectively. One may also alternate static stretches with 
periodic gentle ballistic stretches to enhance the effectiveness of any stretch and one may even carry out ballistic

and conventional dynamic stretching becausc ballistic actions are a frequent component of most sports and other 
forms of stretching usually do not address this specificity of joint action.

repetition (Matveyev, 1981). No further repetitions should be performed if the range o f movement becomes 
impaired by fatigue, an approach which may be applied with equal validity to all other forms of stretching.
3.5.9 Low Flexibility versus Non-functional M uscle Tension
Limitations in functional ROM should not automatically be attributed to joint stiffness alone, because this can 
lead to an unnecessary emphasis on stretching. Limitations to full ROM can also be caused by various forms of 
spurious tension or excessive muscle tension such as coordination tension, which may accompany the appropriate 
muscle tension required by the given movement. This non-functional tension can occur in both phasic and tonic 
muscles before, during and after the movement.
The level of proficiency of the athlete has a marked influence on the reflex ability o f the muscles to contract 
and relax (Fig 3.35). Rapidity of both contraction and relaxation increases with level of mastery, with a decrease 
in relaxation time becoming especially evident. The importance of teaching athletes to relax the muscles rapidly 
and efficiently to enhance the functional range of sporting movement then becomes obvious. 
It is of little 
consequence to have highly flexible joints with well conditioned, supple connective tissues and a large range of 
movement, if action is limited by any spurious muscle tension. Flexibility training, therefore, should always be 
combined with neuromuscular training to produce efficient, functional ROM.

relaxation (sec 7.2).
• Sudden unloading, the sudden removal of external resistance imposed under strong isometric or dynamic 
conditions (e.g. the end of the jerk, completion o f a heavy squat or bench press, throwing of a shot or 
medicine ball, short bursts of strong electromuscular contraction). 
It has been shown that this means 
produces the greatest relaxation response of all the means currently used. They become even more effective if 
the powerful and rapid contraction-relaxation process is related as closely as possible to the given sporting 
actions.
• The change of muscle groups from a state of tension to relaxation in a controlled, gradual manner or in a series 
of stages (e.g. Jacobsen's progressive relaxation method).

1755	STRENGTH TRAINING
1756	Opinion concerning the means and methods of strength training often repeats itself, with the beginning of the 
1757	modem era identifying more clearly the motor mechanisms of sports technique. This has helped to determine the 
1758	means of strength training more precisely. However, with the improvement in sporting achievements, the effect 
1759	of these means became less marked. The volume of the same exercises was increased, but it was found that this 
1760	approach also has its limitations (Verkhoshansky, 1977). Once again, researchers turned to analysis o f sports 
1761	movements, now equipped with better measuring technology.
1762	This new cycle of research initiated further progress in training methodology. This was the case, for example, 
1763	when information regarding the significance of strength in sport emerged from the laboratory and coaches looked 
1764	optimistically to weight training. The next trend was towards specificity, since studies indicated that the strength 
1765	necessary for the successful execution of one movement has little effect on another movement. Naturally, this 
1766	specificity of strength turned attention to the principle of selectivity in the means of special preparation.
1767	In general, the progress of strength preparation methods leads logically to examination of 
1768	the motor 
1769	mechanisms underlying sports movements. This results in new hypotheses being formulated to replace currently 
1770	accepted ones, beginning with an understanding of actual sports movements and the specific level of the athlete's 
1771	physical fitness. Thus, one can understand why it is necessary to devise new means that cannot easily be rejected 
1772	in favour of fashionable techniques which have become established more on the basis of tradition and emotion 
1773	than on scientific grounds (Verkhoshansky, 1977).
1774	Thus, the selection of the strength and other training means based on the motor specifics o f given sports 
1775	exercises, is one of the most important tasks in sport. This has marked a turning point in training science, which 
1776	has identified the progression of all training from a foundation of general physical preparation (GPP) to 
1777	wbsequent specific physical preparation (SPP), guided by an intimate understanding of the specific character of 
1778	the sports activity. The practice of selecting the means of strength preparation, based upon the specifics of the 
1779	athlete's movements, leads one to abandon reliance on intuition alone and find a more objective foundation.
1780	This foundation is expressed in the form of the principle o f dynamic correspondence, which determines how 
1781	closely the means of special strength preparation corresponds to the functioning of the neuromuscular system in a 
1782	given sport (Vcrkhoshansky, 1977).

1785	traces in the body. With repetitive stimulation the traces accumulate, leading to significant modifications which 
1786	raise the functional capability o f the body. A characteristic of every living creature is the relative speed with 
1787	which it adapts to repetitive stimulation. The same regime of stimulation can rapidly produce habituation and 
1788	then fail to elicit any further adaptation, only maintaining the existing levels. Another regime can prove excessive 
1789	and lead to overtraining, which prevents adaptation. An optimum level of stimulation offered in a progressively 
1790	increasing sequence of carefully chosen means is essential for ensuring adaptation at successively higher levels of 
1791	performance (see 1.14).
1792	This, in general and simplified terms, is the physiological foundation of training. In reality it is a very intricate 
1793	process, since systematic exercise as a means of physical conditioning involves a complex of different stimuli 
1794	which affect all systems of the body. 
1795	For example, to successfully increase strength, the load, number of 
1796	repetitions, tempo of execution and workout venue all influence the effectiveness of the training. These variables 
1797	could be listed at great length, since the development of strength is not the only goal o f training. However, 
1798	besides this, it is likely that the coach will select from the vast number of variations, that combination of means 
1799	which he considers will produce the greatest success.

hypertrophy than functional strength, since this is the main aim of'isolation' training.
Some final remarks are warranted. Lest one be tempted to consider that the muscles alone are responsible for 
all stabilisation and mobilisation, we must remember that ligaments, fascia and joint capsules play an important rok 
in passively stabilising some joints to enable the body to actively use the muscles to execute other tasks. Although 
this stabilising role is well known in preventing joint damage when loading threatens to move a joint beyond its 
active structural limits, these soft tissues also play a vital role during non-emergency situations.
For example, spinal ligament involvement during dcadlifting or cleans is invaluable for decreasing the stress <m 
the erector spinae. Spinal flexion during heavy lifts from the ground can damage the intervertebral discs, so
198


===== PDF idx 210 / printed 199 =====
SUPERTRAINING
competent lifters strive to diminish the flattening of the lumbar spine by actively concentrating on increasing 
erector spinae tension. If this is overdone, the various spinal ligaments become slack and most of the load is borne 
by the muscles. Conversely, if the muscles are inadequately contracted, then excessive stress is placed on the 
ligaments. The skilled lifter is able to optimise the required balance between the spinal muscles and ligaments, 
thereby enhancing lifting efficiency and diminishing the likelihood of injury. Similar rhythms and patterns of 
muscular and other soft tissue involvement are essential for all strength training efficiency and safety.
Limitations of Anatom ical M ovem ent Analysis
Standard anatomical textbook approaches describing the action of certain muscle groups in controlling isolated joint 
actions, such as flexion, extension and rotation, frequently are used to identify which musclcs should be trained to 
enhance performance in sport. Virtually every bodybuilding and sports training publication invokes this approach 
in describing how a given exercise or machine ‘works* a given muscle group, as do most of the clinical texts on 
muscle testing and rehabilitation.
The appropriateness of this tradition, however, recently has been questioned on the basis o f biomechanical 
analysis of multi-articular joint actions (Zajac & Gordon, 1989). This classical method of functional anatomy 
defines a given muscic, for instance, as a flexor or extensor, on the basis of the torque that it produces around a 
single joint, but the nature of the body as a linked system of many joints means that muscles which do not span 
other joints can still produce acceleration about those joints.
The anatomical approach implies that complex multi-articular movement is simply the linear superimposition 
of the actions of the individual joints which are involved in that movement. However, the mechanical systems of the 
body are nonlinear and superposition docs not apply, since there is no simple relationship between velocity, angle 
and torque about a single joint in a complex sporting movement. Besides the fact that a single muscle group can 
simultaneously perform several different stabilising and moving actions about one joint, there is also a fundamental 
difference between the dynamics of single and multiple joint movements, namely that forces on one segment can be 
caused by motion of other segments. In the case of uniarticular musclcs or even biarticular muscles (like the biceps 
or triceps), where only one of the joints is constrained to move, the standard approach is acceptable, but not if 
several joints are free to move concurrently.
Because joint acceleration and individual joint torque are linearly related, Zajac and Gordon (1989) consider it 
more accurate to rephrase a statement such as “muscle X flexes joint A” as “muscle X acts to accelerate joint A into 
flexion” Superficially, this may seem a matter of trivial semantics, but the fact that muscles certainly do act to 
accelerate all joints has profound implications for the analysis of movement. For instance, muscles which cross the 
ankle joint can extend and flex the knee joint much more than they do the ankle.
Biomechanical analysis reveals that multi articular muscles may even accelerate a spanned joint in a direction 
opposite to that of the joint to which it is applying torque.
In the apparently simple action of standing, soleus, usually labelled as an extensor of the ankle, accelerates the 
knee (which it does not span) into extension (Fig 3.47) twice as much as it acts to accelerate the ankle (which it 
spans) into extension for positions near upright posture (Zajac & Gordon, 1989).
Ftjure 3.47 Effect of soleus on the angular acceleration o f the knee relative to the ankle (based on Zajac & Gordon, 1989).
199


===== PDF idx 211 / printed 200 =====
SUPERTRAINING
In work derived from Lombard’s Paradox (‘Antagonist muscles can act in the same contraction mode as their] 
agonists’), Andrews (1985, 1987) found that the rectus femoris of the quadriceps and all the hamstrings act in three] 
different ways during cycling, emphasizing that biarticular muscles are considered enigmatic. 
This paradosl 
originally became apparent when it was noticed that in actions such as cycling and squatting, extension of the knee 
and the hip occurs simultaneously, so that the quadriceps and hamstrings are both operating concentrically at the 
same time. Theoretically, according to the concept of concurrent musclc antagonism, the hamstrings should contract 
eccentrically while the quadriceps are contracting concentrically, and vice versa, since they are regarded as opposing 
muscles.
Others have shown that a muscle which is capable o f carrying out several different joint actions, does no( 
necessarily do so in every movement (Andrews, 1982, 1985). For instance, gluteus maximus, which can extend and 
abduct the hip, will not necessarily accelerate the hip simultaneously into extension and abduction, but its extensor 
torque may even accelerate the hip into adduction (Mansour & Pereira, 1987).
Gastrocnemius, which is generally recognised as a flexor of the knee and an extensor of the ankle, actually can cany 
out the following complex tasks (see Fig 3.48):
(a) flex the knee and extend the ankle
(b) flex the knee and flex the ankle
(c) extend the knee and extend the ankle
Figure 3.48 The three possible actions of gastrocnemius revealed by the relative moment-arm ratios of the knee and ankle joints (based 
on Zajac & Gordon, 1989).
During the standing press, which used to be part of Olympic Weightlifting, the back bending action of the trunk is 
due not only to a Newton 111 reaction to the overhead pressing action, but also due to acceleration caused by the 
thrusting backwards of the triceps muscle which crosses the shoulder joint, as well as the elbow joint. This same 
action of the triceps also occurs during several gymnastic moves on the parallel, horizontal and uneven bars. This 
back extending action of the triceps is counteracted by the expected trunk flexing action of rectus abdominis and the 
hip extension action of the hip flexors, accompanied by acceleration of the trunk by the hip flexors.
Appreciation of this frequently ignored type of action by many niultiarticular muscles enables us to select and 
use resistance training exercises far more effectively to meet an athlete's specific sporting needs and to offer 
superior rehabilitation of the injured athlete.
Because of this multiplicity of actions associated with multiarticular complex movement, Zajac and Gordon 
stress a point made by Basmajian (1978), namely that it may be more useful to examine muscle action in terms of 
synergism rather than agonism and antagonism. This is especially important, since a generalised approach to 
understanding human movement on the basis of breaking down all movement into a series of single joint actions fails 
to take into account that muscle action is task dependent.
200


===== PDF idx 212 / printed 201 =====
SUPERTRAINING
THE MEANS OF SPECIAL 
STRENGTH TRAINING
Opinion concerning the means and methods of strength training often repeats itself, with the beginning of the 
modem era identifying more clearly the motor mechanisms of sports technique. This has helped to determine the 
means of strength training more precisely. However, with the improvement in sporting achievements, the effect 
of these means became less marked. The volume of the same exercises was increased, but it was found that this 
approach also has its limitations (Verkhoshansky, 1977). Once again, researchers turned to analysis o f sports 
movements, now equipped with better measuring technology.
This new cycle of research initiated further progress in training methodology. This was the case, for example, 
when information regarding the significance of strength in sport emerged from the laboratory and coaches looked 
optimistically to weight training. The next trend was towards specificity, since studies indicated that the strength 
necessary for the successful execution of one movement has little effect on another movement. Naturally, this 
specificity of strength turned attention to the principle of selectivity in the means of special preparation.
In general, the progress of strength preparation methods leads logically to examination of 
the motor 
mechanisms underlying sports movements. This results in new hypotheses being formulated to replace currently 
accepted ones, beginning with an understanding of actual sports movements and the specific level of the athlete's 
physical fitness. Thus, one can understand why it is necessary to devise new means that cannot easily be rejected 
in favour of fashionable techniques which have become established more on the basis of tradition and emotion 
than on scientific grounds (Verkhoshansky, 1977).
Thus, the selection of the strength and other training means based on the motor specifics o f given sports 
exercises, is one of the most important tasks in sport. This has marked a turning point in training science, which 
has identified the progression of all training from a foundation of general physical preparation (GPP) to 
wbsequent specific physical preparation (SPP), guided by an intimate understanding of the specific character of 
the sports activity. The practice of selecting the means of strength preparation, based upon the specifics of the 
athlete's movements, leads one to abandon reliance on intuition alone and find a more objective foundation.
This foundation is expressed in the form of the principle o f dynamic correspondence, which determines how 
closely the means of special strength preparation corresponds to the functioning of the neuromuscular system in a 
given sport (Vcrkhoshansky, 1977).
4.1 The Problem of Training Means
The process of adaptation involves stimulation from the external or internal environment, which leaves certain 
traces in the body. With repetitive stimulation the traces accumulate, leading to significant modifications which 
raise the functional capability o f the body. A characteristic of every living creature is the relative speed with 
which it adapts to repetitive stimulation. The same regime of stimulation can rapidly produce habituation and 
then fail to elicit any further adaptation, only maintaining the existing levels. Another regime can prove excessive 
and lead to overtraining, which prevents adaptation. An optimum level of stimulation offered in a progressively 
increasing sequence of carefully chosen means is essential for ensuring adaptation at successively higher levels of 
performance (see 1.14).
This, in general and simplified terms, is the physiological foundation of training. In reality it is a very intricate 
process, since systematic exercise as a means of physical conditioning involves a complex of different stimuli 
which affect all systems of the body. 
For example, to successfully increase strength, the load, number of 
repetitions, tempo of execution and workout venue all influence the effectiveness of the training. These variables 
could be listed at great length, since the development of strength is not the only goal o f training. However, 
besides this, it is likely that the coach will select from the vast number of variations, that combination of means 
which he considers will produce the greatest success.
4.1.1 Characteristics of Strength Increase
Strength as a specific result of physical adaptation is determined by the intensity and repetitiveness of the stimuli 
to which the body is exposed during use of the motor apparatus. Only a sufficiently intense level of muscular

1	######## [1] claim--irradiation-effect-raises-prime-mover-force-and-endurance.md
2	---
3	type: library-entry
4	kind: claim
5	domain: strength-and-conditioning
6	book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
7	chapter: "3.4.3"
8	topic: cross-limb irradiation effects on prime mover force
9	category: [neuromuscular, coordination, cross-education]
10	confidence: supported
11	ingest-tier: full-text
12	created: 2026-09-27
13	---
14	
15	# Tensing Additional, Non-Prime-Mover Muscle Groups Can Raise or Lower Working-Limb Force
16	
17	**What it is** — In acyclic movements that require a single instantaneous maximal
18	contraction (so proficiency cannot be judged by the fluid tension-relaxation sequencing
19	used in cyclic movements, unlike the jaw-tension example the authors give for judging a
20	sprinter's mastery), deliberately involving additional muscle groups not directly needed
21	for the task, an "additional movement," can change the working effect. The authors
22	attribute this to "overflow" or "irradiation" from stronger to weaker or more fatigued
23	muscles, a concept from PNF (Knott & Voss, 1968), plus excitation of the dominant motor
24	centre by afferent impulses from the additional muscle groups, which raises effector-process
25	excitability in the prime-mover muscle groups. Concrete numbers (Mukhammedova, 1958): during
26	rhythmic flexing of the right arm, momentarily tensing the left elbow's extensors raised
27	right-arm flexor work capacity by 39-42%, while tensing the left elbow's flexors after first
28	fatiguing the right flexors increased the right's capacity to do more work; tensing the left
29	flexors alone (without prior right-arm fatigue) decreased right-arm work capacity by 8-22%.
30	A large stimulatory effect appeared when the left arm's additional effort reached 25-33% of
31	the right arm's effort. Separately, the authors cite the unexercised-limb "cross-training"
32	phenomenon (training one side of the body increases strength on the unexercised side):
33	Wissler & Richardson, 1900; Davis, 1942; Hellebrant et al, 1947; Laun, 1954; Enoka, 1988.
34	(PDF p. 177, printed p. 166, "3.4.3 Additional Movement.")
35	
36	**Why it works** — The authors give the mechanism directly: afferent impulses from the
37	additional muscle groups raise excitability of the dominant motor centre, which is
38	counter-productive early in an effort (before dominance has formed) but becomes
39	stimulatory once dominance is established (Shatenstein & Yordanskaya, 1955). They also
40	note the size and direction of the effect depends on the athlete's fitness, the type of
41	additional activity (dynamic vs static), and changes in load or work rhythm (Vinogradov,
42	1966), so this is not a fixed-magnitude effect.
43	
44	**When NOT to apply** — The quantified numbers come from one small, dated lab study of
45	contralateral elbow flexion/extension (Mukhammedova, 1958), not from a validated training
46	method; the direction of the effect (raise vs lower) depends on which muscle group is
47	tensed and when, so "add tension elsewhere" is not a safe blanket cue. The authors' own
48	timing caveat matters: involving other muscle groups before the prime-mover motor centre
49	has established dominance in that effort "will be counter-productive." The book gives no
50	applied strength-training protocol built on this effect, only the underlying phenomenon
51	and its role in athletics (they mention pole-vault takeoff as an example of mechanically,
52	not just neurally, mediated additional movement).
53	
54	**Example** — Inference: a coach cueing a lifter to actively grip and brace with the
55	non-working hand or forearm during a heavy unilateral press or pull, once the lifter is
56	already committed to the effort, is consistent with the irradiation effect raising
57	prime-mover output; the book gives no such applied strength-training example itself.
58	
59	**Related** — [[claim--bilateral-deficit-and-limb-training-specificity]] (Ch1, a different
60	cross-limb neural phenomenon: bilateral force deficit vs this irradiation/cross-education
61	effect; both concern neural interaction between limbs but are not the same mechanism).
62	######## [2] claim--multijoint-coordination-compensates-for-disadvantageous-joint-angles.md
63	---
64	type: library-entry
65	kind: claim
66	domain: strength-and-conditioning
67	book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
68	chapter: "3.4.5"
69	topic: coordination redistributes force to offset joint-angle disadvantage
70	category: [coordination, biomechanics, technique]
71	confidence: supported
72	ingest-tier: full-text
73	created: 2026-09-27
74	---
75	
76	# In Multi-Joint Movements, Resultant Force Is Not the Sum of Each Muscle Group's Individual Maximum
77	
78	**What it is** — Coordination changes during a movement can take three forms (Averianov,
79	1963; Moikin, 1964): a change in the sequence of muscle groups participating, a change in
80	the number of muscle groups participating, and a change in the relative degree of
81	participation of different muscles. In complex multi-joint movements, the resulting force
82	does not equal the sum of the individual maximum tensions each contributing muscle group
83	is capable of. The authors' rowing example (Table 3.9, Egorov, 1966): the largest summed
84	force a rower develops occurs at the beginning of the stroke, even though the legs are
85	working at a disadvantageous knee and hip angle at that instant. However, the percentage
86	utilisation of absolute strength (the summed force actually produced relative to the
87	summed maximum each contributing muscle group could individually produce) is also largest
88	at that same instant. The authors' reading: disadvantageous conditions for one muscle
89	group's work can be compensated by more advantageous conditions for another's, through
90	effective coordination of contributory actions (here, the back muscles compensating for
91	the legs' poor angle). Separately, in cyclic movements the duration of active and relative
92	rest phases changes across the movement and the point of maximal muscular contribution
93	shifts from one muscle group to another; and movements against large resistance, or
94	executed at great speed, shift activity toward the muscles of the proximal limb segments
95	(Ivanitsky, 1956; Lebedev, 1962; Moikin, 1964; Averianov & Shibanov, 1964). (PDF pp.
96	178-179, printed pp. 167-168, "3.4.5 Coordination in Muscular Work," Table 3.9.)
97	
98	**Why it works** — This is the authors' own explanation, not an inference: a disadvantaged
99	joint angle for one muscle group's contribution in a multi-joint chain can be offset by
100	another muscle group being in a more mechanically favorable position at that same instant,
101	so the chain's summed output is not simply predictable from summing each joint's isolated
102	strength curve.
103	
104	**When to apply** — Use this when interpreting force output from a multi-joint,
105	multi-phase lift or sport action (e.g., a pull phase of an Olympic lift, a rowing stroke,
106	a jump takeoff) rather than assuming the resultant force can be predicted by summing
107	single-joint isometric or isokinetic test values taken at each joint's own disadvantaged
108	angle. It also cautions against reading a low single-joint strength-curve value at a given
109	angle as a direct limiter of the whole-chain output at that phase of the movement.
110	
111	**When NOT to apply** — Table 3.9's numbers are specific to the rowing stroke and to skill
112	level (Class III, Class II, Class I, Master of Sport), not a universal quantitative model;
113	the authors give no formula for how much compensation occurs in other lifts or chains, only
114	the general principle and one worked example. Do not extend the exact rowing percentages to
115	other movements.
116	
117	**Example** — Inference: a lifter whose limited ankle dorsiflexion forces a more
118	upright, back-angle-dominant front squat may still produce comparable summed force at the
119	sticking point by relying more on hip and back musculature at that phase, rather than
120	losing force output in direct proportion to the knee/ankle angle disadvantage; the book
121	gives no front-squat data, this reasoning only extends the rowing principle.
122	
123	**Related** — [[framework--dynamometric-and-functional-profile-for-weak-link-identification]]
124	(Ch2, strength-topography profiling by joint and muscle group; that entry's isolated
125	joint-angle testing is the kind of single-joint data this entry warns against
126	over-extrapolating to multi-joint output).
127	######## [3] claim--exercise-economy-improves-with-skill-and-interval-style-costs-more.md
128	---
129	type: library-entry
130	kind: claim
131	domain: strength-and-conditioning
132	book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
133	chapter: "3.4.6"
134	topic: energy expenditure differs by skill level, load, and rep style
135	category: [energy-systems, technique, economy]
136	confidence: supported
137	ingest-tier: full-text
138	created: 2026-09-27
139	---
140	
141	# Skilled Lifters Spend Less Energy per Lift, and Discrete Singles Cost More Than a Continuous Set
142	
143	**What it is** — Based on Vorobyev's (1978) weightlifting data (Tables 3.10-3.12), energy
144	expenditure in resistance training varies with bodymass, exercise, and skill level. Rate of
145	energy expenditure (kJ/min, Table 3.10) rises with bodymass class (from 9.9 kJ/min for
146	Class I-II lifters in the 56 kg division to 23.0 kJ/min in the >90 kg division) and is
147	lower at the same bodymass division for Masters of Sport than for Class I-III lifters.
148	Absolute energy expenditure for a 1RM attempt (kcal, Table 3.12) is generally lower for
149	"elite" lifters than for lower-ranked ("ranked") lifters on the same exercise: e.g. clean
150	and jerk, 13.7 kcal (elite) vs 15.5 kcal (ranked); bench press, 8.4 vs 12.2 kcal. (One
151	exception visible in the table but not discussed by the authors: front squat runs slightly
152	higher for elite lifters than ranked, 12.7 vs 11.8 kcal.) Relative to bodymass (Table 3.11),
153	the clean and jerk is the most economical major lift and the press from the rack the most
154	expensive, because its prime movers are the comparatively small arm muscles rather than
155	the large muscle mass used in the clean and jerk. Separately, and independent of the skill
156	tables: the specific energy expenditure of a series of single repetitions performed with
157	rest between each (an "interval" style) is 35% greater than a continuous set of several
158	repetitions with the same load. (PDF pp. 179-180, printed pp. 168-169, "3.4.6 Efficiency of
159	Energy Expenditure," Tables 3.10-3.12, Fig 3.30.)
160	
161	**Why it works** — The authors give the mechanism for the interval-vs-continuous finding
162	directly: continuous-style exercise (as in traditional bodybuilding or circuit training)
163	relies more heavily on momentum and on elastic energy stored in the tendons between
164	repetitions, and minimizes the amount of eccentric, starting-strength, and isometric work,
165	all of which raise the metabolic cost of a discrete single repetition performed from a dead
166	stop. Improving movement efficiency (skill) is described as reducing energy cost for any
167	level of strength, speed-strength, strength-endurance, or other fitness component; the
168	authors give no mechanism for why skill specifically lowers per-lift energy cost beyond
169	this general efficiency claim.
170	
171	**When to apply** — Use this to caution against summing kcal or kJ figures across exercise
172	types to compare training-session cost, and to expect that the same external load performed
173	as discrete singles with rest between reps (e.g., cluster sets) is more metabolically
174	demanding per repetition than the same reps done continuously.
175	
176	**When NOT to apply** — The authors explicitly warn that "a simplistic calculation of
177	energy expenditure... can be very misleading" because it fails to account for rest
178	intervals between exercises or the interaction of successive training sessions; two
179	sessions should not be treated as equivalent training stress just because their summed
180	energy expenditure is similar. The skill/bodymass tables are single-lab, Soviet-era
181	weightlifting data (Vorobyev, 1978) specific to the snatch, clean and jerk, and their
182	component pulls and presses; they are not established as generalizable to other lifts or
183	populations.
184	
185	**Example** — Inference: cluster sets (discrete reps with intra-set rest at a fixed load)
186	likely impose a higher energy cost per repetition than the same reps performed continuously,
187	consistent with the 35% figure above, though the book presents no cluster-set experiment
188	itself.
189	
190	**Related** — None found in the staging library or vault on this specific angle
191	(skill-linked lifting economy); flagged for a reciprocal link if a future entry on cluster
192	sets or lifting economy is added.
193	######## [4] claim--hypnosis-and-social-presence-alter-strength-output.md
194	---
195	type: library-entry
196	kind: claim
197	domain: strength-and-conditioning
198	book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
199	chapter: "3.4.7"
200	topic: hypnosis, emotion, and social presence effects on strength
201	category: [psychology, strength-expression]
202	confidence: supported
203	ingest-tier: full-text
204	created: 2026-09-27
205	---
206	
207	# Emotional State, Hypnosis, and an Audience Can Each Change Measured Strength
208	
209	**What it is** — The authors report several psychological effects on strength expression,
210	each from a single old citation with no modern replication given. Strong positive emotions
211	can immediately increase the energy of muscular contraction by as much as four times
212	(Vinogradov, 1966). Under certain conditions, hypnosis has been shown to increase muscular
213	strength by 22.5% and to decrease it by 31.7% (Ikai & Steinhaus, 1961); the authors give no
214	detail on what conditions produced which direction. Group activities produce greater results
215	than individual activities (Gurnee, 1937; Abel, 1938; Weyner & Zeaman, 1956; Beasley, 1958;
216	Cratty, 1965). The presence of spectators also increases the effectiveness of motor activity
217	(Gates, 1924; Lazaruc et al, 1952; Cratty & Hutten, 1964), with novices showing a
218	significantly greater improvement from an audience than advanced athletes (Singer, 1965).
219	The authors' summary: "carefully directed training creates a specific emotional background
220	which makes strength work more productive." (PDF p. 182, printed p. 171, "3.4.7 Emotion and
221	Other Psychological Factors.")
222	
223	**Why it works** — The author gives no mechanism connecting emotion, hypnosis, or social
224	presence to measured force output beyond naming the findings themselves. Inference: these
225	are most plausibly framed as changes in voluntary activation or willingness to approach the
226	true physiological ceiling (raising the "expressed" fraction of maximal strength) rather
227	than a change in the muscle's underlying contractile capacity, but the source does not state
228	this explanation.
229	
230	**When NOT to apply** — Every figure here rests on a single citation from 1924-1965, with
231	no magnitude-reproducing modern study named; do not treat the 22.5%/31.7% hypnosis figures
232	or the fourfold emotion figure as established, reproducible effect sizes. Hypnosis for
233	performance manipulation is not a documented Baylor Applied Performance or Athletic
234	Performance practice and raises consent and oversight questions this source does not
235	address; this entry documents the claim, it does not endorse using hypnosis as an
236	intervention. The social-facilitation effect is explicitly reported as larger in novices
237	than advanced athletes, so it should not be assumed to transfer to elite competitors
238	unchanged.
239	
240	**Example** — Inference: a coach who has observed that certain athletes perform noticeably
241	better in a full weight room with teammates present than alone is consistent with the
242	group/spectator findings above, though the book gives no team-sport or strength-training
243	example of its own.
244	
245	**Related** — None found in the staging library or vault; this is a distinct angle from
246	[[heuristic--instruction-type-and-verbal-framing-shape-strength-output]] (same source
247	subsection, coaching-instruction effects rather than emotional/social state effects).
248	######## [5] heuristic--instruction-type-and-verbal-framing-shape-strength-output.md
249	---

261	
262	# Split Instruction into "Heuristic" (What) and "Concrete" (How), and Expect Less Return from It as Athletes Advance
263	
264	**What it is** — The authors give two applied findings about verbal coaching input and
265	strength expression. First, a preliminary verbal command about the perceived heaviness of
266	a load can change the tonus of the working muscles without changing the actual load: the
267	words "heavy load" increase tension in the working arm muscles and "light load" decrease it
268	(Farfel, 1961). Second, instruction should always target a precise motor aim and can be
269	divided into two types: **heuristic** instruction (what must be done, leaving the athlete
270	to individually develop the specific technique to accomplish the task) and **concrete**
271	instruction (how it must be done, the coach specifying the execution details). The combined
272	use of both types by an experienced coach increases the effectiveness of strength exercises.
273	Active, qualified guidance produces the optimal force-speed-amplitude combination for a
274	speed-strength movement faster than unguided practice; the authors cite a depth-jump takeoff
275	study (Table 3.13, Verkhoshansky, 1963) where less experienced athletes executing the
276	takeoff faster or slower than usual changed jump height, and a rowing-feedback study
277	(Table 3.14, Egorov, 1966) where telling rowers the actual force contribution of each
278	phase of the stroke raised their stroke force scores across all skill classes. The authors
279	state that instruction effectiveness decreases as athlete qualification rises, because a
280	Master of Sport learns, to a large degree, to mobilise their own potential. (PDF pp.
281	181-182, printed pp. 170-171, "3.4.7 Emotion and Other Psychological Factors.")
282	
283	**Why it works** — The author gives no mechanism for the verbal-framing effect beyond
284	citing the finding itself (Farfel, 1961). Inference: the load-framing result implies verbal
285	cues can shift motor-unit recruitment or intended effort independent of the true
286	mechanical demand, which is consistent with why coaches' language during a lift ("this one's
287	heavy") is not neutral.
288	
289	**When to apply** — Pair heuristic instruction (state the outcome: "get the bar moving as
290	fast as possible off the chest") with concrete instruction (specify execution: "keep your
291	elbows under the bar") deliberately, rather than defaulting to only one type. Expect
292	outcome-based feedback about actual force or timing (as in the rowing example) to improve
293	execution even in already-trained athletes.
294	
295	**When NOT to apply** — The qualification-effectiveness claim ("effectiveness of
296	instruction decreases with the increase in qualification") is stated without a quantified
297	threshold or citation of its own; treat it as the authors' generalization, not a measured
298	result. The supporting studies (Table 3.13, Table 3.14) are single-lab Soviet
299	weightlifting/rowing data collected in testing or lab settings, not shown as a
300	longitudinal training method. The verbal-framing finding (Farfel, 1961) is a single old
301	citation with no magnitude given, only direction.
302	
303	**Example** — Inference: telling a lifter "this set is your top set, make it fast" versus
304	"this is a light warm-up" for the same actual %1RM could, per the Farfel finding, shift bar
305	speed or perceived effort independent of the load itself; the book gives no strength-training
306	example of this specific kind.
307	
308	**Related** — [[heuristic--program-variable-complexity-scales-with-training-age]] (Ch1,
309	also connects training-age to how much a variable, there programming complexity, here
310	coaching instruction, needs to be managed for less-trained athletes).

324	
325	# Brief Cold Exposure May Raise Work Capacity; Prolonged Cold Is Contraindicated as an Ergogenic Aid
326	
327	**What it is** — The authors report that brief application of cold to the body can
328	increase work capacity, citing Michael (1957, via Vorobyev, 1978): cold showers increase
329	work capacity, more so in trained athletes than in the general public. In support, the
330	authors cite older findings (Happ, 1947; Rosen, 1952; O'Rolev, 1956) that cold compresses
331	applied to the abdomen between exercise sets improved performance, and report a similar
332	improvement when Russian weightlifters were sponged with cold water between competition
333	lifts. The application described in every cited case was brief. Prolonged cold exposure
334	that lowers muscle or core temperature is explicitly described as contraindicated as an
335	ergogenic aid. A longer cold application (5-15 minutes, typically ice) is named as
336	effective for a different purpose: treating muscle and other soft-tissue trauma, not
337	boosting performance. (PDF pp. 182-183, printed pp. 171-172, "3.4.8 The Effect of Cold
338	Application.")
339	
340	**Why it works** — The source presents this as Vorobyev's own suggested explanation, not
341	an established mechanism: the muscle contraction induced by shivering, increased adrenal
342	gland activity, and a survival-directed central nervous system reaction to peripheral cold
343	stimulation. The authors do not independently verify this mechanism; it is reported as a
344	proposed explanation, not a demonstrated one.
345	
346	**When to apply** — As a brief, targeted stimulus (cold shower, localized cold compress, or
347	cold sponging) between sets or attempts in a competition or training setting where a
348	trained athlete's work capacity needs a short-term lift, consistent with the cited findings.
349	
350	**When NOT to apply** — Do not use prolonged cold exposure, or any application that lowers
351	muscle or core temperature, as a pre-performance or between-set strategy; the source states
352	this directly as contraindicated. The supporting citations are old (1947-1965) and largely
353	single-source per claim, with no magnitude or dose-response data given (how brief is
354	"brief," how cold is "cold"). The proposed mechanism is the source's own conjecture, not
355	independently tested within this text. This entry is about acute work-capacity effects, not
356	about cold application for recovery or injury treatment, which the source treats as a
357	separate, longer-duration use.
358	
359	**Example** — Inference: a brief cold-water face or forearm splash between attempts at a
360	competition, rather than an ice bath or prolonged cold-water immersion beforehand, is the
361	kind of application consistent with the cited findings; the book gives no specific modern
362	protocol.
363	
364	**Related** — None found in the staging library or vault on acute cold exposure and work
365	capacity specifically (distinct from post-exercise cold-water immersion for recovery,
366	which this entry does not address).
367	######## [7] principle--breath-holding-and-valsalva-support-spinal-stability-in-maximal-lifting.md

380	
381	# Breath-Holding (Valsalva) Stabilises the Spine Under Heavy Load; Exhaling Through Effort Is the Authors' Named Risk, Except for Cardiac or Hypertensive Athletes
382	
383	**What it is** — The authors state that breathing pattern, duration, and rate have a
384	profound effect on strength production. The Valsalva manoeuvre, breath-holding, plays a
385	vital role in raising intra-abdominal pressure to support and stabilise the lumbar spine
386	during heavy lifting, with the abdominal and oblique muscles acting as an anatomical
387	corset. Spinal stress is diminished during high-resistance-loaded movement against
388	resistance when breath is held, and exhalation during lifting increases the risk of lumbar
389	injury; the authors call it unwise to follow the popular medical advice to exhale during
390	effort during strenuous lifting, squatting, or overhead pressing, though they name that
391	advice as appropriate specifically for patients with cardiac disease or hypertension.
392	Common sporting actions, jumping, throwing, pushing against an opponent, striking a ball,
393	standing up from a squat, kicking, elicit involuntary breath-holding because it enhances
394	performance and control accuracy in short-duration movements; archery and pistol shooting
395	stability and accuracy are tied to brief breath-holding phases; other cited research found
396	speed-strength actions are optimally enhanced when lung air volume is held at about 75% of
397	maximum capacity (Vorobyev, 1978). A study of 34 qualified weightlifters (Blokhin &
398	Monastirskii, 1985) recorded bar movement and breathing (spirometry) during the clean and
399	jerk at 60-90% of 1RM and identified three breathing-phase variants (A, B, C) across the
400	pull, rack, and jerk. All lifters held their breath during the pull and during the jerk in
401	every variant; when breathing did occur at other phases, exhalation volume always exceeded
402	inhalation volume by at least 125 ml. Variant B was judged optimal for maximal effort;
403	variant A occurs when the athlete makes technical corrections mid-lift; variant C is
404	characteristic of submaximal lifts. Recommendation: breath-holding should precede and
405	accompany maximal efforts, followed by brief exhalation-inhalation unless a technical
406	correction is needed, in which case breath-holding should persist; submaximal loads can use
407	longer normal-breathing phases and shorter breath-holding phases; neither rapid short
408	hyperventilation nor a forced maximal inhalation is desirable during maximal-effort lifting.
409	(PDF pp. 183-184, printed pp. 172-173, "3.4.9 Breathing and Strength Production," Fig 3.31.)
410	
411	**Why it works** — The authors give the mechanism directly: breath-holding raises
412	intra-abdominal pressure, and the abdominal and oblique muscles use that pressure as an
413	anatomical corset to support and stabilise the lumbar spine, reducing spinal stress under
414	high-resistance loading. Inference: this is broadly consistent with the modern
415	strength-training convention of Valsalva or bracing during heavy compound lifts, though
416	this entry does not independently verify that separate literature.
417	
418	**When to apply** — Cue breath-holding through the concentric drive of a heavy
419	compound lift (squat, deadlift, overhead press), with a brief exhale-inhale at or near
420	lockout rather than exhaling through the sticking point, for healthy athletes lifting near
421	maximal loads. For submaximal work, normal breathing between reps is acceptable, with
422	breath-holding reserved for the effort phase itself.
423	
424	**When NOT to apply** — The authors themselves name the exception: athletes with cardiac
425	disease or hypertension should follow the standard medical advice to exhale during effort,
426	not hold their breath, because Valsalva raises intrathoracic and blood pressure. The source
427	does not discuss that blood-pressure risk itself, or give any guidance on how long a breath
428	hold is safe; it addresses spinal stability and performance, not cardiovascular risk
429	management. The 34-lifter breathing-phase study is specific to the snatch/clean-and-jerk
430	pull-rack-jerk sequence at 60-90% of 1RM; it is not validated for sustained isometric
431	holds, high-rep sets, or other lift patterns.
432	
433	**Example** — Inference: cue a lifter to inhale to roughly the described optimal range,
434	hold through the pull off the floor and the drive through the sticking point of a heavy
435	deadlift or squat, then exhale briefly at lockout before the next rep, rather than exhaling
436	on the way up.
437	
438	**Related** — None found in the staging library or vault on breathing pattern and lifting
439	technique specifically; flagged for a reciprocal link if a future entry addresses
440	intra-abdominal pressure or bracing directly.

454	
455	# Removing Vision During Practice Can Sharpen Proprioceptive Awareness and Technical Skill
456	
457	**What it is** — The authors state that strength, efficiency, and safety of movement are
458	determined primarily by neuromuscular factors, in particular kinaesthesis and the
459	underlying proprioceptive mechanisms that inform the body about the position and motion of
460	its own components, integrated with input from the other senses (sight, sound, hearing,
461	touch). Proprioception receives little dedicated training attention despite its central
462	role in PNF (proprioceptive neuromuscular facilitation) rehabilitation. One way to improve
463	proprioceptive efficiency is to diminish or block input from other sensory systems,
464	particularly vision: training with weights, or executing Olympic or powerlifting movements,
465	blindfolded can enhance technical skill and strength or power production. Research cited
466	(Roman, 1986) found blindfolding does not disrupt motor activity and that, on the contrary,
467	exercises are performed with greater precision and stability when the eyes are closed or in
468	darkness; athletes remember joint angles, degree of muscular tension, movement amplitude,
469	and movement patterns best with eyes closed, and that enhanced motor sensitivity is
470	preserved and improves technical skill once the movement is performed with eyes open again.
471	During normal training an athlete is largely unaware of errors and generally feels the
472	exercise is being done correctly; blindfolded practice increases proprioceptive sensitivity,
473	enabling more accurate internal self-correction. Practical protocol described: eyes are
474	lightly covered with soft, dark material (airline eye-covers are named as suitable); the
475	athlete repeats the starting position with the coach's tactile and verbal correction; the
476	athlete then performs the full movement with light weights, alternating eyes uncovered and
477	covered until it feels natural and stable, then progresses to heavier weights with the same
478	alternation until the movement is mastered blindfolded. The technique is usable for any
479	strength exercise where the body stays in contact with the bar or apparatus, and also for
480	select movements practiced blindfolded to improve proprioception (jumping, track-and-field
481	events, swimming, throwing), as well as in physiotherapy rehabilitation, applying PNF
482	techniques and movement patterns with the client blindfolded. (PDF pp. 184-185, printed pp.
483	173-174, "3.4.10 Strength Development and Proprioception.")
484	
485	**Why it works** — The authors' own explanation: removing visual feedback forces reliance
486	on proprioceptive information, and the resulting heightened internal awareness of joint
487	angle, tension, amplitude, and pattern is retained and improves technique once vision is
488	restored, because the athlete can now form a more accurate internal "visualisation" of the
489	movement to self-correct against.
490	
491	**When to apply** — For refining technique on a movement the athlete already performs
492	safely (not a first exposure), where visual dependence (e.g., watching the bar path in a
493	mirror) may be masking coordination or positioning errors; in supervised rehabilitation
494	using PNF-style pattern drilling with reduced visual input.
495	
496	**When NOT to apply** — The authors give no safety protocol beyond soft eye-covers and a
497	light-to-heavy loading progression; this is not appropriate for a genuinely unfamiliar
498	movement, for high-injury-risk loads, or without a trusted coach spotting and cueing
499	throughout, none of which the source addresses directly. The single supporting citation
500	(Roman, 1986) is dated, and the source reports the rationale and a training procedure, not
501	a quantified measure of how much technical improvement resulted.
502	
503	**Example** — Inference: a lifter who over-relies on watching the bar path during the squat
504	could perform light-load blindfolded reps with a coach's verbal and tactile cueing to build
505	internal proprioceptive awareness of depth and bar position, then remove the blindfold once
506	the pattern feels stable; the book does not give this specific example.
507	
508	**Related** — [[framework--kinaesthetic-system-and-feedforward-visualization]] (Ch1, the
509	kinaesthetic system and mental-visualization content this entry's proprioceptive-training
510	method draws on).

524	
525	# Flexibility Is Joint- and Direction-Specific Range of Movement, Not a Single Trait
526	
527	**What it is** — The authors define flexibility as the range of movement (ROM) of a
528	specific joint with respect to a particular degree of freedom, not a single global trait.
529	Each joint exhibits, statically or dynamically, some or many of: flexion-extension,
530	rotation, adduction-abduction, traction-approximation, protraction-retraction,
531	inversion-eversion, varus-valgus, pronation-supination, and various gliding/rocking
532	actions. Some degrees of freedom are under active muscular control; others occur only
533	passively from external force (the authors' example: a sudden stop during running can
534	glide the femur anteriorly on the tibia). ROM at any joint is determined by: the
535	structural/architectural limits of the joint itself, the mechanical properties of the
536	muscles and other soft tissues, neuromuscular processes controlling muscle tension and
537	length, the level of non-functional muscle tension present, and the individual's pain
538	threshold near end of range. Two types are distinguished: active flexibility (maximum ROM
539	producible under active muscular control) and passive flexibility (maximum ROM producible
540	passively by an external force without causing joint injury). The authors call
541	toe-touching and the "splits" commonly but wrongly treated as general indicators of
542	flexibility or suppleness, when flexibility is joint-specific: it is common for a toe-toucher
543	or a splitter to be unable to sit on their haunches with heels flat. (PDF p. 185, printed
544	p. 174.)
545	
546	A closing caution from the same section: joint tissues must balance mobility (the ability
547	to stretch) against stability (damping ratio, the ability to absorb tensile shocks). A
548	joint whose tissues have low stiffness (stretches easily) but a low damping ratio (absorbs
549	shock poorly) is described as especially susceptible to overload injury (Siff, 1986). (PDF
550	p. 187, printed p. 176.)
551	
552	**Why it works** — This is the authors' definitional framework for organizing the rest of
553	the chapter, not an empirical finding with its own mechanism to evaluate.
554	
555	**When to apply** — Use this to choose or interpret a flexibility test by joint and degree
556	of freedom relevant to the sport skill, rather than defaulting to one generic test (e.g.
557	sit-and-reach) as a stand-in for "flexibility." When a test or exercise is reported to
558	improve "flexibility," ask which joint, which degree of freedom, and active or passive.
559

######## [1] claim--irradiation-effect-raises-prime-mover-force-and-endurance.md
---
type: library-entry
kind: claim
domain: strength-and-conditioning
book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
chapter: "3.4.3"
topic: cross-limb irradiation effects on prime mover force
category: [neuromuscular, coordination, cross-education]
confidence: supported
ingest-tier: full-text
created: 2026-09-27
---

# Tensing Additional, Non-Prime-Mover Muscle Groups Can Raise or Lower Working-Limb Force

**What it is** — In acyclic movements that require a single instantaneous maximal
contraction (so proficiency cannot be judged by the fluid tension-relaxation sequencing
used in cyclic movements, unlike the jaw-tension example the authors give for judging a
sprinter's mastery), deliberately involving additional muscle groups not directly needed
for the task, an "additional movement," can change the working effect. The authors
attribute this to "overflow" or "irradiation" from stronger to weaker or more fatigued
muscles, a concept from PNF (Knott & Voss, 1968), plus excitation of the dominant motor
centre by afferent impulses from the additional muscle groups, which raises effector-process
excitability in the prime-mover muscle groups. Concrete numbers (Mukhammedova, 1958): during
rhythmic flexing of the right arm, momentarily tensing the left elbow's extensors raised
right-arm flexor work capacity by 39-42%, while tensing the left elbow's flexors after first
fatiguing the right flexors increased the right's capacity to do more work; tensing the left
flexors alone (without prior right-arm fatigue) decreased right-arm work capacity by 8-22%.
A large stimulatory effect appeared when the left arm's additional effort reached 25-33% of
the right arm's effort. Separately, the authors cite the unexercised-limb "cross-training"
phenomenon (training one side of the body increases strength on the unexercised side):
Wissler & Richardson, 1900; Davis, 1942; Hellebrant et al, 1947; Laun, 1954; Enoka, 1988.
(PDF p. 177, printed p. 166, "3.4.3 Additional Movement.")

**Why it works** — The authors give the mechanism directly: afferent impulses from the
additional muscle groups raise excitability of the dominant motor centre, which is
counter-productive early in an effort (before dominance has formed) but becomes
stimulatory once dominance is established (Shatenstein & Yordanskaya, 1955). They also
note the size and direction of the effect depends on the athlete's fitness, the type of
additional activity (dynamic vs static), and changes in load or work rhythm (Vinogradov,
1966), so this is not a fixed-magnitude effect.

**When NOT to apply** — The quantified numbers come from one small, dated lab study of
contralateral elbow flexion/extension (Mukhammedova, 1958), not from a validated training
method; the direction of the effect (raise vs lower) depends on which muscle group is
tensed and when, so "add tension elsewhere" is not a safe blanket cue. The authors' own
timing caveat matters: involving other muscle groups before the prime-mover motor centre
has established dominance in that effort "will be counter-productive." The book gives no
applied strength-training protocol built on this effect, only the underlying phenomenon
and its role in athletics (they mention pole-vault takeoff as an example of mechanically,
not just neurally, mediated additional movement).

**Example** — Inference: a coach cueing a lifter to actively grip and brace with the
non-working hand or forearm during a heavy unilateral press or pull, once the lifter is
already committed to the effort, is consistent with the irradiation effect raising
prime-mover output; the book gives no such applied strength-training example itself.

**Related** — [[claim--bilateral-deficit-and-limb-training-specificity]] (Ch1, a different
cross-limb neural phenomenon: bilateral force deficit vs this irradiation/cross-education
effect; both concern neural interaction between limbs but are not the same mechanism).
######## [2] claim--multijoint-coordination-compensates-for-disadvantageous-joint-angles.md
---
type: library-entry

domain: strength-and-conditioning
book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
chapter: "3.4.5"
topic: coordination redistributes force to offset joint-angle disadvantage
category: [coordination, biomechanics, technique]
confidence: supported

---

# In Multi-Joint Movements, Resultant Force Is Not the Sum of Each Muscle Group's Individual Maximum

**What it is** — Coordination changes during a movement can take three forms (Averianov,
1963; Moikin, 1964): a change in the sequence of muscle groups participating, a change in
the number of muscle groups participating, and a change in the relative degree of
participation of different muscles. In complex multi-joint movements, the resulting force
does not equal the sum of the individual maximum tensions each contributing muscle group
is capable of. The authors' rowing example (Table 3.9, Egorov, 1966): the largest summed
force a rower develops occurs at the beginning of the stroke, even though the legs are
working at a disadvantageous knee and hip angle at that instant. However, the percentage
utilisation of absolute strength (the summed force actually produced relative to the
summed maximum each contributing muscle group could individually produce) is also largest
at that same instant. The authors' reading: disadvantageous conditions for one muscle
group's work can be compensated by more advantageous conditions for another's, through
effective coordination of contributory actions (here, the back muscles compensating for
the legs' poor angle). Separately, in cyclic movements the duration of active and relative
rest phases changes across the movement and the point of maximal muscular contribution
shifts from one muscle group to another; and movements against large resistance, or
executed at great speed, shift activity toward the muscles of the proximal limb segments
(Ivanitsky, 1956; Lebedev, 1962; Moikin, 1964; Averianov & Shibanov, 1964). (PDF pp.
178-179, printed pp. 167-168, "3.4.5 Coordination in Muscular Work," Table 3.9.)

**Why it works** — This is the authors' own explanation, not an inference: a disadvantaged
joint angle for one muscle group's contribution in a multi-joint chain can be offset by
another muscle group being in a more mechanically favorable position at that same instant,
so the chain's summed output is not simply predictable from summing each joint's isolated
strength curve.

**When to apply** — Use this when interpreting force output from a multi-joint,
multi-phase lift or sport action (e.g., a pull phase of an Olympic lift, a rowing stroke,
a jump takeoff) rather than assuming the resultant force can be predicted by summing
single-joint isometric or isokinetic test values taken at each joint's own disadvantaged
angle. It also cautions against reading a low single-joint strength-curve value at a given
angle as a direct limiter of the whole-chain output at that phase of the movement.

**When NOT to apply** — Table 3.9's numbers are specific to the rowing stroke and to skill
level (Class III, Class II, Class I, Master of Sport), not a universal quantitative model;
the authors give no formula for how much compensation occurs in other lifts or chains, only
the general principle and one worked example. Do not extend the exact rowing percentages to
other movements.

**Example** — Inference: a lifter whose limited ankle dorsiflexion forces a more
upright, back-angle-dominant front squat may still produce comparable summed force at the
sticking point by relying more on hip and back musculature at that phase, rather than
losing force output in direct proportion to the knee/ankle angle disadvantage; the book
gives no front-squat data, this reasoning only extends the rowing principle.

**Related** — [[framework--dynamometric-and-functional-profile-for-weak-link-identification]]
(Ch2, strength-topography profiling by joint and muscle group; that entry's isolated
joint-angle testing is the kind of single-joint data this entry warns against
over-extrapolating to multi-joint output).

# Skilled Lifters Spend Less Energy per Lift, and Discrete Singles Cost More Than a Continuous Set

**What it is** — Based on Vorobyev's (1978) weightlifting data (Tables 3.10-3.12), energy
expenditure in resistance training varies with bodymass, exercise, and skill level. Rate of
energy expenditure (kJ/min, Table 3.10) rises with bodymass class (from 9.9 kJ/min for
Class I-II lifters in the 56 kg division to 23.0 kJ/min in the >90 kg division) and is
lower at the same bodymass division for Masters of Sport than for Class I-III lifters.
Absolute energy expenditure for a 1RM attempt (kcal, Table 3.12) is generally lower for
"elite" lifters than for lower-ranked ("ranked") lifters on the same exercise: e.g. clean
and jerk, 13.7 kcal (elite) vs 15.5 kcal (ranked); bench press, 8.4 vs 12.2 kcal. (One
exception visible in the table but not discussed by the authors: front squat runs slightly
higher for elite lifters than ranked, 12.7 vs 11.8 kcal.) Relative to bodymass (Table 3.11),
the clean and jerk is the most economical major lift and the press from the rack the most
expensive, because its prime movers are the comparatively small arm muscles rather than
the large muscle mass used in the clean and jerk. Separately, and independent of the skill
tables: the specific energy expenditure of a series of single repetitions performed with
rest between each (an "interval" style) is 35% greater than a continuous set of several
repetitions with the same load. (PDF pp. 179-180, printed pp. 168-169, "3.4.6 Efficiency of
Energy Expenditure," Tables 3.10-3.12, Fig 3.30.)

**Why it works** — The authors give the mechanism for the interval-vs-continuous finding
directly: continuous-style exercise (as in traditional bodybuilding or circuit training)
relies more heavily on momentum and on elastic energy stored in the tendons between
repetitions, and minimizes the amount of eccentric, starting-strength, and isometric work,
all of which raise the metabolic cost of a discrete single repetition performed from a dead
stop. Improving movement efficiency (skill) is described as reducing energy cost for any
level of strength, speed-strength, strength-endurance, or other fitness component; the
authors give no mechanism for why skill specifically lowers per-lift energy cost beyond
this general efficiency claim.

**When to apply** — Use this to caution against summing kcal or kJ figures across exercise
types to compare training-session cost, and to expect that the same external load performed
as discrete singles with rest between reps (e.g., cluster sets) is more metabolically
demanding per repetition than the same reps done continuously.

**When NOT to apply** — The authors explicitly warn that "a simplistic calculation of
energy expenditure... can be very misleading" because it fails to account for rest
intervals between exercises or the interaction of successive training sessions; two
sessions should not be treated as equivalent training stress just because their summed
energy expenditure is similar. The skill/bodymass tables are single-lab, Soviet-era
weightlifting data (Vorobyev, 1978) specific to the snatch, clean and jerk, and their
component pulls and presses; they are not established as generalizable to other lifts or
populations.

**Example** — Inference: cluster sets (discrete reps with intra-set rest at a fixed load)
likely impose a higher energy cost per repetition than the same reps performed continuously,
consistent with the 35% figure above, though the book presents no cluster-set experiment
itself.

**Related** — None found in the staging library or vault on this specific angle
(skill-linked lifting economy); flagged for a reciprocal link if a future entry on cluster
sets or lifting economy is added.

# Emotional State, Hypnosis, and an Audience Can Each Change Measured Strength

**What it is** — The authors report several psychological effects on strength expression,
each from a single old citation with no modern replication given. Strong positive emotions
can immediately increase the energy of muscular contraction by as much as four times
(Vinogradov, 1966). Under certain conditions, hypnosis has been shown to increase muscular
strength by 22.5% and to decrease it by 31.7% (Ikai & Steinhaus, 1961); the authors give no
detail on what conditions produced which direction. Group activities produce greater results
than individual activities (Gurnee, 1937; Abel, 1938; Weyner & Zeaman, 1956; Beasley, 1958;
Cratty, 1965). The presence of spectators also increases the effectiveness of motor activity
(Gates, 1924; Lazaruc et al, 1952; Cratty & Hutten, 1964), with novices showing a
significantly greater improvement from an audience than advanced athletes (Singer, 1965).
The authors' summary: "carefully directed training creates a specific emotional background
which makes strength work more productive." (PDF p. 182, printed p. 171, "3.4.7 Emotion and
Other Psychological Factors.")

**Why it works** — The author gives no mechanism connecting emotion, hypnosis, or social
presence to measured force output beyond naming the findings themselves. Inference: these
are most plausibly framed as changes in voluntary activation or willingness to approach the
true physiological ceiling (raising the "expressed" fraction of maximal strength) rather
than a change in the muscle's underlying contractile capacity, but the source does not state
this explanation.

**When NOT to apply** — Every figure here rests on a single citation from 1924-1965, with
no magnitude-reproducing modern study named; do not treat the 22.5%/31.7% hypnosis figures
or the fourfold emotion figure as established, reproducible effect sizes. Hypnosis for
performance manipulation is not a documented Baylor Applied Performance or Athletic
Performance practice and raises consent and oversight questions this source does not
address; this entry documents the claim, it does not endorse using hypnosis as an
intervention. The social-facilitation effect is explicitly reported as larger in novices
than advanced athletes, so it should not be assumed to transfer to elite competitors
unchanged.

**Example** — Inference: a coach who has observed that certain athletes perform noticeably
better in a full weight room with teammates present than alone is consistent with the
group/spectator findings above, though the book gives no team-sport or strength-training
example of its own.

**Related** — None found in the staging library or vault; this is a distinct angle from
[[heuristic--instruction-type-and-verbal-framing-shape-strength-output]] (same source
subsection, coaching-instruction effects rather than emotional/social state effects).

# Split Instruction into "Heuristic" (What) and "Concrete" (How), and Expect Less Return from It as Athletes Advance

**What it is** — The authors give two applied findings about verbal coaching input and
strength expression. First, a preliminary verbal command about the perceived heaviness of
a load can change the tonus of the working muscles without changing the actual load: the
words "heavy load" increase tension in the working arm muscles and "light load" decrease it
(Farfel, 1961). Second, instruction should always target a precise motor aim and can be
divided into two types: **heuristic** instruction (what must be done, leaving the athlete
to individually develop the specific technique to accomplish the task) and **concrete**
instruction (how it must be done, the coach specifying the execution details). The combined
use of both types by an experienced coach increases the effectiveness of strength exercises.
Active, qualified guidance produces the optimal force-speed-amplitude combination for a
speed-strength movement faster than unguided practice; the authors cite a depth-jump takeoff
study (Table 3.13, Verkhoshansky, 1963) where less experienced athletes executing the
takeoff faster or slower than usual changed jump height, and a rowing-feedback study
(Table 3.14, Egorov, 1966) where telling rowers the actual force contribution of each
phase of the stroke raised their stroke force scores across all skill classes. The authors
state that instruction effectiveness decreases as athlete qualification rises, because a
Master of Sport learns, to a large degree, to mobilise their own potential. (PDF pp.
181-182, printed pp. 170-171, "3.4.7 Emotion and Other Psychological Factors.")

**Why it works** — The author gives no mechanism for the verbal-framing effect beyond
citing the finding itself (Farfel, 1961). Inference: the load-framing result implies verbal
cues can shift motor-unit recruitment or intended effort independent of the true
mechanical demand, which is consistent with why coaches' language during a lift ("this one's
heavy") is not neutral.

**When to apply** — Pair heuristic instruction (state the outcome: "get the bar moving as
fast as possible off the chest") with concrete instruction (specify execution: "keep your
elbows under the bar") deliberately, rather than defaulting to only one type. Expect
outcome-based feedback about actual force or timing (as in the rowing example) to improve
execution even in already-trained athletes.

**When NOT to apply** — The qualification-effectiveness claim ("effectiveness of
instruction decreases with the increase in qualification") is stated without a quantified
threshold or citation of its own; treat it as the authors' generalization, not a measured
result. The supporting studies (Table 3.13, Table 3.14) are single-lab Soviet
weightlifting/rowing data collected in testing or lab settings, not shown as a
longitudinal training method. The verbal-framing finding (Farfel, 1961) is a single old
citation with no magnitude given, only direction.

**Example** — Inference: telling a lifter "this set is your top set, make it fast" versus
"this is a light warm-up" for the same actual %1RM could, per the Farfel finding, shift bar
speed or perceived effort independent of the load itself; the book gives no strength-training
example of this specific kind.

**Related** — [[heuristic--program-variable-complexity-scales-with-training-age]] (Ch1,
also connects training-age to how much a variable, there programming complexity, here
coaching instruction, needs to be managed for less-trained athletes).
