# Brief Cold Exposure May Raise Work Capacity; Prolonged Cold Is Contraindicated as an Ergogenic Aid

**What it is** — The authors report that brief application of cold to the body can
increase work capacity, citing Michael (1957, via Vorobyev, 1978): cold showers increase
work capacity, more so in trained athletes than in the general public. In support, the
authors cite older findings (Happ, 1947; Rosen, 1952; O'Rolev, 1956) that cold compresses
applied to the abdomen between exercise sets improved performance, and report a similar
improvement when Russian weightlifters were sponged with cold water between competition
lifts. The application described in every cited case was brief. Prolonged cold exposure
that lowers muscle or core temperature is explicitly described as contraindicated as an
ergogenic aid. A longer cold application (5-15 minutes, typically ice) is named as
effective for a different purpose: treating muscle and other soft-tissue trauma, not
boosting performance. (PDF pp. 182-183, printed pp. 171-172, "3.4.8 The Effect of Cold
Application.")

**Why it works** — The source presents this as Vorobyev's own suggested explanation, not
an established mechanism: the muscle contraction induced by shivering, increased adrenal
gland activity, and a survival-directed central nervous system reaction to peripheral cold
stimulation. The authors do not independently verify this mechanism; it is reported as a
proposed explanation, not a demonstrated one.

**When to apply** — As a brief, targeted stimulus (cold shower, localized cold compress, or
cold sponging) between sets or attempts in a competition or training setting where a
trained athlete's work capacity needs a short-term lift, consistent with the cited findings.

**When NOT to apply** — Do not use prolonged cold exposure, or any application that lowers
muscle or core temperature, as a pre-performance or between-set strategy; the source states
this directly as contraindicated. The supporting citations are old (1947-1965) and largely
single-source per claim, with no magnitude or dose-response data given (how brief is
"brief," how cold is "cold"). The proposed mechanism is the source's own conjecture, not
independently tested within this text. This entry is about acute work-capacity effects, not
about cold application for recovery or injury treatment, which the source treats as a
separate, longer-duration use.

**Example** — Inference: a brief cold-water face or forearm splash between attempts at a
competition, rather than an ice bath or prolonged cold-water immersion beforehand, is the
kind of application consistent with the cited findings; the book gives no specific modern
protocol.

**Related** — None found in the staging library or vault on acute cold exposure and work
capacity specifically (distinct from post-exercise cold-water immersion for recovery,
which this entry does not address).

# Breath-Holding (Valsalva) Stabilises the Spine Under Heavy Load; Exhaling Through Effort Is the Authors' Named Risk, Except for Cardiac or Hypertensive Athletes

**What it is** — The authors state that breathing pattern, duration, and rate have a
profound effect on strength production. The Valsalva manoeuvre, breath-holding, plays a
vital role in raising intra-abdominal pressure to support and stabilise the lumbar spine
during heavy lifting, with the abdominal and oblique muscles acting as an anatomical
corset. Spinal stress is diminished during high-resistance-loaded movement against
resistance when breath is held, and exhalation during lifting increases the risk of lumbar
injury; the authors call it unwise to follow the popular medical advice to exhale during
effort during strenuous lifting, squatting, or overhead pressing, though they name that
advice as appropriate specifically for patients with cardiac disease or hypertension.
Common sporting actions, jumping, throwing, pushing against an opponent, striking a ball,
standing up from a squat, kicking, elicit involuntary breath-holding because it enhances
performance and control accuracy in short-duration movements; archery and pistol shooting
stability and accuracy are tied to brief breath-holding phases; other cited research found
speed-strength actions are optimally enhanced when lung air volume is held at about 75% of
maximum capacity (Vorobyev, 1978). A study of 34 qualified weightlifters (Blokhin &
Monastirskii, 1985) recorded bar movement and breathing (spirometry) during the clean and
jerk at 60-90% of 1RM and identified three breathing-phase variants (A, B, C) across the
pull, rack, and jerk. All lifters held their breath during the pull and during the jerk in
every variant; when breathing did occur at other phases, exhalation volume always exceeded
inhalation volume by at least 125 ml. Variant B was judged optimal for maximal effort;
variant A occurs when the athlete makes technical corrections mid-lift; variant C is
characteristic of submaximal lifts. Recommendation: breath-holding should precede and
accompany maximal efforts, followed by brief exhalation-inhalation unless a technical
correction is needed, in which case breath-holding should persist; submaximal loads can use
longer normal-breathing phases and shorter breath-holding phases; neither rapid short
hyperventilation nor a forced maximal inhalation is desirable during maximal-effort lifting.
(PDF pp. 183-184, printed pp. 172-173, "3.4.9 Breathing and Strength Production," Fig 3.31.)

**Why it works** — The authors give the mechanism directly: breath-holding raises
intra-abdominal pressure, and the abdominal and oblique muscles use that pressure as an
anatomical corset to support and stabilise the lumbar spine, reducing spinal stress under
high-resistance loading. Inference: this is broadly consistent with the modern
strength-training convention of Valsalva or bracing during heavy compound lifts, though
this entry does not independently verify that separate literature.

**When to apply** — Cue breath-holding through the concentric drive of a heavy
compound lift (squat, deadlift, overhead press), with a brief exhale-inhale at or near
lockout rather than exhaling through the sticking point, for healthy athletes lifting near
maximal loads. For submaximal work, normal breathing between reps is acceptable, with
breath-holding reserved for the effort phase itself.

**When NOT to apply** — The authors themselves name the exception: athletes with cardiac
disease or hypertension should follow the standard medical advice to exhale during effort,
not hold their breath, because Valsalva raises intrathoracic and blood pressure. The source
does not discuss that blood-pressure risk itself, or give any guidance on how long a breath
hold is safe; it addresses spinal stability and performance, not cardiovascular risk
management. The 34-lifter breathing-phase study is specific to the snatch/clean-and-jerk
pull-rack-jerk sequence at 60-90% of 1RM; it is not validated for sustained isometric
holds, high-rep sets, or other lift patterns.

**Example** — Inference: cue a lifter to inhale to roughly the described optimal range,
hold through the pull off the floor and the drive through the sticking point of a heavy
deadlift or squat, then exhale briefly at lockout before the next rep, rather than exhaling
on the way up.

**Related** — None found in the staging library or vault on breathing pattern and lifting
technique specifically; flagged for a reciprocal link if a future entry addresses
intra-abdominal pressure or bracing directly.

# Removing Vision During Practice Can Sharpen Proprioceptive Awareness and Technical Skill

**What it is** — The authors state that strength, efficiency, and safety of movement are
determined primarily by neuromuscular factors, in particular kinaesthesis and the
underlying proprioceptive mechanisms that inform the body about the position and motion of
its own components, integrated with input from the other senses (sight, sound, hearing,
touch). Proprioception receives little dedicated training attention despite its central
role in PNF (proprioceptive neuromuscular facilitation) rehabilitation. One way to improve
proprioceptive efficiency is to diminish or block input from other sensory systems,
particularly vision: training with weights, or executing Olympic or powerlifting movements,
blindfolded can enhance technical skill and strength or power production. Research cited
(Roman, 1986) found blindfolding does not disrupt motor activity and that, on the contrary,
exercises are performed with greater precision and stability when the eyes are closed or in
darkness; athletes remember joint angles, degree of muscular tension, movement amplitude,
and movement patterns best with eyes closed, and that enhanced motor sensitivity is
preserved and improves technical skill once the movement is performed with eyes open again.
During normal training an athlete is largely unaware of errors and generally feels the
exercise is being done correctly; blindfolded practice increases proprioceptive sensitivity,
enabling more accurate internal self-correction. Practical protocol described: eyes are
lightly covered with soft, dark material (airline eye-covers are named as suitable); the
athlete repeats the starting position with the coach's tactile and verbal correction; the
athlete then performs the full movement with light weights, alternating eyes uncovered and
covered until it feels natural and stable, then progresses to heavier weights with the same
alternation until the movement is mastered blindfolded. The technique is usable for any
strength exercise where the body stays in contact with the bar or apparatus, and also for
select movements practiced blindfolded to improve proprioception (jumping, track-and-field
events, swimming, throwing), as well as in physiotherapy rehabilitation, applying PNF
techniques and movement patterns with the client blindfolded. (PDF pp. 184-185, printed pp.
173-174, "3.4.10 Strength Development and Proprioception.")

**Why it works** — The authors' own explanation: removing visual feedback forces reliance
on proprioceptive information, and the resulting heightened internal awareness of joint
angle, tension, amplitude, and pattern is retained and improves technique once vision is
restored, because the athlete can now form a more accurate internal "visualisation" of the
movement to self-correct against.

**When to apply** — For refining technique on a movement the athlete already performs
safely (not a first exposure), where visual dependence (e.g., watching the bar path in a
mirror) may be masking coordination or positioning errors; in supervised rehabilitation
using PNF-style pattern drilling with reduced visual input.

**When NOT to apply** — The authors give no safety protocol beyond soft eye-covers and a
light-to-heavy loading progression; this is not appropriate for a genuinely unfamiliar
movement, for high-injury-risk loads, or without a trusted coach spotting and cueing
throughout, none of which the source addresses directly. The single supporting citation
(Roman, 1986) is dated, and the source reports the rationale and a training procedure, not
a quantified measure of how much technical improvement resulted.

**Example** — Inference: a lifter who over-relies on watching the bar path during the squat
could perform light-load blindfolded reps with a coach's verbal and tactile cueing to build
internal proprioceptive awareness of depth and bar position, then remove the blindfold once
the pattern feels stable; the book does not give this specific example.

**Related** — [[framework--kinaesthetic-system-and-feedforward-visualization]] (Ch1, the
kinaesthetic system and mental-visualization content this entry's proprioceptive-training
method draws on).

# Flexibility Is Joint- and Direction-Specific Range of Movement, Not a Single Trait

**What it is** — The authors define flexibility as the range of movement (ROM) of a
specific joint with respect to a particular degree of freedom, not a single global trait.
Each joint exhibits, statically or dynamically, some or many of: flexion-extension,
rotation, adduction-abduction, traction-approximation, protraction-retraction,
inversion-eversion, varus-valgus, pronation-supination, and various gliding/rocking
actions. Some degrees of freedom are under active muscular control; others occur only
passively from external force (the authors' example: a sudden stop during running can
glide the femur anteriorly on the tibia). ROM at any joint is determined by: the
structural/architectural limits of the joint itself, the mechanical properties of the
muscles and other soft tissues, neuromuscular processes controlling muscle tension and
length, the level of non-functional muscle tension present, and the individual's pain
threshold near end of range. Two types are distinguished: active flexibility (maximum ROM
producible under active muscular control) and passive flexibility (maximum ROM producible
passively by an external force without causing joint injury). The authors call
toe-touching and the "splits" commonly but wrongly treated as general indicators of
flexibility or suppleness, when flexibility is joint-specific: it is common for a toe-toucher
or a splitter to be unable to sit on their haunches with heels flat. (PDF p. 185, printed
p. 174.)

A closing caution from the same section: joint tissues must balance mobility (the ability
to stretch) against stability (damping ratio, the ability to absorb tensile shocks). A
joint whose tissues have low stiffness (stretches easily) but a low damping ratio (absorbs
shock poorly) is described as especially susceptible to overload injury (Siff, 1986). (PDF
p. 187, printed p. 176.)

**Why it works** — This is the authors' definitional framework for organizing the rest of
the chapter, not an empirical finding with its own mechanism to evaluate.

**When to apply** — Use this to choose or interpret a flexibility test by joint and degree
of freedom relevant to the sport skill, rather than defaulting to one generic test (e.g.
sit-and-reach) as a stand-in for "flexibility." When a test or exercise is reported to
improve "flexibility," ask which joint, which degree of freedom, and active or passive.

587	
588	# Four Ways to Increase ROM, Ranked by Speed of Effect and Durability
589	
590	**What it is** — The authors give four practical means of enhancing joint ROM, in order
591	of effectiveness, and note the first limitation on the list (skeletal structure) cannot be
592	overcome by any form of exercise:
593	1. Modifying the neuromuscular processes that control tension and length in the muscle
594	complex. This increases ROM most rapidly and most effectively, but the change tends to be
595	confined to short-term improvements unless the neuromuscular means are used as an ongoing
596	part of all training.
597	2. Increasing the length and strength of the soft tissues comprising the muscle complex,
598	especially collagenous tissues such as fascia. These changes are slower to produce but
599	long-term.
600	3. Lengthening and strengthening other soft tissues, especially those of the joint capsule
601	and ligaments. Also long-lasting, but if promoted to the point of joint laxity, joint
602	stability can be severely compromised.
603	4. Restructuring the articulating surfaces of the joints, a process mediated by many years
604	of regular heavy loading in specific patterns; not a practical training target, more a
605	by-product of loaded full-range sporting movement, and inappropriate/excessive loading can
606	instead produce degenerative changes that reduce ROM.
607	The authors add that stretching and flexibility training are not synonymous: some
608	flexibility exercises increase ROM without being stretching exercises at all, because they
609	work entirely by modifying neuromuscular processes (the stretch and tendon reflexes);
610	conversely, many stretching exercises pay no deliberate attention to neuromuscular
611	processes and instead aim at structural change in soft tissue, so static stretches may
612	change muscle length without adequately affecting the dynamic ROM a given sport requires.
613	(PDF pp. 185-186, printed pp. 174-175.)
614	
615	**Why it works** — The authors give no single unifying mechanism; the ordering reflects
616	which physiological layer (nervous system, muscle/fascia, joint capsule/ligament, bone) is
617	being changed and how quickly each layer adapts, from fastest-and-least-durable
618	(neuromuscular) to slowest-and-most-durable (bone).
619	
620	**When to apply** — Use this ordering to set expectations for a flexibility intervention:
621	a single session aimed at neuromuscular relaxation (e.g. PNF) can produce a same-day ROM
622	gain that will not persist without repetition, while a multi-week soft-tissue-lengthening
623	block is the one that produces a durable change. Match the method to the timeframe: a
624	pre-competition warm-up should rely on method 1 (rapid, neuromuscular, session-specific);
625	an off-season block targeting chronic ROM limits should emphasize methods 2-3.
626	
627	**When NOT to apply** — Do not expect a brief pre-event stretching routine to produce
628	long-term flexibility change; the text is explicit that this is a category error common in
629	"the average stretching programme." Do not pursue method 3 (ligament/capsule lengthening)
630	without limit: the text names joint laxity and compromised stability as the direct cost of
631	overdoing it. Method 4 should never be treated as a deliberate training target.
632	
633	**Example** — Inference: a pre-game mobility routine that relies on PNF contract-relax drills is
634	working through method 1 and will not, by itself, change an athlete's baseline hip ROM
635	measured a week later; that requires a sustained block emphasizing methods 2 and 3.

653	# Active Flexibility, Not Passive, Is the One That Tracks Sporting Proficiency
654	
655	**What it is** — Citing a single Russian study of over 200 adult competitors (Iashvili,
656	1982), the authors report that sporting achievement (rated by competition standards)
657	correlates more strongly with active flexibility than with passive flexibility: R = 0.81
658	versus R = 0.69. The same study found traditional static and passive stretching develop
659	mainly passive flexibility, while combined strength-and-stretching exercises are
660	considerably more effective at developing active flexibility, particularly when the
661	strength conditioning is applied in the zone of active muscular inadequacy (i.e. the end
662	of the joint's active range). (PDF p. 186, printed p. 175.)
663	
664	A later section (3.5.8) returns to the same Iashvili (1982) study across "several Olympic
665	sports" with further detail: joint mobility level tracks sporting proficiency generally;
666	static/passive stretching enhances passive flexibility but only moderately improves active
667	mobility (described as "by far the most important flexibility quality needed in sport");
668	the pattern and range of joint mobility is sport-specific (e.g. backstroke/butterfly
669	swimmers show the greatest shoulder and ankle mobility, breast-strokers the least in those
670	joints but the greatest hip/knee mobility; javelinists show the greatest shoulder
671	mobility among throwers, hurdlers the greatest hip flexibility among track athletes); and
672	the active-passive correlation itself depends on training method, running 0.61-0.73 with
673	primarily static/passive stretching but rising to 0.91 when stretching is combined with
674	strengthening. (PDF pp. 196-197, printed pp. 185-186.)
675	
676	A related measurement framework from the same section (Tumanyan & Dzhanyan, 1980) defines
677	three flexibility indices from a pulley-loaded limb: maximum passive flexibility (PFmax,
678	at the pain threshold), active flexibility (AF, reached by non-ballistic muscular action),
679	and loaded passive flexibility (PF, with a progressively increased sub-pain-threshold
680	load), yielding a maximum active flexibility deficit (FDmax = PFmax - AF), a loaded active
681	flexibility deficit (FD = PF - AF), and an interval of flexibility pain threshold (FPT =
682	PFmax - PF). Using these indices, the same source reports: static/passive stretching
683	increases passive flexibility while leaving the active-passive gap unchanged; full-range
684	strength exercise increases passive flexibility and narrows that gap; and combined
685	strength-plus-flexibility exercise increases both and narrows the gap most. A large
686	active-passive gap ("flexibility deficit") is reported to correlate strongly with the
687	incidence of soft-tissue injury. (PDF p. 197, printed p. 186.)
688	
689	**Why it works** — The book gives no physiological mechanism for why active flexibility
690	specifically tracks proficiency; it reports only the correlational and intervention
691	results above.
692	
693	**When to apply** — Prefer testing and training active ROM (through the athlete's own
694	muscular control) over passive ROM (examiner- or gravity-assisted) when the goal is a
695	proxy for sporting flexibility demands, and prefer combined strength-and-stretch
696	programming over stretching alone when the goal is to close a large active-passive gap.
697	
698	**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence capped at `supported`.** These are single-source,
699	Soviet-era correlational and intervention findings (Iashvili 1982; Tumanyan & Dzhanyan
700	1980) not independently replicated in this corpus; the correlation coefficients describe
701	association within that sample, not a causal mechanism, and "sporting proficiency" is the
702	study's own competition-standard rating, not defined here. Do not treat the specific
703	numbers (0.81, 0.69, 0.91, the sport-by-sport mobility patterns) as generalizable norms for
704	a Baylor football roster without independent verification.
705	
706	**Example** — Inference: two athletes with identical passive hip-flexion ROM on a table test may
707	differ substantially in active hip flexion under their own muscular control during a
708	sprint stride; per this claim, the active measure (and a program that narrows any gap
709	between the two) is the one that tracks performance, not the passive number alone.
710	
711	**Related** — [[framework--flexibility-definition-and-rom-determinants]],
712	[[heuristic--eccentric-quasi-isometrics-for-active-flexibility-and-starting-strength]].

727	# The Book's Stretching-Benefits List Includes Items Modern Evidence Disputes
728	
729	**What it is** — Citing a literature and empirical-evidence review (Keith, 1977; Weiss,
730	1976; Holland, 1968; de Vries, 1966, 1966), the authors list these benefits of stretching:
731	increase in range of useful movement; reduction in the incidence of injury; decrease in
732	the severity of injury; delay in the onset of muscular fatigue; prevention and alleviation
733	of muscle soreness after exercise; increase in the level of skill and muscular efficiency;
734	prolongation of sporting life. In the same section they also caution that inappropriate
735	stretching can be detrimental: tendons and ligaments can be permanently deformed or
736	damaged by over-zealous or prolonged stretching, impairing joint stability; unskilled
737	ballistic stretching can cause muscle soreness and stiffness; and overstretching of the
738	cervical or lumbar spine can damage nerves, discs and blood vessels, particularly in
739	forceful yoga postures or amateur spinal manipulation. (PDF p. 187, printed p. 176.)
740	
741	**Why it works** — The authors give no mechanism for any item on the benefits list; it is
742	presented as a summary of a 1960s-70s literature review, not derived from a stated
743	physiological pathway in this text.
744	
745	**When to apply** — Treat "increase in range of useful movement" as the best-supported
746	item on this list, consistent with the book's own later, more specific claim that ROM
747	gains from routine stretching mainly reflect increased stretch tolerance (see
748	[[claim--static-cyclic-stretching-increases-rom-via-stretch-tolerance-not-tissue-change]]).
749	
750	**When NOT to apply** — **`contested`, named reason:** the muscle-soreness-prevention claim
751	on this list is disputed by a later systematic review of randomized trials: Herbert RD, de
752	Noronha M, Kamper SJ, "Stretching to prevent or reduce muscle soreness after exercise,"
753	Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews 2011, concluded that stretching (before, after, or
754	both) produces little to no reduction in delayed-onset muscle soreness, whether performed
755	pre- or post-exercise. The injury-incidence and injury-severity items are also not
756	supported by a specific modern trial in this entry; do not cite this 1966-1977 review list
757	as current evidence for injury prevention or soreness reduction without independent
758	verification. Inference: several items (skill/efficiency increase, prolongation of
759	sporting life) are broad, difficult-to-falsify claims not tied to a specific outcome
760	measure in the cited sources, and should be treated as unverified assertions rather than
761	established findings.
762	
763	**Example** — Inference: a staff member citing "stretching reduces soreness" to justify a mandatory
764	post-lift static stretching block would be relying on the disputed half of this list; the
765	Cochrane review found this benefit does not hold up under randomized-trial evidence.

782	# The Muscle Spindle, Golgi Tendon Organ, and the Stretch Reflex Family
783	
784	**What it is** — Joint flexibility is shaped not only by tissue structure and mechanical
785	properties but by the degree of motor unit activity in the relevant muscles: muscle
786	contraction raises muscle tension, which counteracts stretching. Two receptor types govern
787	this: muscle spindles (Fig 3.32), which detect changes in muscle fibre length and rate of
788	length change, and Golgi tendon organs (GTOs), which monitor tension in the muscle tendon
789	during contraction or stretching. The spindle produces the "stretch reflex" (contraction in
790	response to lengthening); the GTO produces the "inverse stretch reflex" (relaxing a
791	contracting muscle if its tension becomes excessive). Spindles contain 3-10 intrafusal
792	fibres of two types (nuclear bag and nuclear chain), innervated by primary (large type Ia)
793	and secondary (smaller type II) sensory receptors; primary receptors innervate both fibre
794	types and are held responsible for the strong dynamic response, while nuclear chain fibres
795	(innervated by both receptor types) are held responsible for the static response. Gamma
796	efferent fibres split similarly into gamma-dynamic (exciting bag fibres, powerful dynamic
797	response) and gamma-static (exciting chain fibres, persistent static response) (Guyton,
798	1984). The full stretch reflex (myotatic reflex, Fig 3.33) comprises a dynamic (phasic)
799	reflex (strong but brief contraction on sudden length change), a static (tonic) reflex
800	(weaker but sustained for up to several hours while tension persists), and a negative
801	stretch reflex (inhibitory relaxation when a muscle is suddenly shortened, opposing
802	shortening the way the myotatic reflex opposes lengthening). GTO firing shows the same
803	dynamic/static split: an intense initial (dynamic) response to sudden tension change,
804	settling to a lower steady-state (static) response proportional to tension; it is now
805	understood to continuously monitor, not just protect against excess, muscle tension
806	(Matthews, 1973). Repeated reflex production, like voluntary effort, fatigues: reflex
807	tension diminishes with repeated stimulation, and "rebound" (a second reflex of the same
808	type becoming progressively harder to elicit for a time after the first) is named as a
809	likely contributor to cyclic activities such as locomotion, swimming and cycling (Guyton,
810	1984). (PDF pp. 187-189, printed pp. 176-178, Figs 3.32-3.33.)
811	
812	**Why it works** — This is established, independent-of-text mammalian neurophysiology
813	(muscle spindle and GTO structure and reflex function, per Guyton and Matthews, cited in
814	the text); the book's own extensions (rebound's role in specific cyclic sports, the
815	practical stretching implications below) are less established and are flagged separately
816	in Related entries.
817	
818	**When to apply** — Use the dynamic-vs-static split to explain why a fast, sudden stretch
819	provokes a strong protective contraction (via the dynamic stretch reflex) while a slow,
820	sustained stretch allows the muscle to relax further into the new length (the dynamic
821	component fades quickly, leaving only the weaker static response): this is the
822	physiological basis for preferring slow entry into a static stretch over a fast one.
823	
824	**When NOT to apply** — This entry covers the basic reflex arcs only; it does not by
825	itself justify any specific stretching protocol, duration, or frequency. **Confidence is
826	`proven` for the core spindle/GTO/stretch-reflex mechanisms described (established,
827	independent physiology); it is not proven** for the book's applied claims about rebound's
828	role in specific sports or the fatigue-of-reflex claim's magnitude, which are stated
829	without a specific citation beyond Guyton (1984).
830	
831	**Example** — The book's own example: many "plyometric drills" are performed too slowly to
832	elicit the powerful dynamic spindle response essential for speed-strength development,
833	because the dynamic response requires a rapid rate of length change, not just any
834	stretch-shorten action (printed 177).
835	
836	**Related** — [[heuristic--reflex-based-techniques-for-flexibility-training]],
837	[[framework--joint-stabilization-sequence-across-range-of-motion]].

852	# Two Reflex Phenomena With Direct Stretching Applications: The Positive Supportive Reaction and Voluntary Relaxation
853	
854	**What it is** — Two specific, named reflex phenomena the authors connect directly to
855	stretching practice. First, the positive supportive reaction (Guyton, 1984): any form of
856	stretching that exerts pressure on the soles of the feet or palms of the hands produces
857	strong reflex extension of the limb concerned, stiffening and stabilizing it against
858	external pressure (including body/trunk weight). The authors state this makes toe-touching
859	stretches in standing versus seated positions neuromuscularly different procedures,
860	because the locus of pressure on the sole or palm determines which limb extends, a
861	mechanism physiotherapists use in PNF to guide a patient into a specific pattern. Second,
862	electromyographic (EMG) silence can persist in muscles being passively stretched,
863	regardless of stretch speed, meaning subjects can consciously relax a muscle below the
864	tension normal stretch reflexes would otherwise produce (Basmajian, 1978); the authors
865	infer from this that voluntary mental control or biofeedback techniques can play a useful
866	role in stretching and flexibility procedures. (PDF pp. 188-189, printed pp. 177-178.)
867	
868	**Why it works** — The positive supportive reaction is presented as an established reflex
869	(Guyton, 1984) without further mechanism given here. The EMG-silence finding (Basmajian,
870	1978) demonstrates that voluntary control can override the expected reflex response, but
871	the book does not explain how; Inference: this implies stretch reflex tension is not a
872	fixed floor and can be reduced by conscious relaxation or biofeedback training, independent
873	of any change in the tissue's mechanical properties.
874	
875	**When to apply** — Standing toe-touch and seated toe-touch are not neuromuscularly
876	interchangeable tests or stretches, per this entry, because standing loads the sole with
877	body weight (triggering the positive supportive reaction in the leg) while seated does
878	not. Consider cueing conscious relaxation or using biofeedback/visualization during static
879	stretching, on the premise that voluntary relaxation can reduce reflex-driven resistance
880	independent of tissue length change.
881	
882	**When NOT to apply** — This is a Guyton-textbook physiology citation and a single
883	Basmajian (1978) EMG finding, not a study of stretching outcomes; the book does not report
884	that biofeedback-assisted stretching produces measurably greater ROM gains than
885	conventional stretching. Do not treat "voluntary relaxation matters" as license to ignore
886	tissue-level stretching methods (see
887	[[framework--four-methods-of-enhancing-rom-ranked-by-effectiveness]]).
888	
889	**Example** — Inference: cueing an athlete to consciously "let the hamstring go" while
890	holding a static stretch, rather than relying only on time-under-tension, is an attempt to
891	use the voluntary-override pathway described here on top of the tissue-mechanical effect of
892	the stretch itself.
893	
894	**Related** — [[framework--stretch-reflex-types-and-neuromuscular-control-of-flexibility]].

909	# What Each Soft Tissue Contributes to Joint Stiffness, and Short- vs Long-Term Stretch Change
910	
911	**What it is** — With stretch reflex mechanisms minimally involved and muscles relaxed
912	(rarely the case during dynamic functional movement), the relative contribution of soft
913	tissues to joint stiffness is given as (Johns & Wright, 1962): muscles and their fascial
914	sheaths 41%, structures of the joint capsule including ligaments 35%, skin 11%, tendons and
915	their sheaths 10%. Since nothing can be done to alter joint structure itself, appropriate
916	stretching must target these soft tissues to increase flexibility, and stretching can
917	produce short-term (elastic), long-term (plastic), or combined short/long-term changes in
918	tissue characteristics. The authors state the average pre-event or pre-training warm-up
919	stretching session mainly targets short-term flexibility, and that this distinction is
920	often insufficiently emphasized: changing long-term flexibility requires a specific,
921	regularly repeated conditioning component built into the overall training programme, not
922	just brief preparatory sessions. (PDF p. 189, printed p. 178.)
923	
924	**Why it works** — The percentage breakdown is the authors' cited figure (Johns & Wright,
925	1962) with no further mechanism given; the elastic-vs-plastic distinction follows directly
926	from standard viscoelastic tissue behavior (elastic deformation recovers, plastic
927	deformation persists), which the book treats as background rather than derives here.
928	
929	**When to apply** — Use the percentage breakdown to set expectations: muscle/fascia is the
930	largest single lever (41%) for stretching-driven ROM change, but joint-capsule/ligament
931	tissue is a close second (35%) and carries the injury-risk caveat that lengthening it too
932	far compromises joint stability (see
933	[[framework--four-methods-of-enhancing-rom-ranked-by-effectiveness]]). Distinguish, when
934	programming, whether a stretching block is meant to produce same-session (short-term,
935	elastic) readiness or multi-week (long-term, plastic) ROM change, since a warm-up-style
936	session will not reliably produce the latter.
937	
938	**When NOT to apply** — The 1962 percentages describe relaxed-muscle, minimal-reflex
939	conditions; the authors state this rarely reflects dynamic functional movement, where
940	muscle tension (not passive tissue mechanics alone) dominates joint stiffness. Do not treat
941	a single pre-training stretch session as sufficient to produce durable ROM change; the text
942	is explicit that this is a common but mistaken programming assumption.
943	
944	**Example** — The book's own contrast: a brief pre-event stretch is "obvious[ly]...intended
945	primarily to enhance short-term flexibility for the physical activity which is just about
946	to commence," while durable change "requires a specific type of regular conditioning to be
947	built into the overall training programme" (printed 178).
948	
949	**Related** — [[framework--flexibility-definition-and-rom-determinants]],
950	[[claim--ligament-tendon-adaptation-and-detraining-response]].

964	
965	# Six Factors That Shift an Individual's Flexibility
966	
967	**What it is** — The authors list six factors that influence flexibility in general:
968	1. **Exercise and training history.** Regular full-range exercise generally enhances
969	flexibility. Athletes develop patterns of flexibility characteristic of their sport;
970	long-term flexibility can be reduced by a sedentary lifestyle, by training that rarely
971	uses full-range joint motion, by excessive hypertrophy focus, or by soft-tissue injury.
972	Short-term flexibility can be decreased by overtraining-induced soreness, stiffness, or
973	injury; tissue mechanical stiffness stays fairly constant during exercise, but damping
974	ratio invariably increases (Siff, 1986). As a specific instance of this factor, the authors
975	report that Russian and Eastern European scientists discourage cycling for athletes who
976	need large trunk and hip ROM, because cycling is held to decrease functional ROM in those
977	joints; they instead favor intensive sprinting and interval training, and similarly
978	discourage conventional push-ups and sit-ups (which limit shoulder and trunk ROM
979	respectively) in favor of push-ups on dip bars/parallel bars and backward sit-ups over a
980	pommel horse or "Roman chair."
981	2. **Age.** Flexibility generally decreases with age, raising soft-tissue injury
982	susceptibility during intensive exercise; regular exercise combined with flexibility
983	training can minimize this. Maximum flexibility is not at its peak in the youngest infants
984	but is reached between ages 10 and 12, depending on gender (Beaulieu, 1986).
985	3. **Gender.** Females tend to be more flexible than males at equivalent joints; the
986	damping ratio of females' joint soft tissues is greater than males', implying females are
987	intrinsically better equipped to absorb elastic stretch, and the pain threshold for joint
988	torsion is generally significantly lower in females (Siff, 1986).
989	4. **Temperature.** Increased muscle temperature (active warm-up, passive massage,
990	ultrasound) increases flexibility, including improved plastic deformation of collagenous
991	tissue during stretching; a gentle rhythmic warm-up is recommended before flexibility
992	training. Prolonged heat or cold can produce analgesia or otherwise modify the
993	neuromuscular processes behind the stretch and tendon reflexes, enhancing relaxation and
994	stretching; cooling tissue with ice for the final minutes of stretching is reported to
995	stabilize connective tissue at its new length (Sapega et al., 1981).
996	5. **Type of joint.** Flexibility is specific to each joint; an overall flexibility index
997	can be built by averaging a representative sample of joints, but what matters
998	practically is establishing static and dynamic ROM for the specific joints most important
999	to a given sport.
1000	6. **Type of movement.** The relative degree of flexibility differs for each degree of
1001	joint freedom; increasing flexibility in a direction that would compromise a joint's
1002	stability during a specific movement should be avoided. Optimum, not maximum, static and
1003	dynamic flexibility is required for each degree of freedom; subjects hypermobile in
1004	certain joints should avoid increasing flexibility further at the expense of stability.
1005	(PDF pp. 189-191, printed pp. 178-180.)
1006	
1007	**Why it works** — No single mechanism unifies these six; each is the authors' summary of
1008	a separate cited source (Siff 1986; Beaulieu 1986; Sapega et al. 1981) or an unsourced
1009	general observation.
1010	
1011	**When to apply** — Use factor 6 as a direct programming caution: do not chase additional
1012	ROM in a hypermobile athlete's already-loose joint, since the goal is optimum, not maximum,
1013	flexibility per degree of freedom. Use factor 4 to sequence a session: warm before
1014	stretching, and consider a brief cooling period at the end of a stretch to help "lock in"
1015	a new tissue length (Sapega et al., 1981).
1016	
1017	**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence capped at `supported`.** The cycling/push-up/sit-up
1018	recommendation under factor 1 is attributed only to unnamed "Russian and Eastern European
1019	scientists," with no specific citation or study design given; treat it as a single
1020	tradition's programming preference, not an established finding, and do not extend it to
1021	justify removing cycling or sit-ups from a Baylor program without independent evidence.
1022	The gender pain-threshold and damping-ratio claims (Siff, 1986) are also single-source and
1023	not cross-checked against a modern sex-differences study in this entry.
1024	
1025	**Example** — The book's own example: breast-stroke swimmers versus backstroke/butterfly
1026	swimmers show opposite shoulder/ankle-versus-hip/knee mobility patterns, illustrating that
1027	"type of joint" and training history jointly produce sport-specific flexibility profiles
1028	rather than one general flexibility trait (see also
1029	[[claim--active-flexibility-correlates-more-with-sporting-proficiency-than-passive]]).
1030	
1031	**Related** — [[framework--flexibility-definition-and-rom-determinants]],
1032	[[claim--active-flexibility-correlates-more-with-sporting-proficiency-than-passive]].

1047	# Ordinary Stretching Increases ROM by Raising Stretch Tolerance, Not by Changing Muscle Viscoelastic Properties
1048	
1049	**What it is** — The authors state: "Static and cyclic stretching, as commonly performed
1050	by athletes (up to 90 seconds duration each), increases joint range of motion by
1051	increasing stretch tolerance while the viscoelastic characteristics of the muscle remain
1052	unaltered" (Magnussen et al., 1998). (PDF p. 191, printed p. 181.)
1053	
1054	**Why it works** — The authors give no further mechanism for why stretch tolerance itself
1055	increases; the citation (Magnussen et al., 1998) is offered as the source of the finding,
1056	not explained here. Inference: "stretch tolerance" implies the limiting factor in a typical
1057	short-duration static/cyclic stretch is the point at which the nervous system perceives the
1058	stretch as uncomfortable or reaches a reflex-protective threshold, not the muscle-tendon
1059	unit's actual length-tension (stiffness) properties, which this citation reports as
1060	unchanged.
1061	
1062	**When to apply** — Use this to set an accurate expectation for a single stretching
1063	session or short block: an acute or short-term ROM gain from static/cyclic stretching in
1064	this duration range should be read as increased tolerance to the sensation of stretch, not
1065	as evidence the muscle-tendon unit itself has become mechanically more compliant. This is
1066	consistent with, and gives a mechanism for, the book's separate claim that brief
1067	pre-training stretching mainly produces short-term (not tissue-level, long-term) flexibility
1068	change (see
1069	[[framework--four-methods-of-enhancing-rom-ranked-by-effectiveness]]).
1070	
1071	**When NOT to apply** — Do not extend this specific claim (static/cyclic stretching, up to
1072	90 seconds per stretch) to other stretching modes (ballistic, PNF, long-duration static
1073	holds well beyond 90 seconds) without separate evidence; the book does not state this
1074	mechanism applies to those. Do not use "stretch tolerance increased, tissue unchanged" to
1075	argue stretching has no tissue-level benefit at all: this entry describes the mechanism of
1076	short-duration ROM gain specifically, not the long-term soft-tissue adaptations covered
1077	elsewhere (see [[claim--ligament-tendon-adaptation-and-detraining-response]]).
1078	
1079	**Example** — Inference: an athlete who gains 5 degrees of hip flexion after a single
1080	90-second hamstring stretch has very likely become more tolerant of that stretch sensation
1081	in that session, not changed the mechanical stiffness of the hamstring muscle-tendon unit;
1082	retesting the next day without further stretching would be expected to show the gain has
1083	mostly reverted.
1084

# Four Ways to Increase ROM, Ranked by Speed of Effect and Durability

**What it is** — The authors give four practical means of enhancing joint ROM, in order
of effectiveness, and note the first limitation on the list (skeletal structure) cannot be
overcome by any form of exercise:
1. Modifying the neuromuscular processes that control tension and length in the muscle
complex. This increases ROM most rapidly and most effectively, but the change tends to be
confined to short-term improvements unless the neuromuscular means are used as an ongoing
part of all training.
2. Increasing the length and strength of the soft tissues comprising the muscle complex,
especially collagenous tissues such as fascia. These changes are slower to produce but
long-term.
3. Lengthening and strengthening other soft tissues, especially those of the joint capsule
and ligaments. Also long-lasting, but if promoted to the point of joint laxity, joint
stability can be severely compromised.
4. Restructuring the articulating surfaces of the joints, a process mediated by many years
of regular heavy loading in specific patterns; not a practical training target, more a
by-product of loaded full-range sporting movement, and inappropriate/excessive loading can
instead produce degenerative changes that reduce ROM.
The authors add that stretching and flexibility training are not synonymous: some
flexibility exercises increase ROM without being stretching exercises at all, because they
work entirely by modifying neuromuscular processes (the stretch and tendon reflexes);
conversely, many stretching exercises pay no deliberate attention to neuromuscular
processes and instead aim at structural change in soft tissue, so static stretches may
change muscle length without adequately affecting the dynamic ROM a given sport requires.
(PDF pp. 185-186, printed pp. 174-175.)

**Why it works** — The authors give no single unifying mechanism; the ordering reflects
which physiological layer (nervous system, muscle/fascia, joint capsule/ligament, bone) is
being changed and how quickly each layer adapts, from fastest-and-least-durable
(neuromuscular) to slowest-and-most-durable (bone).

**When to apply** — Use this ordering to set expectations for a flexibility intervention:
a single session aimed at neuromuscular relaxation (e.g. PNF) can produce a same-day ROM
gain that will not persist without repetition, while a multi-week soft-tissue-lengthening
block is the one that produces a durable change. Match the method to the timeframe: a
pre-competition warm-up should rely on method 1 (rapid, neuromuscular, session-specific);
an off-season block targeting chronic ROM limits should emphasize methods 2-3.

**When NOT to apply** — Do not expect a brief pre-event stretching routine to produce
long-term flexibility change; the text is explicit that this is a category error common in
"the average stretching programme." Do not pursue method 3 (ligament/capsule lengthening)
without limit: the text names joint laxity and compromised stability as the direct cost of
overdoing it. Method 4 should never be treated as a deliberate training target.

**Example** — Inference: a pre-game mobility routine that relies on PNF contract-relax drills is
working through method 1 and will not, by itself, change an athlete's baseline hip ROM
measured a week later; that requires a sustained block emphasizing methods 2 and 3.

[[framework--joint-stabilization-sequence-across-range-of-motion]].

# Active Flexibility, Not Passive, Is the One That Tracks Sporting Proficiency

**What it is** — Citing a single Russian study of over 200 adult competitors (Iashvili,
1982), the authors report that sporting achievement (rated by competition standards)
correlates more strongly with active flexibility than with passive flexibility: R = 0.81
versus R = 0.69. The same study found traditional static and passive stretching develop
mainly passive flexibility, while combined strength-and-stretching exercises are
considerably more effective at developing active flexibility, particularly when the
strength conditioning is applied in the zone of active muscular inadequacy (i.e. the end
of the joint's active range). (PDF p. 186, printed p. 175.)

A later section (3.5.8) returns to the same Iashvili (1982) study across "several Olympic
sports" with further detail: joint mobility level tracks sporting proficiency generally;
static/passive stretching enhances passive flexibility but only moderately improves active
mobility (described as "by far the most important flexibility quality needed in sport");
the pattern and range of joint mobility is sport-specific (e.g. backstroke/butterfly
swimmers show the greatest shoulder and ankle mobility, breast-strokers the least in those
joints but the greatest hip/knee mobility; javelinists show the greatest shoulder
mobility among throwers, hurdlers the greatest hip flexibility among track athletes); and
the active-passive correlation itself depends on training method, running 0.61-0.73 with
primarily static/passive stretching but rising to 0.91 when stretching is combined with
strengthening. (PDF pp. 196-197, printed pp. 185-186.)

A related measurement framework from the same section (Tumanyan & Dzhanyan, 1980) defines
three flexibility indices from a pulley-loaded limb: maximum passive flexibility (PFmax,
at the pain threshold), active flexibility (AF, reached by non-ballistic muscular action),
and loaded passive flexibility (PF, with a progressively increased sub-pain-threshold
load), yielding a maximum active flexibility deficit (FDmax = PFmax - AF), a loaded active
flexibility deficit (FD = PF - AF), and an interval of flexibility pain threshold (FPT =
PFmax - PF). Using these indices, the same source reports: static/passive stretching
increases passive flexibility while leaving the active-passive gap unchanged; full-range
strength exercise increases passive flexibility and narrows that gap; and combined
strength-plus-flexibility exercise increases both and narrows the gap most. A large
active-passive gap ("flexibility deficit") is reported to correlate strongly with the
incidence of soft-tissue injury. (PDF p. 197, printed p. 186.)

**Why it works** — The book gives no physiological mechanism for why active flexibility
specifically tracks proficiency; it reports only the correlational and intervention
results above.

**When to apply** — Prefer testing and training active ROM (through the athlete's own
muscular control) over passive ROM (examiner- or gravity-assisted) when the goal is a
proxy for sporting flexibility demands, and prefer combined strength-and-stretch
programming over stretching alone when the goal is to close a large active-passive gap.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence capped at `supported`.** These are single-source,
Soviet-era correlational and intervention findings (Iashvili 1982; Tumanyan & Dzhanyan
1980) not independently replicated in this corpus; the correlation coefficients describe
association within that sample, not a causal mechanism, and "sporting proficiency" is the
study's own competition-standard rating, not defined here. Do not treat the specific
numbers (0.81, 0.69, 0.91, the sport-by-sport mobility patterns) as generalizable norms for
a Baylor football roster without independent verification.

**Example** — Inference: two athletes with identical passive hip-flexion ROM on a table test may
differ substantially in active hip flexion under their own muscular control during a
sprint stride; per this claim, the active measure (and a program that narrows any gap
between the two) is the one that tracks performance, not the passive number alone.

[[heuristic--eccentric-quasi-isometrics-for-active-flexibility-and-starting-strength]].

# The Book's Stretching-Benefits List Includes Items Modern Evidence Disputes

**What it is** — Citing a literature and empirical-evidence review (Keith, 1977; Weiss,
1976; Holland, 1968; de Vries, 1966, 1966), the authors list these benefits of stretching:
increase in range of useful movement; reduction in the incidence of injury; decrease in
the severity of injury; delay in the onset of muscular fatigue; prevention and alleviation
of muscle soreness after exercise; increase in the level of skill and muscular efficiency;
prolongation of sporting life. In the same section they also caution that inappropriate
stretching can be detrimental: tendons and ligaments can be permanently deformed or
damaged by over-zealous or prolonged stretching, impairing joint stability; unskilled
ballistic stretching can cause muscle soreness and stiffness; and overstretching of the
cervical or lumbar spine can damage nerves, discs and blood vessels, particularly in
forceful yoga postures or amateur spinal manipulation. (PDF p. 187, printed p. 176.)

**Why it works** — The authors give no mechanism for any item on the benefits list; it is
presented as a summary of a 1960s-70s literature review, not derived from a stated
physiological pathway in this text.

**When to apply** — Treat "increase in range of useful movement" as the best-supported
item on this list, consistent with the book's own later, more specific claim that ROM
gains from routine stretching mainly reflect increased stretch tolerance (see
[[claim--static-cyclic-stretching-increases-rom-via-stretch-tolerance-not-tissue-change]]).

**When NOT to apply** — **`contested`, named reason:** the muscle-soreness-prevention claim
on this list is disputed by a later systematic review of randomized trials: Herbert RD, de
Noronha M, Kamper SJ, "Stretching to prevent or reduce muscle soreness after exercise,"
Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews 2011, concluded that stretching (before, after, or
both) produces little to no reduction in delayed-onset muscle soreness, whether performed
pre- or post-exercise. The injury-incidence and injury-severity items are also not
supported by a specific modern trial in this entry; do not cite this 1966-1977 review list
as current evidence for injury prevention or soreness reduction without independent
verification. Inference: several items (skill/efficiency increase, prolongation of
sporting life) are broad, difficult-to-falsify claims not tied to a specific outcome
measure in the cited sources, and should be treated as unverified assertions rather than
established findings.

**Example** — Inference: a staff member citing "stretching reduces soreness" to justify a mandatory
post-lift static stretching block would be relying on the disputed half of this list; the
Cochrane review found this benefit does not hold up under randomized-trial evidence.

# The Muscle Spindle, Golgi Tendon Organ, and the Stretch Reflex Family

**What it is** — Joint flexibility is shaped not only by tissue structure and mechanical
properties but by the degree of motor unit activity in the relevant muscles: muscle
contraction raises muscle tension, which counteracts stretching. Two receptor types govern
this: muscle spindles (Fig 3.32), which detect changes in muscle fibre length and rate of
length change, and Golgi tendon organs (GTOs), which monitor tension in the muscle tendon
during contraction or stretching. The spindle produces the "stretch reflex" (contraction in
response to lengthening); the GTO produces the "inverse stretch reflex" (relaxing a
contracting muscle if its tension becomes excessive). Spindles contain 3-10 intrafusal
fibres of two types (nuclear bag and nuclear chain), innervated by primary (large type Ia)
and secondary (smaller type II) sensory receptors; primary receptors innervate both fibre
types and are held responsible for the strong dynamic response, while nuclear chain fibres
(innervated by both receptor types) are held responsible for the static response. Gamma
efferent fibres split similarly into gamma-dynamic (exciting bag fibres, powerful dynamic
response) and gamma-static (exciting chain fibres, persistent static response) (Guyton,
1984). The full stretch reflex (myotatic reflex, Fig 3.33) comprises a dynamic (phasic)
reflex (strong but brief contraction on sudden length change), a static (tonic) reflex
(weaker but sustained for up to several hours while tension persists), and a negative
stretch reflex (inhibitory relaxation when a muscle is suddenly shortened, opposing
shortening the way the myotatic reflex opposes lengthening). GTO firing shows the same
dynamic/static split: an intense initial (dynamic) response to sudden tension change,
settling to a lower steady-state (static) response proportional to tension; it is now
understood to continuously monitor, not just protect against excess, muscle tension
(Matthews, 1973). Repeated reflex production, like voluntary effort, fatigues: reflex
tension diminishes with repeated stimulation, and "rebound" (a second reflex of the same
type becoming progressively harder to elicit for a time after the first) is named as a
likely contributor to cyclic activities such as locomotion, swimming and cycling (Guyton,
1984). (PDF pp. 187-189, printed pp. 176-178, Figs 3.32-3.33.)

**Why it works** — This is established, independent-of-text mammalian neurophysiology
(muscle spindle and GTO structure and reflex function, per Guyton and Matthews, cited in
the text); the book's own extensions (rebound's role in specific cyclic sports, the
practical stretching implications below) are less established and are flagged separately
in Related entries.

**When to apply** — Use the dynamic-vs-static split to explain why a fast, sudden stretch
provokes a strong protective contraction (via the dynamic stretch reflex) while a slow,
sustained stretch allows the muscle to relax further into the new length (the dynamic
component fades quickly, leaving only the weaker static response): this is the
physiological basis for preferring slow entry into a static stretch over a fast one.

**When NOT to apply** — This entry covers the basic reflex arcs only; it does not by
itself justify any specific stretching protocol, duration, or frequency. **Confidence is
`proven` for the core spindle/GTO/stretch-reflex mechanisms described (established,
independent physiology); it is not proven** for the book's applied claims about rebound's
role in specific sports or the fatigue-of-reflex claim's magnitude, which are stated
without a specific citation beyond Guyton (1984).

**Example** — The book's own example: many "plyometric drills" are performed too slowly to
elicit the powerful dynamic spindle response essential for speed-strength development,
because the dynamic response requires a rapid rate of length change, not just any
stretch-shorten action (printed 177).

**Related** — [[heuristic--reflex-based-techniques-for-flexibility-training]],
[[framework--joint-stabilization-sequence-across-range-of-motion]].

# Two Reflex Phenomena With Direct Stretching Applications: The Positive Supportive Reaction and Voluntary Relaxation

**What it is** — Two specific, named reflex phenomena the authors connect directly to
stretching practice. First, the positive supportive reaction (Guyton, 1984): any form of
stretching that exerts pressure on the soles of the feet or palms of the hands produces
strong reflex extension of the limb concerned, stiffening and stabilizing it against
external pressure (including body/trunk weight). The authors state this makes toe-touching
stretches in standing versus seated positions neuromuscularly different procedures,
because the locus of pressure on the sole or palm determines which limb extends, a
mechanism physiotherapists use in PNF to guide a patient into a specific pattern. Second,
electromyographic (EMG) silence can persist in muscles being passively stretched,
regardless of stretch speed, meaning subjects can consciously relax a muscle below the
tension normal stretch reflexes would otherwise produce (Basmajian, 1978); the authors
infer from this that voluntary mental control or biofeedback techniques can play a useful
role in stretching and flexibility procedures. (PDF pp. 188-189, printed pp. 177-178.)

**Why it works** — The positive supportive reaction is presented as an established reflex
(Guyton, 1984) without further mechanism given here. The EMG-silence finding (Basmajian,
1978) demonstrates that voluntary control can override the expected reflex response, but
the book does not explain how; Inference: this implies stretch reflex tension is not a
fixed floor and can be reduced by conscious relaxation or biofeedback training, independent
of any change in the tissue's mechanical properties.

**When to apply** — Standing toe-touch and seated toe-touch are not neuromuscularly
interchangeable tests or stretches, per this entry, because standing loads the sole with
body weight (triggering the positive supportive reaction in the leg) while seated does
not. Consider cueing conscious relaxation or using biofeedback/visualization during static
stretching, on the premise that voluntary relaxation can reduce reflex-driven resistance
independent of tissue length change.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a Guyton-textbook physiology citation and a single
Basmajian (1978) EMG finding, not a study of stretching outcomes; the book does not report
that biofeedback-assisted stretching produces measurably greater ROM gains than
conventional stretching. Do not treat "voluntary relaxation matters" as license to ignore
tissue-level stretching methods (see
[[framework--four-methods-of-enhancing-rom-ranked-by-effectiveness]]).

**Example** — Inference: cueing an athlete to consciously "let the hamstring go" while
holding a static stretch, rather than relying only on time-under-tension, is an attempt to
use the voluntary-override pathway described here on top of the tissue-mechanical effect of
the stretch itself.

# What Each Soft Tissue Contributes to Joint Stiffness, and Short- vs Long-Term Stretch Change

**What it is** — With stretch reflex mechanisms minimally involved and muscles relaxed
(rarely the case during dynamic functional movement), the relative contribution of soft
tissues to joint stiffness is given as (Johns & Wright, 1962): muscles and their fascial
sheaths 41%, structures of the joint capsule including ligaments 35%, skin 11%, tendons and
their sheaths 10%. Since nothing can be done to alter joint structure itself, appropriate
stretching must target these soft tissues to increase flexibility, and stretching can
produce short-term (elastic), long-term (plastic), or combined short/long-term changes in
tissue characteristics. The authors state the average pre-event or pre-training warm-up
stretching session mainly targets short-term flexibility, and that this distinction is
often insufficiently emphasized: changing long-term flexibility requires a specific,
regularly repeated conditioning component built into the overall training programme, not
just brief preparatory sessions. (PDF p. 189, printed p. 178.)

**Why it works** — The percentage breakdown is the authors' cited figure (Johns & Wright,
1962) with no further mechanism given; the elastic-vs-plastic distinction follows directly
from standard viscoelastic tissue behavior (elastic deformation recovers, plastic
deformation persists), which the book treats as background rather than derives here.

**When to apply** — Use the percentage breakdown to set expectations: muscle/fascia is the
largest single lever (41%) for stretching-driven ROM change, but joint-capsule/ligament
tissue is a close second (35%) and carries the injury-risk caveat that lengthening it too
far compromises joint stability (see
[[framework--four-methods-of-enhancing-rom-ranked-by-effectiveness]]). Distinguish, when
programming, whether a stretching block is meant to produce same-session (short-term,
elastic) readiness or multi-week (long-term, plastic) ROM change, since a warm-up-style
session will not reliably produce the latter.

**When NOT to apply** — The 1962 percentages describe relaxed-muscle, minimal-reflex
conditions; the authors state this rarely reflects dynamic functional movement, where
muscle tension (not passive tissue mechanics alone) dominates joint stiffness. Do not treat
a single pre-training stretch session as sufficient to produce durable ROM change; the text
is explicit that this is a common but mistaken programming assumption.

**Example** — The book's own contrast: a brief pre-event stretch is "obvious[ly]...intended
primarily to enhance short-term flexibility for the physical activity which is just about
to commence," while durable change "requires a specific type of regular conditioning to be
built into the overall training programme" (printed 178).

**Related** — [[framework--flexibility-definition-and-rom-determinants]],
[[claim--ligament-tendon-adaptation-and-detraining-response]].

# Six Factors That Shift an Individual's Flexibility

**What it is** — The authors list six factors that influence flexibility in general:
1. **Exercise and training history.** Regular full-range exercise generally enhances
flexibility. Athletes develop patterns of flexibility characteristic of their sport;
long-term flexibility can be reduced by a sedentary lifestyle, by training that rarely
uses full-range joint motion, by excessive hypertrophy focus, or by soft-tissue injury.
Short-term flexibility can be decreased by overtraining-induced soreness, stiffness, or
injury; tissue mechanical stiffness stays fairly constant during exercise, but damping
ratio invariably increases (Siff, 1986). As a specific instance of this factor, the authors
report that Russian and Eastern European scientists discourage cycling for athletes who
need large trunk and hip ROM, because cycling is held to decrease functional ROM in those
joints; they instead favor intensive sprinting and interval training, and similarly
discourage conventional push-ups and sit-ups (which limit shoulder and trunk ROM
respectively) in favor of push-ups on dip bars/parallel bars and backward sit-ups over a
pommel horse or "Roman chair."
2. **Age.** Flexibility generally decreases with age, raising soft-tissue injury
susceptibility during intensive exercise; regular exercise combined with flexibility
training can minimize this. Maximum flexibility is not at its peak in the youngest infants
but is reached between ages 10 and 12, depending on gender (Beaulieu, 1986).
3. **Gender.** Females tend to be more flexible than males at equivalent joints; the
damping ratio of females' joint soft tissues is greater than males', implying females are
intrinsically better equipped to absorb elastic stretch, and the pain threshold for joint
torsion is generally significantly lower in females (Siff, 1986).
4. **Temperature.** Increased muscle temperature (active warm-up, passive massage,
ultrasound) increases flexibility, including improved plastic deformation of collagenous
tissue during stretching; a gentle rhythmic warm-up is recommended before flexibility
training. Prolonged heat or cold can produce analgesia or otherwise modify the
neuromuscular processes behind the stretch and tendon reflexes, enhancing relaxation and
stretching; cooling tissue with ice for the final minutes of stretching is reported to
stabilize connective tissue at its new length (Sapega et al., 1981).
5. **Type of joint.** Flexibility is specific to each joint; an overall flexibility index
can be built by averaging a representative sample of joints, but what matters
practically is establishing static and dynamic ROM for the specific joints most important
to a given sport.
6. **Type of movement.** The relative degree of flexibility differs for each degree of
joint freedom; increasing flexibility in a direction that would compromise a joint's
stability during a specific movement should be avoided. Optimum, not maximum, static and
dynamic flexibility is required for each degree of freedom; subjects hypermobile in
certain joints should avoid increasing flexibility further at the expense of stability.
(PDF pp. 189-191, printed pp. 178-180.)

**Why it works** — No single mechanism unifies these six; each is the authors' summary of
a separate cited source (Siff 1986; Beaulieu 1986; Sapega et al. 1981) or an unsourced
general observation.

**When to apply** — Use factor 6 as a direct programming caution: do not chase additional
ROM in a hypermobile athlete's already-loose joint, since the goal is optimum, not maximum,
flexibility per degree of freedom. Use factor 4 to sequence a session: warm before
stretching, and consider a brief cooling period at the end of a stretch to help "lock in"
a new tissue length (Sapega et al., 1981).

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence capped at `supported`.** The cycling/push-up/sit-up
recommendation under factor 1 is attributed only to unnamed "Russian and Eastern European
scientists," with no specific citation or study design given; treat it as a single
tradition's programming preference, not an established finding, and do not extend it to
justify removing cycling or sit-ups from a Baylor program without independent evidence.
The gender pain-threshold and damping-ratio claims (Siff, 1986) are also single-source and
not cross-checked against a modern sex-differences study in this entry.

**Example** — The book's own example: breast-stroke swimmers versus backstroke/butterfly
swimmers show opposite shoulder/ankle-versus-hip/knee mobility patterns, illustrating that
"type of joint" and training history jointly produce sport-specific flexibility profiles
rather than one general flexibility trait (see also
[[claim--active-flexibility-correlates-more-with-sporting-proficiency-than-passive]]).

**Related** — [[framework--flexibility-definition-and-rom-determinants]],
[[claim--active-flexibility-correlates-more-with-sporting-proficiency-than-passive]].

# Ordinary Stretching Increases ROM by Raising Stretch Tolerance, Not by Changing Muscle Viscoelastic Properties

**What it is** — The authors state: "Static and cyclic stretching, as commonly performed
by athletes (up to 90 seconds duration each), increases joint range of motion by
increasing stretch tolerance while the viscoelastic characteristics of the muscle remain
unaltered" (Magnussen et al., 1998). (PDF p. 191, printed p. 181.)

**Why it works** — The authors give no further mechanism for why stretch tolerance itself
increases; the citation (Magnussen et al., 1998) is offered as the source of the finding,
not explained here. Inference: "stretch tolerance" implies the limiting factor in a typical
short-duration static/cyclic stretch is the point at which the nervous system perceives the
stretch as uncomfortable or reaches a reflex-protective threshold, not the muscle-tendon
unit's actual length-tension (stiffness) properties, which this citation reports as
unchanged.

**When to apply** — Use this to set an accurate expectation for a single stretching
session or short block: an acute or short-term ROM gain from static/cyclic stretching in
this duration range should be read as increased tolerance to the sensation of stretch, not
as evidence the muscle-tendon unit itself has become mechanically more compliant. This is
consistent with, and gives a mechanism for, the book's separate claim that brief
pre-training stretching mainly produces short-term (not tissue-level, long-term) flexibility
change (see
[[framework--four-methods-of-enhancing-rom-ranked-by-effectiveness]]).

**When NOT to apply** — Do not extend this specific claim (static/cyclic stretching, up to

retesting the next day without further stretching would be expected to show the gain has
mostly reverted.

1150	
1151	# What Actually Stabilizes a Joint Changes as It Approaches End-Range
1152	
1153	**What it is** — Against the "widespread opinion that muscles act as efficient synergistic
1154	stabilisers," the authors argue muscle cannot always respond quickly enough to protect a
1155	joint against a large, rapid (particularly torsional) impact (Pope et al., 1978), and
1156	propose joint stabilization instead works in a sequence:
1157	1. The contractile element (activated by the stretch reflex complex) together with the
1158	muscle's series elastic component (SEC) act as primary stabilizers, if the loading rate
1159	allows the muscle to respond in time.
1160	2. If the joint reaches the physical limits of muscle length, strength, or endurance,
1161	protection shifts to the ligaments and the SEC; if the inverse stretch reflex (GTO) signals
1162	the muscle to relax at its maximum length, the muscle's parallel elastic component (PEC)
1163	also contributes to stabilization. Receptors resembling Golgi tendon organs have been found
1164	on the surface of cruciate ligaments (Schultz et al., 1984), and muscles show reflex
1165	contraction if ligaments are stretched to the point of pain (Basmajian, 1978).
1166	3. If the joint is extended to its limit without sufficient muscle contraction, primary
1167	stabilization is provided by ligaments and the PEC; once the initial latency period for
1168	muscle excitation passes, the contracting muscle and its SEC contribute as secondary
1169	stabilizers.
1170	4. In certain joints, skeletal structure itself can act as the final stabilizer at the
1171	limits of joint movement.
1172	(PDF p. 193, printed p. 182.)
1173	
1174	**Why it works** — The sequence follows from the mechanical roles already established for
1175	the SEC, PEC, and stretch/inverse-stretch reflexes elsewhere in the text (see
1176	[[framework--series-and-parallel-elastic-components]] and
1177	[[framework--stretch-reflex-types-and-neuromuscular-control-of-flexibility]]), combined
1178	with the cited finding that ligaments themselves carry GTO-like tension receptors (Schultz
1179	et al., 1984) and can trigger protective muscle contraction (Basmajian, 1978).
1180	
1181	**When to apply** — Use this sequence to explain why a joint can be injured even with
1182	strong, well-conditioned muscles around it: at high loading rates (stage 1's premise
1183	fails), stabilization falls to ligament and PEC tissue that may not be conditioned to the
1184	same standard as the muscle. This reframes injury-prevention conditioning as needing to
1185	address ligament/capsule tissue specifically, not only muscular strength.
1186	
1187	**When NOT to apply** — This is the authors' synthesized model, not a single cited
1188	experimental finding; treat the four numbered stages as an organizing framework for
1189	reasoning about joint stabilization, not as a validated, measured sequence with defined
1190	timing thresholds. Confidence is capped at `supported` because the sequence itself
1191	(as opposed to the individual cited facts feeding it) is not independently attributed to a
1192	specific study.
1193	
1194	**Example** — Inference: a sudden, high-velocity valgus torque to the knee arrives faster
1195	than stage 1's muscular response can engage, meaning stages 2-3 (ligament and PEC) bear
1196	more of the load than they would under a slower, anticipated movement, which is consistent
1197	with why acute ligament injuries often occur on unanticipated contact.
1198	
1199	**Related** — [[framework--stretch-reflex-types-and-neuromuscular-control-of-flexibility]],
1200	[[framework--series-and-parallel-elastic-components]].

1214	
1215	# "There Is No Unsafe Stretch, Only an Unsafe Way of Executing It"
1216	
1217	**What it is** — In a bulleted list of biomechanical points on stretching, the authors
1218	state: "There is generally no such thing as an unsafe stretch or exercise: only an unsafe
1219	way of executing any movement for a specific individual at a specific time." (PDF p. 192,
1220	printed p. 181.) This appears alongside a related claim in the same list that
1221	physiotherapeutic PNF shows rapid or powerful recruitment of the different stretch
1222	reflexes can be safely applied to rehabilitate and strengthen tissue, "contrary to common
1223	belief."
1224	
1225	**Why it works** — The authors give no supporting mechanism, study, or citation for this
1226	specific aphorism; it reads as a stated position, not a derived or evidenced conclusion in
1227	this passage.
1228	
1229	**When to apply** — Useful as a reframing prompt when an exercise or stretch is being
1230	categorically banned ("we never do ballistic stretching," "no PNF for this population"):
1231	ask whether the concern is really about the movement class itself, or about a specific
1232	athlete's readiness, technique, loading rate, or tissue state for that movement at that
1233	time.
1234	
1235	**When NOT to apply** — **`untested`, unlabeled aphorism with no supporting citation in
1236	this passage.** Do not use this claim to override a specific, evidence-based
1237	contraindication (e.g. a known ligament laxity, an acute strain, a post-surgical range
1238	restriction) on the reasoning that "there's no unsafe stretch, only unsafe execution": the
1239	book gives no criteria here for what counts as safe execution, and the claim is broad
1240	enough to be difficult to falsify. Treat it as a coaching-philosophy prompt, not a safety
1241	rule.
1242	
1243	**Example** — The book's own paired example: it treats the popular blanket rule "ballistic
1244	stretching should be avoided at all costs" as the kind of overgeneralization this heuristic
1245	is meant to counter, arguing instead that rate and technique determine ballistic
1246	stretching's safety (see
1247	[[heuristic--ballistic-stretching-safe-with-gradual-progressive-protocol]]).
1248	
1249	**Related** — [[heuristic--ballistic-stretching-safe-with-gradual-progressive-protocol]].
