1263	
1264	# Tendon Stretching Must Not Compromise the Tendon's Ability to Store Elastic Energy
1265	
1266	**What it is** — The authors state tendons, unlike ligaments, are not simply passive
1267	joint stabilizers: together with strongly contracted muscle fibres (particularly during
1268	eccentric contraction), they play a vital role in storing elastic energy during running and
1269	other impulsive motor acts, saving energy and increasing the efficiency of muscular
1270	activity (Goldspink, 1978). From this they draw a direct programming rule: no stretching
1271	manoeuvre should compromise the strength or ability of the tendons to store elastic energy
1272	throughout their range of movement; tendon stretching exercises should therefore be
1273	accompanied by strength conditioning against adequate resistance. They add that tendons and
1274	ligaments, being viscoelastic, are sensitive to loading rate and undergo stress relaxation,
1275	creep, and hysteresis. (PDF p. 192, printed p. 181.)
1276	
1277	**Why it works** — Goldspink (1978) is cited as the source of the tendon-energy-storage
1278	mechanism itself; the programming rule (pair tendon stretching with resistance work) is the
1279	authors' own inference from that mechanism, not a separately cited intervention finding.
1280	
1281	**When to apply** — When programming flexibility work for tendon-dependent qualities
1282	(sprinting, jumping, change of direction), pair any deliberate tendon-lengthening or
1283	stretching work with resistance training against that tendon, rather than stretching it in
1284	isolation, on the reasoning that a lengthened but under-strengthened tendon may store
1285	elastic energy less effectively.
1286	
1287	**When NOT to apply** — The book does not give a specific dose, duration, or exercise
1288	example for "adequate resistance" alongside tendon stretching; treat this as a general
1289	programming principle, not a prescribed protocol. Do not use this rule to avoid all tendon
1290	flexibility work; the claim is about pairing, not avoiding, stretching.
1291	
1292	**Example** — Inference: an athlete doing calf-tendon stretching for ankle dorsiflexion
1293	ROM would, per this rule, also need loaded calf-raise or plyometric work in that same block
1294	so the lengthened gastrocnemius-soleus tendon complex retains its elastic energy-storage
1295	capacity for sprinting and jumping.
1296	
1297	**Related** — [[claim--tendon-insertion-transitional-stiffness-gradient-disrupted-by-steroids]],
1298	[[principle--short-amortization-preserves-elastic-energy]].

1312	
1313	# Ligaments and Tendons Thicken and Strengthen With Training, Weaken With Inactivity
1314	
1315	**What it is** — The authors report that physical training strengthens the attachments of
1316	tendons and ligaments to bone: trained ligaments are thicker and heavier, though the
1317	increase in mass is not necessarily associated with a greater concentration of collagen,
1318	a process described as still poorly understood (Booth & Gould, 1975); controlled strain on
1319	soft tissue may increase fibre formation, contributing to enhanced elasticity and strength
1320	(Holland, 1968). Regular resistance training increases not only muscle hypertrophy but also
1321	the collagen content of ligaments and the connective tissue surrounding muscle fibres
1322	(Tipton et al., 1975); training also increases the activity of an enzyme involved in
1323	collagen synthesis, an effect possibly stimulated by lactic acid production during exercise
1324	(Booth & Gould, 1975). By contrast, moderate-intensity treadmill training in rats produces
1325	neither muscle hypertrophy nor increased intramuscular connective tissue growth; prolonged
1326	low-intensity training conditions the cardiovascular system but not the musculoskeletal
1327	system. The authors state it is anaerobic, muscle-endurance training specifically that most
1328	strengthens collagenous tissue and its junction zones, making progressive stretching
1329	alongside this type of training especially valuable. In contrast to chronic training,
1330	single exercise sessions, occasional stretching, or sprint training alone do not produce
1331	significant increases in junction strength, although sprinting does markedly increase
1332	ligament mass and concentration (Tipton et al., 1974). Just as ligaments strengthen and
1333	stiffen under increased stress, they become weaker and less stiff with decreased stress,
1334	immobilization, and inactivity (Tipton et al., 1970); the authors note the similar changes
1335	seen with ageing may partly reflect inactivity rather than degeneration alone. (PDF pp.
1336	193-194, printed p. 182.)
1337	
1338	**Why it works** — This is presented as a summary of cited animal and human exercise
1339	physiology findings (Tipton et al. 1970, 1974, 1975; Booth & Gould, 1975; Holland, 1968);
1340	the authors do not add a mechanism beyond what each citation states.
1341	
1342	**When to apply** — Use this to set expectations for how long connective tissue
1343	conditioning takes: this entry supports chronic, repeated anaerobic/muscle-endurance
1344	training as the driver of ligament and tendon strengthening, not occasional or single-bout
1345	stretching or training. It also supports resuming ligament/tendon-specific loading
1346	gradually after a period of inactivity or immobilization (e.g. post-injury), since the same
1347	literature reports detraining weakens and destiffens these tissues.
1348	
1349	**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence capped at `supported`.** Much of the underlying
1350	evidence is animal-model research (rat treadmill studies; Tipton's ligament work), not
1351	human athlete data, and the collagen-concentration-vs-mass distinction is itself described
1352	in the source as poorly understood. Do not assume a single stretching or sprint session
1353	meaningfully strengthens ligament-bone junctions; the text is explicit this requires
1354	chronic training.
1355	
1356	**Example** — The book's own example: sprint training increases ligament mass and
1357	concentration even from acute exposure, but this is distinguished in the text from junction
1358	*strength*, which the authors say requires chronic training rather than occasional
1359	exposure (printed 182).
1360	
1361	**Related** — [[framework--soft-tissue-contribution-to-joint-stiffness-and-stretch-duration-type]],
1362	[[claim--differential-tissue-adaptation-rates]].

1381	"Olympic Weightlifters are amongst the most supple of all athletes, despite beliefs to the

1421	
1422	# Stretch-Then-Shorten Is Not the Same as Shorten-Then-Stretch: Force History Depends on Order
1423	
1424	**What it is** — The authors state that stretch-shortening is not synonymous or
1425	commutative with shortening-stretch: stretch-shortening and shortening-stretch cycles are
1426	not commutative with respect to the isometric forces following the length changes, i.e.
1427	stretch activation before muscle shortening does not produce the same result as muscle
1428	shortening before stretch activation. Prior stretching of a muscle is well known to
1429	decrease the isometric and maximal force the muscle can subsequently produce (force
1430	depression following muscle shortening); this force depression is virtually unaffected by
1431	previous stretching of the muscle, but force enhancement following stretch-shortening
1432	depends, in a dose-dependent manner, on the amount of muscle shortening that precedes the
1433	stretch (Herzog & Leonard, 2000). The history-dependence of isometric force following
1434	stretch-shortening cycles is reported as independent of the stretch preceding the
1435	shortening, except when stretching occurs at very high velocity (roughly 6-10 times fibre
1436	length per second, as in ballistic movement). (PDF p. 195, printed p. 184.)
1437	
1438	**Why it works** — The authors give no mechanism beyond citing Herzog & Leonard (2000) for
1439	the specific dose-dependence and velocity-threshold findings; the general fact that prior
1440	stretch reduces subsequent isometric/maximal force output is treated as established without
1441	further explanation in this passage.
1442	
1443	**When to apply** — Use this to interpret force-plate or barbell-velocity data collected
1444	immediately after a stretch-shortening action versus a shortening-stretch action; the order
1445	of length change, not just the total length excursion, affects the force the muscle can
1446	then produce. Relevant when sequencing a warm-up or a complex/contrast-training pairing
1447	that alternates stretch and shortening actions.
1448	
1449	**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence `supported`: single citation (Herzog & Leonard,
1450	2000), no independent replication given in this text.** Do not generalize the specific
1451	numeric velocity threshold (6-10 fibre lengths/second) beyond the ballistic-movement context
1452	it is given in, and do not assume this history-dependence effect has the same magnitude
1453	across all muscle groups or contraction intensities; the text does not state that.
1454	
1455	**Example** — Inference: a depth jump (stretch immediately preceding shortening, at high
1456	velocity) and a paused, held-stretch-then-jump sequence are not mechanically interchangeable
1457	by this claim, even if the total ROM and final shortening are similar, because the order
1458	and velocity of the length change independently affect the resulting force.
1459	
1460	**Related** — [[principle--short-amortization-preserves-elastic-energy]],
1461	[[framework--series-and-parallel-elastic-components]].

1475	
1476	# Three "Functional" Flexibility Qualities: Flexibility-Speed, Flexibility-Strength, Flexibility-Endurance
1477	
1478	**What it is** — Beyond raw ROM, the authors define three additional, sport-relevant
1479	flexibility qualities that "functional" stretching conditioning must also address, each
1480	having static and dynamic forms: **flexibility-speed**, the ability to produce efficient
1481	full ROM at speed; **flexibility-strength**, the ability to produce efficient, powerful
1482	static and dynamic movements over a full ROM; and **flexibility-endurance**, the ability to
1483	repetitively produce efficient full ROM under static and dynamic conditions. The authors
1484	state the importance of these qualities is why a wide variety of carefully sequenced
1485	stretching methods, cyclically periodized in intensity, duration and complexity, is needed,
1486	rather than a single stretching method or a fixed routine. (PDF p. 197, printed p. 186.)
1487	
1488	**Why it works** — The authors give no separate mechanism for why these three qualities
1489	are distinct from raw ROM; the definitions function as a vocabulary for specifying *how* a
1490	given ROM must be produced (fast, forceful, or repeated) in a sport skill, extending the
1491	active-vs-passive flexibility distinction already covered (see
1492	[[claim--active-flexibility-correlates-more-with-sporting-proficiency-than-passive]]).
1493	
1494	**When to apply** — Use this vocabulary when specifying a flexibility training goal beyond
1495	"improve hip mobility": ask whether the sport skill needs that ROM produced quickly
1496	(flexibility-speed), forcefully (flexibility-strength), or repeatedly across a competition
1497	(flexibility-endurance), since these imply different training methods (e.g. active/PNF
1498	stretching against resistance for flexibility-strength, versus repeated-exposure work for
1499	flexibility-endurance).
1500	
1501	**When NOT to apply** — This is a definitional vocabulary, not an empirically validated
1502	set of independently measurable qualities; the book gives no test or normative data for
1503	flexibility-speed, flexibility-strength, or flexibility-endurance separately from general
1504	active/passive ROM measures. Do not treat these as three distinct, separately trainable
1505	capacities without further evidence that they dissociate from one another.
1506	
1507	**Example** — Inference: a hurdler's trail-leg hip ROM needed within a single stride cycle
1508	is a flexibility-speed demand, while the same joint's ROM held under load during an
1509	isometric hip-flexor stretch-strengthening exercise is closer to a flexibility-strength
1510	demand; per this framework, a program addressing only one would not necessarily transfer to
1511	the other.
1512

1529	# A Two-Branch, Load/State-Based Taxonomy of Stretching Techniques
1530	
1531	**What it is** — The authors argue the traditional four categories of stretching (static,
1532	ballistic, passive, PNF/contract-relax) are an incomplete and sometimes overlapping way to
1533	describe technique, and propose instead a model (Fig 3.34) built from two variables: the
1534	rate of stretching, and the type of load and state of the muscle. This yields two broad
1535	types, each with sub-categories:
1536	1. **Static Stretching**: Free Static Stretching (no external load, under (a) muscle
1537	relaxation or (b) isometric contraction, sometimes called Active Static Stretching), and
1538	Passive Static Stretching (external load applied to (a) relaxed or (b) isometrically
1539	contracted muscle).
1540	2. **Dynamic Stretching**: Ballistic Stretching (passive momentum exceeds static ROM, on
1541	(a) relaxed or (b) contracted muscle, done slowly or rapidly); Active Stretching
1542	(continuous muscle activity exceeds static ROM, as in normal full-range sporting
1543	movement); PNF Stretching (intermittent or continuous phases of static or dynamic muscle
1544	action plus relaxation or passive movement, in specific activation/relaxation patterns);
1545	and Plyometric (Impulsive) Stretching (rapid termination of eccentric loading, a brief
1546	isometric phase, then an explosive rebound using stored elastic energy and powerful reflex
1547	contraction; not intended to increase ROM but to increase speed-strength of movement,
1548	viewable as a form of ballistic stretching done impulsively). The authors state PNF is
1549	misleadingly regarded as a specialized flexibility-only system: in professional practice it
1550	conditions neuromuscular processes, isometric and dynamic strength, muscular endurance, and
1551	functional flexibility more completely than many machine-based routines, using
1552	three-dimensional spiral and diagonal movement patterns, so several "distinct" stretching
1553	types may be seen as a subset of PNF's full discipline. (PDF pp. 194-195, printed pp.
1554	183-184.)
1555	
1556	**Why it works** — The authors' rationale for the taxonomy is that specificity of exercise
1557	means each category can be used effectively and safely for specific subjects at a specific
1558	training stage to achieve optimal stability and mobility; they state active and PNF
1559	stretching involving progressive contraction against external load, through and beyond the
1560	static ROM, appear to offer the most effective means of improving full-range functional
1561	sporting performance, though no comparative data are given in this passage.
1562	
1563	**When to apply** — Use this two-variable scheme (rate x load/muscle-state) to classify
1564	any named stretching modality encountered elsewhere, and to select a category matched to
1565	training goal and stage: static stretching for the average person mainly targeting static
1566	flexibility; active/PNF stretching against external load when the target is full-range
1567	functional performance.
1568	
1569	**When NOT to apply** — This is the authors' own reorganization of stretching
1570	terminology, not an experimentally validated hierarchy of effectiveness; the claim that
1571	active/PNF stretching is "the most effective" is stated without a comparative citation in
1572	this passage. Confidence is capped at `supported` because the taxonomy is a classification
1573	tool, not itself an empirical finding.
1574	
1575	**Example** — The book's own example: gently bouncing ballistic stretching performed over
1576	a gradually increasing ROM is, per this taxonomy, a special case of contract-relax/hold-relax
1577	PNF activity, not a separate, inherently more dangerous category (printed 186; see
1578	[[heuristic--ballistic-stretching-safe-with-gradual-progressive-protocol]]).

1596	# Ballistic Stretching Can Be Applied Safely if Rate and Progression Are Controlled
1597	
1598	**What it is** — Against the "well-meaning, but very misleading" blanket statement that
1599	ballistic stretching is generally harmful and should be avoided, the authors argue this
1600	makes no distinction between the rates and techniques used to apply it. They state most
1601	forms of ballistic stretching could safely be included within the scope of PNF: gentle
1602	bouncing ballistic stretching over a gradually increasing ROM is a special type of
1603	contract-relax/hold-relax PNF activity and can be applied safely and effectively; static
1604	stretches can also be alternated with periodic gentle ballistic stretches, or carried out
1605	against the resistance of stretched elastic bands, as further variants. A "principle of
1606	progressive gradual stretching increase" (increasing speed and range safely and
1607	effectively up to the level of plyometric activity) is proposed to extend this. Citing
1608	Russian research (Matveyev, 1981), the authors give a specific protocol: ballistic
1609	stretching can be most effectively and safely used in 3-5 sets of 8-12 repetitions, with
1610	amplitude of movement gradually increasing with each repetition; no further repetitions
1611	should be performed once ROM becomes impaired by fatigue, a rule the authors suggest may

1613	186-187.)
1614

1616	rate and technique (uncontrolled, high-amplitude, unprogressed bouncing), not from the

1618	tissue's current adapted range rather than exceeding it, and stopping once fatigue impairs
1619	ROM avoids stretching an already-compromised, less-controlled muscle.
1620

1622	sport-specific preparation, since ballistic actions are a frequent component of most
1623	sports and conventional static/dynamic stretching does not always address that specific
1624	joint-action demand), apply it as 3-5 sets of 8-12 reps with amplitude increasing gradually

1629	ballistic stretching abruptly at full amplitude from the first repetition; that is the
1630	specific pattern the authors' own argument depends on avoiding. Do not continue a ballistic

# What Actually Stabilizes a Joint Changes as It Approaches End-Range

**What it is** — Against the "widespread opinion that muscles act as efficient synergistic
stabilisers," the authors argue muscle cannot always respond quickly enough to protect a
joint against a large, rapid (particularly torsional) impact (Pope et al., 1978), and
propose joint stabilization instead works in a sequence:
1. The contractile element (activated by the stretch reflex complex) together with the
muscle's series elastic component (SEC) act as primary stabilizers, if the loading rate
allows the muscle to respond in time.
2. If the joint reaches the physical limits of muscle length, strength, or endurance,
protection shifts to the ligaments and the SEC; if the inverse stretch reflex (GTO) signals
the muscle to relax at its maximum length, the muscle's parallel elastic component (PEC)
also contributes to stabilization. Receptors resembling Golgi tendon organs have been found
on the surface of cruciate ligaments (Schultz et al., 1984), and muscles show reflex
contraction if ligaments are stretched to the point of pain (Basmajian, 1978).
3. If the joint is extended to its limit without sufficient muscle contraction, primary
stabilization is provided by ligaments and the PEC; once the initial latency period for
muscle excitation passes, the contracting muscle and its SEC contribute as secondary
stabilizers.
4. In certain joints, skeletal structure itself can act as the final stabilizer at the
limits of joint movement.
(PDF p. 193, printed p. 182.)

**Why it works** — The sequence follows from the mechanical roles already established for
the SEC, PEC, and stretch/inverse-stretch reflexes elsewhere in the text (see
[[framework--series-and-parallel-elastic-components]] and
[[framework--stretch-reflex-types-and-neuromuscular-control-of-flexibility]]), combined
with the cited finding that ligaments themselves carry GTO-like tension receptors (Schultz
et al., 1984) and can trigger protective muscle contraction (Basmajian, 1978).

**When to apply** — Use this sequence to explain why a joint can be injured even with
strong, well-conditioned muscles around it: at high loading rates (stage 1's premise
fails), stabilization falls to ligament and PEC tissue that may not be conditioned to the
same standard as the muscle. This reframes injury-prevention conditioning as needing to
address ligament/capsule tissue specifically, not only muscular strength.

**When NOT to apply** — This is the authors' synthesized model, not a single cited
experimental finding; treat the four numbered stages as an organizing framework for
reasoning about joint stabilization, not as a validated, measured sequence with defined
timing thresholds. Confidence is capped at `supported` because the sequence itself
(as opposed to the individual cited facts feeding it) is not independently attributed to a
specific study.

**Example** — Inference: a sudden, high-velocity valgus torque to the knee arrives faster
than stage 1's muscular response can engage, meaning stages 2-3 (ligament and PEC) bear
more of the load than they would under a slower, anticipated movement, which is consistent
with why acute ligament injuries often occur on unanticipated contact.

**Related** — [[framework--stretch-reflex-types-and-neuromuscular-control-of-flexibility]],
[[framework--series-and-parallel-elastic-components]].

# "There Is No Unsafe Stretch, Only an Unsafe Way of Executing It"

**What it is** — In a bulleted list of biomechanical points on stretching, the authors
state: "There is generally no such thing as an unsafe stretch or exercise: only an unsafe
way of executing any movement for a specific individual at a specific time." (PDF p. 192,
printed p. 181.) This appears alongside a related claim in the same list that
physiotherapeutic PNF shows rapid or powerful recruitment of the different stretch
reflexes can be safely applied to rehabilitate and strengthen tissue, "contrary to common
belief."

**Why it works** — The authors give no supporting mechanism, study, or citation for this
specific aphorism; it reads as a stated position, not a derived or evidenced conclusion in
this passage.

**When to apply** — Useful as a reframing prompt when an exercise or stretch is being
categorically banned ("we never do ballistic stretching," "no PNF for this population"):
ask whether the concern is really about the movement class itself, or about a specific
athlete's readiness, technique, loading rate, or tissue state for that movement at that
time.

**When NOT to apply** — **`untested`, unlabeled aphorism with no supporting citation in
this passage.** Do not use this claim to override a specific, evidence-based
contraindication (e.g. a known ligament laxity, an acute strain, a post-surgical range
restriction) on the reasoning that "there's no unsafe stretch, only unsafe execution": the
book gives no criteria here for what counts as safe execution, and the claim is broad
enough to be difficult to falsify. Treat it as a coaching-philosophy prompt, not a safety
rule.

**Example** — The book's own paired example: it treats the popular blanket rule "ballistic
stretching should be avoided at all costs" as the kind of overgeneralization this heuristic
is meant to counter, arguing instead that rate and technique determine ballistic
stretching's safety (see
[[heuristic--ballistic-stretching-safe-with-gradual-progressive-protocol]]).

# Tendon Stretching Must Not Compromise the Tendon's Ability to Store Elastic Energy

**What it is** — The authors state tendons, unlike ligaments, are not simply passive
joint stabilizers: together with strongly contracted muscle fibres (particularly during
eccentric contraction), they play a vital role in storing elastic energy during running and
other impulsive motor acts, saving energy and increasing the efficiency of muscular
activity (Goldspink, 1978). From this they draw a direct programming rule: no stretching
manoeuvre should compromise the strength or ability of the tendons to store elastic energy
throughout their range of movement; tendon stretching exercises should therefore be
accompanied by strength conditioning against adequate resistance. They add that tendons and
ligaments, being viscoelastic, are sensitive to loading rate and undergo stress relaxation,
creep, and hysteresis. (PDF p. 192, printed p. 181.)

**Why it works** — Goldspink (1978) is cited as the source of the tendon-energy-storage
mechanism itself; the programming rule (pair tendon stretching with resistance work) is the
authors' own inference from that mechanism, not a separately cited intervention finding.

**When to apply** — When programming flexibility work for tendon-dependent qualities
(sprinting, jumping, change of direction), pair any deliberate tendon-lengthening or
stretching work with resistance training against that tendon, rather than stretching it in
isolation, on the reasoning that a lengthened but under-strengthened tendon may store
elastic energy less effectively.

**When NOT to apply** — The book does not give a specific dose, duration, or exercise
example for "adequate resistance" alongside tendon stretching; treat this as a general
programming principle, not a prescribed protocol. Do not use this rule to avoid all tendon
flexibility work; the claim is about pairing, not avoiding, stretching.

**Example** — Inference: an athlete doing calf-tendon stretching for ankle dorsiflexion
ROM would, per this rule, also need loaded calf-raise or plyometric work in that same block
so the lengthened gastrocnemius-soleus tendon complex retains its elastic energy-storage
capacity for sprinting and jumping.

**Related** — [[claim--tendon-insertion-transitional-stiffness-gradient-disrupted-by-steroids]],
[[principle--short-amortization-preserves-elastic-energy]].

# Ligaments and Tendons Thicken and Strengthen With Training, Weaken With Inactivity

**What it is** — The authors report that physical training strengthens the attachments of
tendons and ligaments to bone: trained ligaments are thicker and heavier, though the
increase in mass is not necessarily associated with a greater concentration of collagen,
a process described as still poorly understood (Booth & Gould, 1975); controlled strain on
soft tissue may increase fibre formation, contributing to enhanced elasticity and strength
(Holland, 1968). Regular resistance training increases not only muscle hypertrophy but also
the collagen content of ligaments and the connective tissue surrounding muscle fibres
(Tipton et al., 1975); training also increases the activity of an enzyme involved in
collagen synthesis, an effect possibly stimulated by lactic acid production during exercise
(Booth & Gould, 1975). By contrast, moderate-intensity treadmill training in rats produces
neither muscle hypertrophy nor increased intramuscular connective tissue growth; prolonged
low-intensity training conditions the cardiovascular system but not the musculoskeletal
system. The authors state it is anaerobic, muscle-endurance training specifically that most
strengthens collagenous tissue and its junction zones, making progressive stretching
alongside this type of training especially valuable. In contrast to chronic training,
single exercise sessions, occasional stretching, or sprint training alone do not produce
significant increases in junction strength, although sprinting does markedly increase
ligament mass and concentration (Tipton et al., 1974). Just as ligaments strengthen and
stiffen under increased stress, they become weaker and less stiff with decreased stress,
immobilization, and inactivity (Tipton et al., 1970); the authors note the similar changes
seen with ageing may partly reflect inactivity rather than degeneration alone. (PDF pp.
193-194, printed p. 182.)

**Why it works** — This is presented as a summary of cited animal and human exercise
physiology findings (Tipton et al. 1970, 1974, 1975; Booth & Gould, 1975; Holland, 1968);
the authors do not add a mechanism beyond what each citation states.

**When to apply** — Use this to set expectations for how long connective tissue
conditioning takes: this entry supports chronic, repeated anaerobic/muscle-endurance
training as the driver of ligament and tendon strengthening, not occasional or single-bout
stretching or training. It also supports resuming ligament/tendon-specific loading
gradually after a period of inactivity or immobilization (e.g. post-injury), since the same
literature reports detraining weakens and destiffens these tissues.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence capped at `supported`.** Much of the underlying
evidence is animal-model research (rat treadmill studies; Tipton's ligament work), not
human athlete data, and the collagen-concentration-vs-mass distinction is itself described
in the source as poorly understood. Do not assume a single stretching or sprint session
meaningfully strengthens ligament-bone junctions; the text is explicit this requires
chronic training.

**Example** — The book's own example: sprint training increases ligament mass and
concentration even from acute exposure, but this is distinguished in the text from junction
*strength*, which the authors say requires chronic training rather than occasional
exposure (printed 182).

**Related** — [[framework--soft-tissue-contribution-to-joint-stiffness-and-stretch-duration-type]],
[[claim--differential-tissue-adaptation-rates]].

# Stretch-Then-Shorten Is Not the Same as Shorten-Then-Stretch: Force History Depends on Order

**What it is** — The authors state that stretch-shortening is not synonymous or
commutative with shortening-stretch: stretch-shortening and shortening-stretch cycles are
not commutative with respect to the isometric forces following the length changes, i.e.
stretch activation before muscle shortening does not produce the same result as muscle
shortening before stretch activation. Prior stretching of a muscle is well known to
decrease the isometric and maximal force the muscle can subsequently produce (force
depression following muscle shortening); this force depression is virtually unaffected by
previous stretching of the muscle, but force enhancement following stretch-shortening
depends, in a dose-dependent manner, on the amount of muscle shortening that precedes the
stretch (Herzog & Leonard, 2000). The history-dependence of isometric force following
stretch-shortening cycles is reported as independent of the stretch preceding the
shortening, except when stretching occurs at very high velocity (roughly 6-10 times fibre
length per second, as in ballistic movement). (PDF p. 195, printed p. 184.)

**Why it works** — The authors give no mechanism beyond citing Herzog & Leonard (2000) for
the specific dose-dependence and velocity-threshold findings; the general fact that prior
stretch reduces subsequent isometric/maximal force output is treated as established without
further explanation in this passage.

**When to apply** — Use this to interpret force-plate or barbell-velocity data collected
immediately after a stretch-shortening action versus a shortening-stretch action; the order
of length change, not just the total length excursion, affects the force the muscle can
then produce. Relevant when sequencing a warm-up or a complex/contrast-training pairing
that alternates stretch and shortening actions.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence `supported`: single citation (Herzog & Leonard,
2000), no independent replication given in this text.** Do not generalize the specific
numeric velocity threshold (6-10 fibre lengths/second) beyond the ballistic-movement context
it is given in, and do not assume this history-dependence effect has the same magnitude
across all muscle groups or contraction intensities; the text does not state that.

**Example** — Inference: a depth jump (stretch immediately preceding shortening, at high
velocity) and a paused, held-stretch-then-jump sequence are not mechanically interchangeable
by this claim, even if the total ROM and final shortening are similar, because the order
and velocity of the length change independently affect the resulting force.

[[framework--series-and-parallel-elastic-components]].

# Three "Functional" Flexibility Qualities: Flexibility-Speed, Flexibility-Strength, Flexibility-Endurance

**What it is** — Beyond raw ROM, the authors define three additional, sport-relevant
flexibility qualities that "functional" stretching conditioning must also address, each
having static and dynamic forms: **flexibility-speed**, the ability to produce efficient
full ROM at speed; **flexibility-strength**, the ability to produce efficient, powerful
static and dynamic movements over a full ROM; and **flexibility-endurance**, the ability to
repetitively produce efficient full ROM under static and dynamic conditions. The authors
state the importance of these qualities is why a wide variety of carefully sequenced
stretching methods, cyclically periodized in intensity, duration and complexity, is needed,
rather than a single stretching method or a fixed routine. (PDF p. 197, printed p. 186.)

**Why it works** — The authors give no separate mechanism for why these three qualities
are distinct from raw ROM; the definitions function as a vocabulary for specifying *how* a
given ROM must be produced (fast, forceful, or repeated) in a sport skill, extending the
active-vs-passive flexibility distinction already covered (see
[[claim--active-flexibility-correlates-more-with-sporting-proficiency-than-passive]]).

**When to apply** — Use this vocabulary when specifying a flexibility training goal beyond
"improve hip mobility": ask whether the sport skill needs that ROM produced quickly
(flexibility-speed), forcefully (flexibility-strength), or repeatedly across a competition
(flexibility-endurance), since these imply different training methods (e.g. active/PNF
stretching against resistance for flexibility-strength, versus repeated-exposure work for
flexibility-endurance).

**When NOT to apply** — This is a definitional vocabulary, not an empirically validated
set of independently measurable qualities; the book gives no test or normative data for
flexibility-speed, flexibility-strength, or flexibility-endurance separately from general
active/passive ROM measures. Do not treat these as three distinct, separately trainable
capacities without further evidence that they dissociate from one another.

**Example** — Inference: a hurdler's trail-leg hip ROM needed within a single stride cycle
is a flexibility-speed demand, while the same joint's ROM held under load during an
isometric hip-flexor stretch-strengthening exercise is closer to a flexibility-strength
demand; per this framework, a program addressing only one would not necessarily transfer to
the other.

**Related** — [[claim--active-flexibility-correlates-more-with-sporting-proficiency-than-passive]],
[[heuristic--eccentric-quasi-isometrics-for-active-flexibility-and-starting-strength]].

# A Two-Branch, Load/State-Based Taxonomy of Stretching Techniques

**What it is** — The authors argue the traditional four categories of stretching (static,
ballistic, passive, PNF/contract-relax) are an incomplete and sometimes overlapping way to
describe technique, and propose instead a model (Fig 3.34) built from two variables: the
rate of stretching, and the type of load and state of the muscle. This yields two broad
types, each with sub-categories:
1. **Static Stretching**: Free Static Stretching (no external load, under (a) muscle
relaxation or (b) isometric contraction, sometimes called Active Static Stretching), and
Passive Static Stretching (external load applied to (a) relaxed or (b) isometrically
contracted muscle).
2. **Dynamic Stretching**: Ballistic Stretching (passive momentum exceeds static ROM, on
(a) relaxed or (b) contracted muscle, done slowly or rapidly); Active Stretching
(continuous muscle activity exceeds static ROM, as in normal full-range sporting
movement); PNF Stretching (intermittent or continuous phases of static or dynamic muscle
action plus relaxation or passive movement, in specific activation/relaxation patterns);
and Plyometric (Impulsive) Stretching (rapid termination of eccentric loading, a brief
isometric phase, then an explosive rebound using stored elastic energy and powerful reflex
contraction; not intended to increase ROM but to increase speed-strength of movement,
viewable as a form of ballistic stretching done impulsively). The authors state PNF is
misleadingly regarded as a specialized flexibility-only system: in professional practice it
conditions neuromuscular processes, isometric and dynamic strength, muscular endurance, and
functional flexibility more completely than many machine-based routines, using
three-dimensional spiral and diagonal movement patterns, so several "distinct" stretching
types may be seen as a subset of PNF's full discipline. (PDF pp. 194-195, printed pp.
183-184.)

**Why it works** — The authors' rationale for the taxonomy is that specificity of exercise
means each category can be used effectively and safely for specific subjects at a specific
training stage to achieve optimal stability and mobility; they state active and PNF
stretching involving progressive contraction against external load, through and beyond the
static ROM, appear to offer the most effective means of improving full-range functional
sporting performance, though no comparative data are given in this passage.

**When to apply** — Use this two-variable scheme (rate x load/muscle-state) to classify
any named stretching modality encountered elsewhere, and to select a category matched to
training goal and stage: static stretching for the average person mainly targeting static
flexibility; active/PNF stretching against external load when the target is full-range
functional performance.

**When NOT to apply** — This is the authors' own reorganization of stretching
terminology, not an experimentally validated hierarchy of effectiveness; the claim that
active/PNF stretching is "the most effective" is stated without a comparative citation in
this passage. Confidence is capped at `supported` because the taxonomy is a classification
tool, not itself an empirical finding.

**Example** — The book's own example: gently bouncing ballistic stretching performed over
a gradually increasing ROM is, per this taxonomy, a special case of contract-relax/hold-relax
PNF activity, not a separate, inherently more dangerous category (printed 186; see
[[heuristic--ballistic-stretching-safe-with-gradual-progressive-protocol]]).

**Related** — [[heuristic--ballistic-stretching-safe-with-gradual-progressive-protocol]],
[[framework--flexibility-speed-strength-endurance-qualities]].

# Ballistic Stretching Can Be Applied Safely if Rate and Progression Are Controlled

**What it is** — Against the "well-meaning, but very misleading" blanket statement that
ballistic stretching is generally harmful and should be avoided, the authors argue this
makes no distinction between the rates and techniques used to apply it. They state most
forms of ballistic stretching could safely be included within the scope of PNF: gentle
bouncing ballistic stretching over a gradually increasing ROM is a special type of
contract-relax/hold-relax PNF activity and can be applied safely and effectively; static
stretches can also be alternated with periodic gentle ballistic stretches, or carried out
against the resistance of stretched elastic bands, as further variants. A "principle of
progressive gradual stretching increase" (increasing speed and range safely and
effectively up to the level of plyometric activity) is proposed to extend this. Citing
Russian research (Matveyev, 1981), the authors give a specific protocol: ballistic
stretching can be most effectively and safely used in 3-5 sets of 8-12 repetitions, with
amplitude of movement gradually increasing with each repetition; no further repetitions
should be performed once ROM becomes impaired by fatigue, a rule the authors suggest may
apply with equal validity to other forms of stretching. (PDF pp. 197-198, printed pp.
186-187.)

**Why it works** — The authors' argument is that ballistic stretching's risk comes from
rate and technique (uncontrolled, high-amplitude, unprogressed bouncing), not from the
ballistic action itself; gradually increasing amplitude keeps each repetition within the
tissue's current adapted range rather than exceeding it, and stopping once fatigue impairs
ROM avoids stretching an already-compromised, less-controlled muscle.

**When to apply** — Where ballistic or dynamic stretching is wanted (e.g. as
sport-specific preparation, since ballistic actions are a frequent component of most
sports and conventional static/dynamic stretching does not always address that specific
joint-action demand), apply it as 3-5 sets of 8-12 reps with amplitude increasing gradually
each rep, and stop the set once fatigue starts to reduce ROM.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence capped at `supported`: single Soviet-era citation
(Matveyev, 1981), no independent replication located in this library.** Do not apply
ballistic stretching abruptly at full amplitude from the first repetition; that is the
specific pattern the authors' own argument depends on avoiding. Do not continue a ballistic
stretching set once ROM is visibly reduced by fatigue; the text states this explicitly as
the stopping rule.

**Example** — The book's own contrast: the "well-meaning, but very misleading" advice to
avoid ballistic stretching "at all costs" is the position this heuristic is written
against; the authors instead prescribe the specific graduated protocol above rather than a
blanket avoidance rule (printed 186).

**Related** — [[heuristic--no-unsafe-stretch-only-unsafe-execution-for-individual]],
[[framework--stretching-techniques-taxonomy-static-vs-dynamic]].

# Eccentric Quasi-Isometrics: Loading a Joint Slowly Past Its Static Flexibility Limit to Build Active Range

**What it is** — Quasi-isometric activity (defined generally in
[[framework--precise-muscle-action-terminology]]) is presented here specifically as a
method for developing active flexibility: exercising a limb through a full ROM against a
resistance allowed to stretch the joint gently beyond its limit of static flexibility,
without sudden movement that would recruit the myotatic (stretch) reflex. Free weights,
pulleys, and functional training machines are named as versatile tools for this, executing
natural resistance patterns. Eccentric quasi-isometrics specifically use the load to force
the joint to move slowly and eccentrically beyond its static flexibility limit; this does
not require very heavy loads, and the authors recommend starting with small loads and
applying progressive overload toward near-maximal loads over time, using multiple
repetitions that gradually increase ROM with each one. Both quasi-isometric modes can be
combined with PNF patterns to improve static strength, static flexibility, dynamic
flexibility, flexibility-strength, and flexibility-endurance. Separately, the authors state
starting-strength (force production very early in a contraction) is important to human
performance, and injudicious stretching or part-range resistance training that impairs this
quality should be discouraged; most isokinetic machines have a small lag in their early
phase and are described as inadequate for developing starting-strength or functional
flexibility in that critical joint zone, whereas progressively sequenced isometric
contractions at varied joint angles, or work against elastic bands, are named as
particularly useful, including for early rehabilitation. (PDF pp. 196-197, printed p.
186.)

1719	# A Flexible, Well-Conditioned Joint Can Still Have Limited Functional ROM From Spurious Muscle Tension
1720	
1721	**What it is** — The authors state that limitations in functional ROM should not
1722	automatically be attributed to joint stiffness alone, since this can lead to an
1723	unnecessary emphasis on stretching. Limitations to full ROM can also be caused by "spurious
1724	tension" or excessive, non-functional muscle tension such as coordination tension, which
1725	may accompany the appropriate tension a given movement requires; this non-functional
1726	tension can occur in both phasic and tonic muscles, before, during, or after the movement.
1727	Athlete proficiency level has a marked influence on the reflex ability of muscles to
1728	contract and relax: rapidity of both contraction and relaxation increases with mastery,
1729	with a decrease in relaxation time being especially evident (Fig 3.35, data from Matveyev,
1730	1981, measured by EMG across five qualification levels from novice to Master of Sport,
1731	showing relaxation time dropping from about 0.4s at Level 1 to about 0.22s at Level 5,
1732	converging with contraction time). The authors conclude it is of little consequence to have
1733	highly flexible joints with well-conditioned, supple connective tissue if action is limited
1734	by spurious muscle tension instead; flexibility training should therefore always be
1735	combined with neuromuscular training aimed at efficient, functional ROM, not tissue
1736	stretching alone. (PDF pp. 199-200, printed pp. 187-188, Fig 3.35.)
1737	
1738	**Why it works** — The authors give no separate mechanism for why proficiency specifically
1739	speeds relaxation more than contraction; the Matveyev (1981) EMG data are reported as the
1740	empirical basis for the mastery-relaxation relationship, without further explanation.
1741	
1742	**When to apply** — When an athlete presents with apparently limited functional ROM in a
1743	sport movement despite passing a passive flexibility screen, consider spurious/coordination
1744	tension and relaxation ability as an alternative or additional target, rather than
1745	defaulting to more stretching.
1746	
1747	**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence capped at `supported`: the Fig 3.35 data are a single
1748	cited source (Matveyev, 1981) with an unspecified sample, and the five qualification
1749	levels (novice through Master of Sport) are specific to that source's population, not
1750	necessarily transferable as normative relaxation-time targets for a Baylor roster.** Do not
1751	use this claim to dismiss a genuine tissue-flexibility deficit; the authors frame this as an
1752	additional cause of limited ROM, not a replacement for checking tissue-level flexibility.
1753	
1754	**Example** — The book's own example, via Fig 3.35: a novice athlete's slower reflex
1755	relaxation (about 0.4s) compared to a Master of Sport's faster relaxation (about 0.22s) at
1756	the same level of tissue flexibility illustrates that training age/mastery, not just
1757	tissue conditioning, changes how quickly non-functional tension clears during a movement.
1758	
1759	**Related** — [[framework--methods-for-improving-voluntary-muscle-relaxation]],
1760	[[heuristic--reflex-based-techniques-for-flexibility-training]].

1775	# Ten Ways Coaches Can Train an Athlete's Ability to Relax Muscles on Demand

1777	**What it is** — Following the claim that spurious muscle tension, not just tissue

1781	hold-relax, and other PNF methods using stretch reflexes to promote relaxation; (2) sudden
1782	unloading, the abrupt removal of external resistance under strong isometric or dynamic
1783	conditions (e.g. the end of a jerk, completion of a heavy squat/bench press, releasing a
1784	thrown shot or medicine ball, short bursts of strong electromuscular contraction), reported
1785	as producing the greatest relaxation response of all listed means, and becoming more
1786	effective the more closely the contraction-relaxation process is tied to the actual
1787	sporting action; (3) changing muscle groups from tension to relaxation in a controlled,
1788	gradual manner or through a series of stages (e.g. Jacobsen's progressive relaxation
1789	method); (4) controlling spurious tension in the face and hands specifically, since these
1790	tend to reflect general body tension well; (5) controlled visualization of muscles
1791	progressing from contraction to relaxation and back; (6) autogenic training, progressive
1792	relaxation, meditation, or massage; (7) breathing pattern control, on the basis that
1793	tension is associated with inhalation and breath-holding (the Valsalva manoeuvre, used
1794	where maximal force and spinal stabilization are needed) while relaxation is associated
1795	with gentle, controlled exhalation; appropriate breathing should be combined with all
1796	phases of movement to enhance mobility, stability, and relaxation; (8) the "pre-exhaustion

1843	# The Stretching Matrix: Any Stretch Is the Reverse of the Action That Contracts the Same Muscle Group
1844	
1845	**What it is** — The authors present a generalized system, built from standard muscle
1846	action charts, for devising a stretch for any major muscle group: "the reverse of any
1847	action to contract a given muscle group becomes a stretch for that same muscle group." A
1848	series of matrices (Figs 3.36-3.40, in this excerpt covering trunk/neck, upper arm,
1849	forearm, lower extremity, and foot) list each muscle against the joint actions that stretch
1850	it. The system requires identifying which joints a given muscle crosses before deciding how
1851	to stretch it, since a muscle's action, and therefore its stretch, can differ depending on
1852	which joint's chart is consulted; using only one matrix for a biarticular or multiarticular
1853	muscle can produce a less-than-maximal stretch. The authors' worked example: psoas (as part
1854	of iliopsoas) is stretched by hip extension and medial rotation per the lower-extremity
1855	matrix, but as a trunk muscle it is also stretched by combined trunk extension and lateral
1856	extension per the trunk/neck matrix; a fencer's front lunge maximally stretches iliacus
1857	(hip extension alone) but will not maximally stretch psoas unless the trunk is also
1858	extended and laterally flexed toward the leading leg. A second worked example: the oblique
1859	muscles and quadratus lumborum both perform lateral trunk flexion, but only the obliques
1860	also rotate the trunk and only quadratus lumborum extends it, so only concurrent trunk
1861	flexion plus lateral extension maximally stretches quadratus lumborum, while flexion plus
1862	lateral extension plus rotation is needed to maximally stretch the obliques. (PDF pp.
1863	199-202, printed pp. 188-191, Figs 3.36-3.39.)
1864	
1865	**Why it works** — The mechanism is definitional, not empirical: if muscle contraction
1866	produces a given joint action, moving the joint through the opposite action necessarily
1867	lengthens (stretches) that muscle, following directly from standard functional anatomy
1868	rather than a cited study.
1869	
1870	**When to apply** — Use the matrices to design a novel stretch for any muscle by first
1871	identifying every joint and degree of freedom the muscle crosses (via multiple figures if
1872	needed), then combining the reverse actions simultaneously rather than one at a time, to
1873	achieve a maximal stretch. Useful for building or auditing a stretching routine's actual
1874	target versus its intended target.
1875	
1876	**When NOT to apply** — This is an anatomical design method, not an outcome-tested
1877	training system; the book does not report ROM-gain or performance data from using this
1878	matrix approach specifically. Confidence is capped at `supported` because it is a
1879	logically-derived tool, not itself an empirical claim. Do not assume a single-joint stretch
1880	fully stretches a muscle that crosses multiple joints; the authors are explicit this is the
1881	main pitfall the matrices are meant to prevent.
1882	
1883	**Example** — The book's own example: to stretch biceps brachii (which crosses both
1884	elbow and shoulder), the elbow must be extended and the shoulder extended and abducted with
1885	the forearm pronated simultaneously (per Figs 3.37-3.38); consulting only the forearm
1886	matrix (elbow extension alone) would under-stretch the muscle (printed 189).
1887	
1888	**Related** — [[framework--movement-matrix-system-for-multiarticular-exercise-selection]].

1903	# A Sport's Own Movements, Progressively Loaded, Can Replace a Dedicated Stretching Session
1904	
1905	**What it is** — The authors call it "possibly the most heretical remark to make about
1906	stretching" that dedicated stretching sessions may not even be necessary, noting many
1907	athletes dispense entirely with special stretching or even warm-up sessions without
1908	suffering injury in training or competition; the prescription of stretching and warm-up
1909	or cool-down has become "a well-accepted ritual," which the authors state does not by
1910	itself make it essential. They propose a "principle of gradual progressive stretching and
1911	activity increase": the athlete begins each movement gently and non-ballistically under
1912	limited static and dynamic conditions, then progressively increases range, speed,
1913	complexity, intensity and other aspects of movement until the actual sporting movements
1914	themselves are performed under light and eventually near-competitive conditions. In weight
1915	training, the same principle is applied by beginning every exercise with a few preparatory
1916	repetitions at a light load, progressively increasing the load over a few sets, and using a
1917	narrower-than-normal grip or stance early in the progression (e.g. bench press, squat) to
1918	reduce range/speed of movement and tissue/joint stress at the start. The authors' concluding
1919	position: it is unnecessary to devise many highly specific individual flexibility drills
1920	for the whole body, since this would be time-consuming and inefficient; functional
1921	movements already used in the sport, combined with the stretching techniques discussed
1922	earlier, can replace a prolonged session of dozens of single-joint stretches, provided the
1923	routine still increases both passive/static ROM and functional flexibility-strength for all
1924	static, dynamic, and necessary ballistic joint actions. (PDF pp. 203-204, printed pp.
1925	192-193.)
1926	
1927	**Why it works** — The authors give no controlled comparison (stretching vs. no
1928	stretching, or dedicated-stretch vs. movement-based warm-up) for injury or performance
1929	outcomes in this passage; the claim rests on informal observation ("many athletes dispense
1930	entirely...without suffering injury") rather than a cited study.
1931	
1932	**When to apply** — Where session time is limited, consider replacing a block of isolated,
1933	single-joint stretches with a progressively loaded, sport-specific movement warm-up
1934	(narrow-grip/stance light sets building toward working load and range), on the premise

1967	# A Muscle's Anatomical "Flexor/Extensor" Label Does Not Reliably Predict What It Actually Accelerates
1968	
1969	**What it is** — The authors report that classical functional anatomy, which labels a
1970	muscle as a flexor or extensor of a joint it crosses based on the torque it produces about
1971	that single joint, has been challenged by biomechanical analysis of multi-articular joint
1972	actions (Zajac & Gordon, 1989). Because the body is a linked system of joints, muscles that
1973	do not even span a given joint can still produce acceleration about it, and the actions of
1974	individual joints do not simply superimpose linearly in a multi-joint movement (no simple
1975	relationship holds between velocity, angle, and torque about a single joint in a complex
1976	movement). Zajac and Gordon argue it is more accurate to say "muscle X accelerates joint A
1977	into flexion" than "muscle X flexes joint A." Their worked example: soleus, an ankle-only
1978	muscle usually labelled an ankle extensor, accelerates the knee (which it does not span)
1979	into extension up to about twice as much as it accelerates the ankle (which it does span)
1980	into extension, near upright standing posture (Fig 3.47). Separately, work derived from
1981	Lombard's Paradox ("antagonist muscles can act in the same contraction mode as their
1982	agonists") found the rectus femoris and hamstrings act in three different ways during
1983	cycling (Andrews, 1985, 1987), since in actions like cycling and squatting the quadriceps
1984	and hamstrings can both contract concentrically at the same time despite being classically
1985	regarded as opposing muscles. A muscle capable of several different joint actions does not
1986	necessarily perform all of them in every movement: gluteus maximus, which can extend and
1987	abduct the hip, does not necessarily accelerate the hip into both simultaneously, and its
1988	extensor torque may even accelerate the hip into adduction instead (Andrews, 1982, 1985;
1989	Mansour & Pereira, 1987). Gastrocnemius, usually described simply as a knee flexor and
1990	ankle extensor, can in fact perform three different combined actions depending on knee
1991	angle (Fig 3.48): flex the knee and extend the ankle, flex the knee and flex the ankle, or
1992	extend the knee and extend the ankle. (PDF pp. 210-211, printed pp. 199-200, Figs 3.47-3.48.)
1993	
1994	**Why it works** — The mechanism is the linked, non-linear dynamics of a multi-joint
1995	skeletal system (induced-acceleration analysis, per Zajac & Gordon, 1989): because segments
1996	are connected, a force applied by a muscle at one joint propagates through the chain and can
1997	accelerate a joint that muscle does not cross, and the net effect at any joint depends on
1998	the whole system's configuration (joint angles) at that instant, not on the muscle's
1999	anatomical classification alone.
2000	
2001	**When to apply** — Use this to caution against selecting or excluding an exercise based
2002	solely on a muscle's textbook flexor/extensor label; the authors argue, following Zajac and
2003	Gordon, that it is more useful to examine muscle action in terms of synergism (how muscles
2004	work together across the whole kinetic chain) than in terms of isolated agonism/antagonism
2005	(Basmajian, 1978, as cited by Zajac & Gordon), since a generalized approach that reduces
2006	movement to single-joint actions fails to capture that muscle action is task-dependent.
2007	
2008	**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is `supported`: the cited induced-acceleration analysis
2009	method (Zajac & Gordon, 1989) is a well-established biomechanical modeling approach, but
2010	this entry reports the book's specific worked examples (soleus/knee, gluteus
2011	maximus/adduction, gastrocnemius's three actions) as given, without independently
2012	re-deriving them; treat the specific numeric ratios (e.g. "twice as much") as reported by
2013	the cited source rather than independently verified here. Do not use this claim to argue
2014	anatomical muscle-action charts are useless; the authors use those same charts elsewhere
2015	(see [[framework--movement-matrix-system-for-multiarticular-exercise-selection]]) as a
2016	starting point, with this entry as the stated caveat on their limits for complex,
2017	multi-joint movement.
2018	
2019	**Example** — The book's own example: during a standing overhead press that used to be
2020	part Olympic Weightlifting, the trunk's back-bending action is caused not only by a
2021	Newton's-third-law reaction to the overhead press but also by the triceps (which crosses
2022	both elbow and shoulder) accelerating the trunk backward as it extends the elbow, an effect
2023	counteracted by rectus abdominis (trunk flexion) and the hip flexors (hip extension)
2024	(printed 200).
2025	
2026	**Related** — [[framework--movement-matrix-system-for-multiarticular-exercise-selection]],
2027	[[heuristic--identify-moved-stabilized-and-both-joints-before-selecting-exercises]].

2045	cleans is valuable for reducing the stress placed on the erector spinae, and that spinal

2049	most of the load is instead borne by the muscles; conversely, if the muscles are
2050	inadequately contracted, excessive stress is placed on the ligaments. The authors describe
2051	a skilled lifter as one able to optimize the balance between spinal muscles and ligaments,
2052	enhancing lifting efficiency and reducing injury likelihood; they state similar rhythms and

2054	efficiency and safety generally. (PDF p. 209, printed pp. 198-199.)

2100	# The Movement Matrix System: Reading Off Muscles From a Joint Action, or Actions From a Muscle
2101	
2102	**What it is** — The authors present a companion series of Movement Matrices (Figs 3.41-3.46
2103	in this excerpt: lower extremity, foot, shoulder, arm/humerus, forearm, trunk and neck) that
2104	can be read two ways: to find the muscles corresponding to a given joint action, or to find
2105	the actions produced by a given muscle group. The authors state these are needed whenever a
2106	reader wants to analyse or devise exercises, and that it is often necessary to apply more
2107	than one Movement Matrix simultaneously, because some muscles cross more than one joint.
2108	Their worked examples: gastrocnemius crosses both the knee and ankle, so Figs 3.41 and 3.42
2109	(lower extremity, foot) must both be consulted to determine whether a single-joint or a
2110	combined multi-joint exercise is more appropriate for a given goal; biceps brachii crosses
2111	the elbow and shoulder, so maximal training of biceps requires extending both joints from a
2112	position of full pre-stretch to full flexion at the end position (Figs 3.43-3.44). This
2113	dual-joint action of gastrocnemius (knee flexion plus ankle plantarflexion together) occurs
2114	naturally during the double-knee-bend (scoop) phase of the weightlifting clean, or in
2115	"glute-ham-gastroc raises," a modified prone hyperextension over a pommel horse with the
2116	feet pressed against a vertical plate (Yessis, 1992). (PDF pp. 204-208, printed pp. 193-197,
2117	Figs 3.41-3.46.)
2118	
2119	**Why it works** — As with the Stretching Matrix, this is a definitional reading of
2120	standard functional-anatomy relationships (which muscles produce which joint actions), not
2121	an empirical finding with its own separate mechanism.
2122	
2123	**When to apply** — Use the paired-matrix approach when selecting or designing an exercise
2124	for a multiarticular muscle: check every matrix the target muscle appears in before
2125	concluding a single-joint exercise trains it fully, and consider whether a combined,
2126	multi-joint version (like the clean's double-knee bend, for gastrocnemius) better matches
2127	the muscle's natural dual action than an isolated single-joint exercise would.
2128	
2129	**When NOT to apply** — This is a reference and design tool built from standard anatomical
2130	muscle-action data, not a validated training-outcome comparison between single-joint and
2131	multi-joint exercise selection; the book does not report performance or hypertrophy data
2132	comparing the two approaches here. See also
2133	[[claim--multiarticular-muscle-action-cannot-be-predicted-from-joints-spanned]] for the
2134	authors' own caution that even this matrix approach is an incomplete model of real
2135	multiarticular muscle function.
2136	
2137	**Example** — The book's own example: because gastrocnemius flexes the knee and
2138	plantarflexes the ankle, the glute-ham-gastroc raise (a modified prone hyperextension with
2139	feet braced) trains both actions together, unlike a standing calf raise (ankle only) or a
2140	leg curl (knee only) performed in isolation (printed 193).
2141

2143	[[heuristic--identify-moved-stabilized-and-both-joints-before-selecting-exercises]].

2158	# Before Picking an Exercise: Identify Which Joints Are Moved, Which Are Stabilized, and Which Are Both
2159	
2160	**What it is** — The authors argue it is preferable to think in terms of joint actions,
2161	rather than muscle actions, when analysing which muscles are involved in a movement or
2162	trained by a specific machine. They criticize the popular practice (common in weight-training
2163	and bodybuilding publications) of identifying only the "prime movers" as a partial and
2164	misleading view, since stabilizing muscles may be contracting far more vigorously than the
2165	movers during some exercises, and there is no situation in which stabilizers are not also
2166	contracting while the movers carry out their dynamic role. The recommended process for
2167	analysing any movement is to identify: (1) which joints are being moved; (2) which joints
2168	are being stabilized; and (3) which joints are being stabilized and moved concurrently. Only
2169	after this should the relevant muscles for moving and stabilizing tasks be determined via
2170	the Movement Matrices. The authors add that even this three-step process gives an
2171	incomplete mechanical picture, because it can still reinforce several inaccurate popular
2172	assumptions: that the same movement is always produced by the same muscles; that the same
2173	muscles always produce the same movement; that the same muscles are dominant throughout the
2174	full ROM; that muscles only act as active tissues; that muscles only act as movers or
2175	stabilizers; and that muscles are the only important tissues controlling movement. (PDF pp.
2176	206-207, printed pp. 195-196.)
2177	
2178	**Why it works** — Inference: this follows directly from the book's broader point that
2179	muscle action is task- and configuration-dependent (see
2180	[[claim--multiarticular-muscle-action-cannot-be-predicted-from-joints-spanned]]); a
2181	prime-mover-only analysis assumes a fixed muscle-to-movement mapping that the authors argue
2182	does not hold across a joint's full range or across different tasks.
2183	
2184	**When to apply** — Use this three-step process (moved / stabilized / both) before
2185	selecting an exercise meant to train or rehabilitate a specific joint action, rather than
2186	relying on a machine's or exercise's marketed "prime mover" label. Particularly relevant
2187	when evaluating whether an exercise adequately trains stabilizer demand, not just the
2188	visible moving joint.
2189	
2190	**When NOT to apply** — The authors explicitly flag this three-step process itself as
2191	still incomplete (it can reinforce the six listed misconceptions if applied mechanically);
2192	do not treat it as a complete biomechanical model, only as an improvement on prime-mover-only
2193	analysis. Confidence capped at `supported`: this is the authors' recommended process, not an
2194	outcome-tested comparison of exercise-selection methods.
2195	
2196	**Example** — Inference: evaluating a leg-press machine by asking only "what does it move"
2197	(knee and hip extension) would miss that trunk and hip stabilizers are working hard
2198	throughout, even though they do not visibly move; the three-step process asks explicitly
2199	which joints are stabilized as well as which are moved.
2200	
2201	**Related** — [[claim--multiarticular-muscle-action-cannot-be-predicted-from-joints-spanned]],
2202	[[framework--movement-matrix-system-for-multiarticular-exercise-selection]].

# A Flexible, Well-Conditioned Joint Can Still Have Limited Functional ROM From Spurious Muscle Tension

**What it is** — The authors state that limitations in functional ROM should not
automatically be attributed to joint stiffness alone, since this can lead to an
unnecessary emphasis on stretching. Limitations to full ROM can also be caused by "spurious
tension" or excessive, non-functional muscle tension such as coordination tension, which
may accompany the appropriate tension a given movement requires; this non-functional
tension can occur in both phasic and tonic muscles, before, during, or after the movement.
Athlete proficiency level has a marked influence on the reflex ability of muscles to
contract and relax: rapidity of both contraction and relaxation increases with mastery,
with a decrease in relaxation time being especially evident (Fig 3.35, data from Matveyev,
1981, measured by EMG across five qualification levels from novice to Master of Sport,
showing relaxation time dropping from about 0.4s at Level 1 to about 0.22s at Level 5,
converging with contraction time). The authors conclude it is of little consequence to have
highly flexible joints with well-conditioned, supple connective tissue if action is limited
by spurious muscle tension instead; flexibility training should therefore always be
combined with neuromuscular training aimed at efficient, functional ROM, not tissue
stretching alone. (PDF pp. 199-200, printed pp. 187-188, Fig 3.35.)

**Why it works** — The authors give no separate mechanism for why proficiency specifically
speeds relaxation more than contraction; the Matveyev (1981) EMG data are reported as the
empirical basis for the mastery-relaxation relationship, without further explanation.

**When to apply** — When an athlete presents with apparently limited functional ROM in a
sport movement despite passing a passive flexibility screen, consider spurious/coordination
tension and relaxation ability as an alternative or additional target, rather than
defaulting to more stretching.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence capped at `supported`: the Fig 3.35 data are a single
cited source (Matveyev, 1981) with an unspecified sample, and the five qualification
levels (novice through Master of Sport) are specific to that source's population, not
necessarily transferable as normative relaxation-time targets for a Baylor roster.** Do not
use this claim to dismiss a genuine tissue-flexibility deficit; the authors frame this as an
additional cause of limited ROM, not a replacement for checking tissue-level flexibility.

**Example** — The book's own example, via Fig 3.35: a novice athlete's slower reflex
relaxation (about 0.4s) compared to a Master of Sport's faster relaxation (about 0.22s) at
the same level of tissue flexibility illustrates that training age/mastery, not just
tissue conditioning, changes how quickly non-functional tension clears during a movement.

**Related** — [[framework--methods-for-improving-voluntary-muscle-relaxation]],
[[heuristic--reflex-based-techniques-for-flexibility-training]].

# Ten Ways Coaches Can Train an Athlete's Ability to Relax Muscles on Demand

**What it is** — Following the claim that spurious muscle tension, not just tissue
stiffness, can limit functional ROM (see
[[claim--spurious-muscle-tension-limits-rom-independent-of-tissue-flexibility]]), the
authors list methods for improving the ability to relax muscles: (1) contract-relax,
hold-relax, and other PNF methods using stretch reflexes to promote relaxation; (2) sudden
unloading, the abrupt removal of external resistance under strong isometric or dynamic
conditions (e.g. the end of a jerk, completion of a heavy squat/bench press, releasing a
thrown shot or medicine ball, short bursts of strong electromuscular contraction), reported
as producing the greatest relaxation response of all listed means, and becoming more
effective the more closely the contraction-relaxation process is tied to the actual
sporting action; (3) changing muscle groups from tension to relaxation in a controlled,
gradual manner or through a series of stages (e.g. Jacobsen's progressive relaxation
method); (4) controlling spurious tension in the face and hands specifically, since these
tend to reflect general body tension well; (5) controlled visualization of muscles
progressing from contraction to relaxation and back; (6) autogenic training, progressive
relaxation, meditation, or massage; (7) breathing pattern control, on the basis that
tension is associated with inhalation and breath-holding (the Valsalva manoeuvre, used
where maximal force and spinal stabilization are needed) while relaxation is associated
with gentle, controlled exhalation; appropriate breathing should be combined with all
phases of movement to enhance mobility, stability, and relaxation; (8) the "pre-exhaustion
principle," exercising against a background of exhaustion of selected muscle groups
(common in bodybuilding) to increase stress on chosen groups, provided movement technique
does not suffer; (9) distracting or focusing activities that direct attention away from
stimuli tied to the sporting action (music, conversation with a training partner, pleasant
thoughts), which may work through internal or external focus depending on the individual;
(10) gentle rhythmic, cyclical, swinging, shaking, or circling movements of the body and
limbs to relax muscles just strongly contracted (as in some dance, swimming, or Tai Chi
movements). (PDF pp. 200-201, printed pp. 187-188.)

**Why it works** — The authors state method 2 (sudden unloading) produces the greatest
relaxation response "of all the means currently used," without giving the underlying
mechanism in this passage; the other methods are listed without comparative effectiveness
data or a stated mechanism beyond their general description.

**When to apply** — Use this list as a menu when an athlete needs targeted work on
reflexive muscle relaxation rather than (or alongside) tissue stretching: sudden-unloading
drills tied closely to the actual sport action are named as the single most effective
listed method, so pairing method 2 with the specific sporting movement (rather than a
generic drill) is the book's own emphasis.

**When NOT to apply** — No dosage, frequency, or measured outcome data are given for any
of the ten methods in this passage; treat this as a menu of techniques the authors report
as used in practice, not a validated, ranked protocol (apart from the single stated
observation that method 2 is most effective). Confidence is capped at `supported`.

**Example** — The book's own example: the abrupt release of tension at the top of a jerk,
or immediately after a heavy squat or bench press rep, is offered as a sudden-unloading
relaxation drill that is more effective the more closely it mirrors the athlete's actual
competitive movement (printed 187).

**Related** — [[claim--spurious-muscle-tension-limits-rom-independent-of-tissue-flexibility]],
[[heuristic--reflex-based-techniques-for-flexibility-training]].

# The Stretching Matrix: Any Stretch Is the Reverse of the Action That Contracts the Same Muscle Group

**What it is** — The authors present a generalized system, built from standard muscle
action charts, for devising a stretch for any major muscle group: "the reverse of any
action to contract a given muscle group becomes a stretch for that same muscle group." A
series of matrices (Figs 3.36-3.40, in this excerpt covering trunk/neck, upper arm,
forearm, lower extremity, and foot) list each muscle against the joint actions that stretch
it. The system requires identifying which joints a given muscle crosses before deciding how
to stretch it, since a muscle's action, and therefore its stretch, can differ depending on
which joint's chart is consulted; using only one matrix for a biarticular or multiarticular
muscle can produce a less-than-maximal stretch. The authors' worked example: psoas (as part
of iliopsoas) is stretched by hip extension and medial rotation per the lower-extremity
matrix, but as a trunk muscle it is also stretched by combined trunk extension and lateral
extension per the trunk/neck matrix; a fencer's front lunge maximally stretches iliacus
(hip extension alone) but will not maximally stretch psoas unless the trunk is also
extended and laterally flexed toward the leading leg. A second worked example: the oblique
muscles and quadratus lumborum both perform lateral trunk flexion, but only the obliques
also rotate the trunk and only quadratus lumborum extends it, so only concurrent trunk
flexion plus lateral extension maximally stretches quadratus lumborum, while flexion plus
lateral extension plus rotation is needed to maximally stretch the obliques. (PDF pp.
199-202, printed pp. 188-191, Figs 3.36-3.39.)

**Why it works** — The mechanism is definitional, not empirical: if muscle contraction
produces a given joint action, moving the joint through the opposite action necessarily
lengthens (stretches) that muscle, following directly from standard functional anatomy
rather than a cited study.

**When to apply** — Use the matrices to design a novel stretch for any muscle by first
identifying every joint and degree of freedom the muscle crosses (via multiple figures if
needed), then combining the reverse actions simultaneously rather than one at a time, to
achieve a maximal stretch. Useful for building or auditing a stretching routine's actual
target versus its intended target.

**When NOT to apply** — This is an anatomical design method, not an outcome-tested
training system; the book does not report ROM-gain or performance data from using this
matrix approach specifically. Confidence is capped at `supported` because it is a
logically-derived tool, not itself an empirical claim. Do not assume a single-joint stretch
fully stretches a muscle that crosses multiple joints; the authors are explicit this is the
main pitfall the matrices are meant to prevent.

**Example** — The book's own example: to stretch biceps brachii (which crosses both
elbow and shoulder), the elbow must be extended and the shoulder extended and abducted with
the forearm pronated simultaneously (per Figs 3.37-3.38); consulting only the forearm
matrix (elbow extension alone) would under-stretch the muscle (printed 189).

**Related** — [[framework--movement-matrix-system-for-multiarticular-exercise-selection]].
######## [32] heuristic--dedicated-stretching-may-be-unnecessary-with-progressive-movement-preparation.md
---
type: library-entry
kind: heuristic
domain: strength-and-conditioning
book: supertraining--verkhoshansky

topic: alternative to dedicated stretching sessions
category: [flexibility, warm-up, programming]
confidence: untested
ingest-tier: full-text
created: 2026-09-27
