# A Sport's Own Movements, Progressively Loaded, Can Replace a Dedicated Stretching Session

**What it is** — The authors call it "possibly the most heretical remark to make about
stretching" that dedicated stretching sessions may not even be necessary, noting many
athletes dispense entirely with special stretching or even warm-up sessions without
suffering injury in training or competition; the prescription of stretching and warm-up
or cool-down has become "a well-accepted ritual," which the authors state does not by
itself make it essential. They propose a "principle of gradual progressive stretching and
activity increase": the athlete begins each movement gently and non-ballistically under
limited static and dynamic conditions, then progressively increases range, speed,
complexity, intensity and other aspects of movement until the actual sporting movements
themselves are performed under light and eventually near-competitive conditions. In weight
training, the same principle is applied by beginning every exercise with a few preparatory
repetitions at a light load, progressively increasing the load over a few sets, and using a
narrower-than-normal grip or stance early in the progression (e.g. bench press, squat) to
reduce range/speed of movement and tissue/joint stress at the start. The authors' concluding
position: it is unnecessary to devise many highly specific individual flexibility drills
for the whole body, since this would be time-consuming and inefficient; functional
movements already used in the sport, combined with the stretching techniques discussed
earlier, can replace a prolonged session of dozens of single-joint stretches, provided the
routine still increases both passive/static ROM and functional flexibility-strength for all
static, dynamic, and necessary ballistic joint actions. (PDF pp. 203-204, printed pp.
192-193.)

**Why it works** — The authors give no controlled comparison (stretching vs. no
stretching, or dedicated-stretch vs. movement-based warm-up) for injury or performance
outcomes in this passage; the claim rests on informal observation ("many athletes dispense
entirely...without suffering injury") rather than a cited study.

**When to apply** — Where session time is limited, consider replacing a block of isolated,
single-joint stretches with a progressively loaded, sport-specific movement warm-up
(narrow-grip/stance light sets building toward working load and range), on the premise
that this can achieve the same flexibility-preparation goal more efficiently, provided full
ROM and the necessary joint actions for that sport are actually included.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence `untested`: no controlled outcome data given in this
passage.** Do not use this as a blanket argument against ever including dedicated
flexibility work; the authors' own surrounding sections (see
[[framework--four-methods-of-enhancing-rom-ranked-by-effectiveness]]) state that durable,
long-term ROM change requires a specific, regularly repeated conditioning component, which
a purely movement-based warm-up may not supply for an athlete with a genuine long-term ROM
deficit in a specific joint.

**Example** — The book's own example: beginning a bench press session with a narrower
grip and lighter load, then progressively widening/loading toward the working set, applies
this principle by using the exercise itself (rather than a separate stretch) to prepare the
shoulder joint's ROM and tissue tolerance (printed 192).

**Related** — [[framework--four-methods-of-enhancing-rom-ranked-by-effectiveness]],
[[framework--stretching-matrix-system-reverse-of-contraction-action]].
######## [33] claim--multiarticular-muscle-action-cannot-be-predicted-from-joints-spanned.md
---
type: library-entry
kind: claim
domain: strength-and-conditioning
book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
chapter: "3.7"
topic: limits of standard anatomical muscle-action analysis
category: [biomechanics, exercise-selection, contested]
confidence: supported
ingest-tier: full-text
created: 2026-09-27
---

# A Muscle's Anatomical "Flexor/Extensor" Label Does Not Reliably Predict What It Actually Accelerates

**What it is** — The authors report that classical functional anatomy, which labels a
muscle as a flexor or extensor of a joint it crosses based on the torque it produces about
that single joint, has been challenged by biomechanical analysis of multi-articular joint
actions (Zajac & Gordon, 1989). Because the body is a linked system of joints, muscles that
do not even span a given joint can still produce acceleration about it, and the actions of
individual joints do not simply superimpose linearly in a multi-joint movement (no simple
relationship holds between velocity, angle, and torque about a single joint in a complex
movement). Zajac and Gordon argue it is more accurate to say "muscle X accelerates joint A
into flexion" than "muscle X flexes joint A." Their worked example: soleus, an ankle-only
muscle usually labelled an ankle extensor, accelerates the knee (which it does not span)
into extension up to about twice as much as it accelerates the ankle (which it does span)
into extension, near upright standing posture (Fig 3.47). Separately, work derived from
Lombard's Paradox ("antagonist muscles can act in the same contraction mode as their
agonists") found the rectus femoris and hamstrings act in three different ways during
cycling (Andrews, 1985, 1987), since in actions like cycling and squatting the quadriceps
and hamstrings can both contract concentrically at the same time despite being classically
regarded as opposing muscles. A muscle capable of several different joint actions does not
necessarily perform all of them in every movement: gluteus maximus, which can extend and
abduct the hip, does not necessarily accelerate the hip into both simultaneously, and its
extensor torque may even accelerate the hip into adduction instead (Andrews, 1982, 1985;
Mansour & Pereira, 1987). Gastrocnemius, usually described simply as a knee flexor and
ankle extensor, can in fact perform three different combined actions depending on knee
angle (Fig 3.48): flex the knee and extend the ankle, flex the knee and flex the ankle, or
extend the knee and extend the ankle. (PDF pp. 210-211, printed pp. 199-200, Figs 3.47-3.48.)

**Why it works** — The mechanism is the linked, non-linear dynamics of a multi-joint
skeletal system (induced-acceleration analysis, per Zajac & Gordon, 1989): because segments
are connected, a force applied by a muscle at one joint propagates through the chain and can
accelerate a joint that muscle does not cross, and the net effect at any joint depends on
the whole system's configuration (joint angles) at that instant, not on the muscle's
anatomical classification alone.

**When to apply** — Use this to caution against selecting or excluding an exercise based
solely on a muscle's textbook flexor/extensor label; the authors argue, following Zajac and
Gordon, that it is more useful to examine muscle action in terms of synergism (how muscles
work together across the whole kinetic chain) than in terms of isolated agonism/antagonism
(Basmajian, 1978, as cited by Zajac & Gordon), since a generalized approach that reduces
movement to single-joint actions fails to capture that muscle action is task-dependent.

**When NOT to apply** — Confidence is `supported`: the cited induced-acceleration analysis
method (Zajac & Gordon, 1989) is a well-established biomechanical modeling approach, but
this entry reports the book's specific worked examples (soleus/knee, gluteus
maximus/adduction, gastrocnemius's three actions) as given, without independently
re-deriving them; treat the specific numeric ratios (e.g. "twice as much") as reported by
the cited source rather than independently verified here. Do not use this claim to argue
anatomical muscle-action charts are useless; the authors use those same charts elsewhere
(see [[framework--movement-matrix-system-for-multiarticular-exercise-selection]]) as a
starting point, with this entry as the stated caveat on their limits for complex,
multi-joint movement.

**Example** — The book's own example: during a standing overhead press that used to be
part Olympic Weightlifting, the trunk's back-bending action is caused not only by a
Newton's-third-law reaction to the overhead press but also by the triceps (which crosses
both elbow and shoulder) accelerating the trunk backward as it extends the elbow, an effect
counteracted by rectus abdominis (trunk flexion) and the hip flexors (hip extension)
(printed 200).

**Related** — [[framework--movement-matrix-system-for-multiarticular-exercise-selection]],
[[heuristic--identify-moved-stabilized-and-both-joints-before-selecting-exercises]].
######## [34] claim--spinal-ligaments-share-load-with-erector-spinae-in-heavy-pulls.md

type: library-entry

confidence: untested

# Spinal Ligaments Share Load With the Erector Spinae During Heavy Pulls From the Ground

**What it is** — The authors state spinal ligament involvement during deadlifting or
cleans is valuable for reducing the stress placed on the erector spinae, and that spinal
flexion during heavy lifts from the ground can damage intervertebral discs; a competent
lifter actively increases erector spinae tension to diminish flattening of the lumbar spine
during the lift. If this active tension is overdone, the spinal ligaments become slack and
most of the load is instead borne by the muscles; conversely, if the muscles are
inadequately contracted, excessive stress is placed on the ligaments. The authors describe
a skilled lifter as one able to optimize the balance between spinal muscles and ligaments,
enhancing lifting efficiency and reducing injury likelihood; they state similar rhythms and
patterns of muscular and other soft-tissue involvement are essential for strength-training
efficiency and safety generally. (PDF p. 209, printed pp. 198-199.)

**Why it works** — The authors give no cited source or measured data for this specific
muscle-ligament load-sharing claim in this passage; it follows logically from the joint
stabilization sequence described elsewhere in the chapter (muscle/SEC as primary
stabilizer, ligament/PEC engaging as muscular contribution changes; see
[[framework--joint-stabilization-sequence-across-range-of-motion]]), applied here
specifically to the lumbar spine during a pull, but is not derived from a named study.

**When to apply** — Useful as a coaching frame for cueing lumbar position during heavy
deadlifts and cleans: the goal is neither maximal erector spinae tension (which the text
says can make ligaments too slack to share load appropriately) nor minimal tension
(overloading the ligaments and discs), but an actively maintained, non-flexed lumbar
position that keeps both tissues sharing the load as intended.

**When NOT to apply** — **Confidence `untested`: no citation or measured data given for
this specific claim in this passage.** Do not present this as an established biomechanical
finding to Athletic Medicine or in athlete-facing injury-risk communication without
independent verification; it is the authors' own technique-coaching synthesis. This entry
is about muscle-ligament load *sharing*, distinct from the moment-arm/torque-reduction
principle already in this library (see
[[principle--torque-optimization-in-lifting-technique]]), which addresses keeping the bar
path close to the body rather than the muscle-versus-ligament balance at the lumbar spine
itself.

**Example** — Inference: a lifter who rounds the lower back on a heavy deadlift (excess
lumbar flexion, per this claim, meaning inadequately contracted erector spinae) shifts more
stress onto the spinal ligaments and discs than a lifter who maintains a neutral,
actively-braced lumbar spine throughout the pull.

**Related** — [[framework--joint-stabilization-sequence-across-range-of-motion]],
[[principle--torque-optimization-in-lifting-technique]].

type: library-entry

# The Movement Matrix System: Reading Off Muscles From a Joint Action, or Actions From a Muscle

**What it is** — The authors present a companion series of Movement Matrices (Figs 3.41-3.46
in this excerpt: lower extremity, foot, shoulder, arm/humerus, forearm, trunk and neck) that
can be read two ways: to find the muscles corresponding to a given joint action, or to find
the actions produced by a given muscle group. The authors state these are needed whenever a
reader wants to analyse or devise exercises, and that it is often necessary to apply more
than one Movement Matrix simultaneously, because some muscles cross more than one joint.
Their worked examples: gastrocnemius crosses both the knee and ankle, so Figs 3.41 and 3.42
(lower extremity, foot) must both be consulted to determine whether a single-joint or a
combined multi-joint exercise is more appropriate for a given goal; biceps brachii crosses
the elbow and shoulder, so maximal training of biceps requires extending both joints from a
position of full pre-stretch to full flexion at the end position (Figs 3.43-3.44). This
dual-joint action of gastrocnemius (knee flexion plus ankle plantarflexion together) occurs
naturally during the double-knee-bend (scoop) phase of the weightlifting clean, or in
"glute-ham-gastroc raises," a modified prone hyperextension over a pommel horse with the
feet pressed against a vertical plate (Yessis, 1992). (PDF pp. 204-208, printed pp. 193-197,
Figs 3.41-3.46.)

**Why it works** — As with the Stretching Matrix, this is a definitional reading of
standard functional-anatomy relationships (which muscles produce which joint actions), not
an empirical finding with its own separate mechanism.

**When to apply** — Use the paired-matrix approach when selecting or designing an exercise
for a multiarticular muscle: check every matrix the target muscle appears in before
concluding a single-joint exercise trains it fully, and consider whether a combined,
multi-joint version (like the clean's double-knee bend, for gastrocnemius) better matches
the muscle's natural dual action than an isolated single-joint exercise would.

**When NOT to apply** — This is a reference and design tool built from standard anatomical
muscle-action data, not a validated training-outcome comparison between single-joint and
multi-joint exercise selection; the book does not report performance or hypertrophy data
comparing the two approaches here. See also
[[claim--multiarticular-muscle-action-cannot-be-predicted-from-joints-spanned]] for the
authors' own caution that even this matrix approach is an incomplete model of real
multiarticular muscle function.

**Example** — The book's own example: because gastrocnemius flexes the knee and
plantarflexes the ankle, the glute-ham-gastroc raise (a modified prone hyperextension with
feet braced) trains both actions together, unlike a standing calf raise (ankle only) or a
leg curl (knee only) performed in isolation (printed 193).

**Related** — [[framework--stretching-matrix-system-reverse-of-contraction-action]],
[[heuristic--identify-moved-stabilized-and-both-joints-before-selecting-exercises]].
######## [36] heuristic--identify-moved-stabilized-and-both-joints-before-selecting-exercises.md
---
type: library-entry
kind: heuristic
domain: strength-and-conditioning
book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
chapter: "3.7"
topic: joint-action analysis process for exercise selection
category: [exercise-selection, biomechanics, coaching-process]
confidence: supported
ingest-tier: full-text
created: 2026-09-27
---

# Before Picking an Exercise: Identify Which Joints Are Moved, Which Are Stabilized, and Which Are Both

**What it is** — The authors argue it is preferable to think in terms of joint actions,
rather than muscle actions, when analysing which muscles are involved in a movement or
trained by a specific machine. They criticize the popular practice (common in weight-training
and bodybuilding publications) of identifying only the "prime movers" as a partial and
misleading view, since stabilizing muscles may be contracting far more vigorously than the
movers during some exercises, and there is no situation in which stabilizers are not also
contracting while the movers carry out their dynamic role. The recommended process for
analysing any movement is to identify: (1) which joints are being moved; (2) which joints
are being stabilized; and (3) which joints are being stabilized and moved concurrently. Only
after this should the relevant muscles for moving and stabilizing tasks be determined via
the Movement Matrices. The authors add that even this three-step process gives an
incomplete mechanical picture, because it can still reinforce several inaccurate popular
assumptions: that the same movement is always produced by the same muscles; that the same
muscles always produce the same movement; that the same muscles are dominant throughout the
full ROM; that muscles only act as active tissues; that muscles only act as movers or
stabilizers; and that muscles are the only important tissues controlling movement. (PDF pp.
206-207, printed pp. 195-196.)

**Why it works** — Inference: this follows directly from the book's broader point that
muscle action is task- and configuration-dependent (see
[[claim--multiarticular-muscle-action-cannot-be-predicted-from-joints-spanned]]); a
prime-mover-only analysis assumes a fixed muscle-to-movement mapping that the authors argue
does not hold across a joint's full range or across different tasks.

**When to apply** — Use this three-step process (moved / stabilized / both) before
selecting an exercise meant to train or rehabilitate a specific joint action, rather than
relying on a machine's or exercise's marketed "prime mover" label. Particularly relevant
when evaluating whether an exercise adequately trains stabilizer demand, not just the
visible moving joint.

**When NOT to apply** — The authors explicitly flag this three-step process itself as
still incomplete (it can reinforce the six listed misconceptions if applied mechanically);
do not treat it as a complete biomechanical model, only as an improvement on prime-mover-only
analysis. Confidence capped at `supported`: this is the authors' recommended process, not an
outcome-tested comparison of exercise-selection methods.

**Example** — Inference: evaluating a leg-press machine by asking only "what does it move"
(knee and hip extension) would miss that trunk and hip stabilizers are working hard
throughout, even though they do not visibly move; the three-step process asks explicitly
which joints are stabilized as well as which are moved.

**Related** — [[claim--multiarticular-muscle-action-cannot-be-predicted-from-joints-spanned]],
[[framework--movement-matrix-system-for-multiarticular-exercise-selection]].

13:tags: ["post-exercise-recovery", "doms", "perceived-fatigue", "meta-analysis", "massage", "water-immersion"]
22:> Dupuy, O., Douzi, W., Theurot, D., Bosquet, L., & Dugué, B. (2018). An evidence-based approach for choosing post-exercise recovery techniques to reduce markers of muscle damage, soreness, fatigue, and inflammation: A systematic review with meta-analysis. *Frontiers in Physiology, 9*, 403. http
26:This review informs selection of post-exercise recovery modalities when the immediate goals are reducing soreness, perceived fatigue, muscle-damage markers, or inflammation.
30:How do commonly used post-exercise recovery techniques compare for delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS), perceived fatigue, muscle-damage markers, and inflammatory markers?
34:- Participants: Healthy adults aged 18 to under 65 across 99 eligible studies; 1,188 participants contributed to the DOMS analysis and 266 to perceived fatigue.
35:- Sport and level: Competitive athletes, recreational athletes, and inactive adults across varied exercise models.
42:- Exposure or intervention: Active recovery, stretching, massage, compression garments, electrostimulation, immersion, contrast water therapy, cryotherapy, and hyperbaric therapy.
44:- Measurements and outcomes: DOMS, perceived fatigue, creatine kinase, C-reactive protein, and interleukin-6.
47:## Key findings
49:- Across modalities, recovery interventions reduced DOMS (SMD -0.78, 95% CI -0.94 to -0.61; I² 56.62%) and perceived fatigue (SMD -1.40, 95% CI -1.92 to -0.89; I² 33%). [p. 4]
50:- Active recovery, massage, compression garments, immersion, contrast water therapy, and cryotherapy produced small-to-large reductions in DOMS (Hedges' g range -2.26 to -0.40), whereas the other reviewed methods did not. [p. 5]
52:- Stretching and electrostimulation did not significantly improve DOMS or fatigue in the pooled analyses. [p. 11]
59:- Performance recovery was not evaluated, repeated use and combined modalities were excluded, and changes in soreness or biomarkers should not be assumed to equal restored performance. [pp. 11-12]
64:Massage, compression garments, and water immersion are reasonable options when short-term soreness or perceived fatigue is the target, but the expected benefit is outcome-specific. Recovery decisions should be individualized and should not substitute subjective recovery changes or biomarker chang
=== strength-and-conditioning/fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer/heuristic--passive-vs-active-rom-decision-rule-sprint.md
7:topic: passive vs active ROM
14:# The Passive-vs-Active Range Rule: What the Gap Tells You to Train
16:**What it is** — Moyer's triage rule for any sprint fault that could have a range-of-motion cause. Test the relevant joint **passively** (you move it) and **actively** (the athlete moves it under their own muscle), then branch:
17:1. **Passive range is lacking** → address the range first (loaded stretches, "time and/or tension"). "First and foremost, they have to have passive. That's number one."
18:2. **Passive range is adequate but active falls short** (you can lift the thigh high; they cannot) → the gap "should be filled with specific strength exercises": **strength in that range** (PAILs/RAILs, isometrics at end range, special strength exercises).
20:The goal is to make passive and active "as close to each other as possible — it's never going to be a perfect one to one."
22:**Why it works** — Passive range tells you whether the tissue and joint *allow* the position. Active range tells you whether the athlete can *produce and control* it. A sprint needs the active version at speed. A drill cannot give range the tissue does not have, and stretching cannot give contr
24:**When to apply** — Before prescribing any sprint corrective for projection (hip extension, ankle, big toe), switching (hamstring at the knee and hip flexion for a long lever), or toe-off (dorsiflexion, plantar flexion, tibial rotation). In RTP, it gives a clean hand-off: the athletic trainer o
26:**When NOT to apply** — Reactivity/stiffness faults are usually not range problems. Moyer himself says range "isn't usually going to be a problem" there; it is a strength-quality issue. Range measured on a table is slow and unloaded, so adequate numbers do not guarantee the range is available a
28:**Example** — A safety cannot fold his swing leg. Prone passive knee flexion: heel to butt, fine. Active: heel stops a hand-span short. That is branch 2, so he gets hamstring PAILs/RAILs and GHR variations, not more butt-kick drills and not more stretching.
=== strength-and-conditioning/fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer/heuristic--pails-rails-close-active-passive-gap-sprint.md
14:# PAILs/RAILs to Close the Active–Passive Gap (Hamstring, Dorsiflexion)
16:**What it is** — Moyer's main tool for branch 2 of the range rule (passive range present, active range short). It is borrowed from FRC/FRS, which he names as his bias. His framing: range improves with **"time and/or tension."**
17:- **PAILs** (progressive angular isometric loading): at end range, the athlete contracts *into* the stretch. Hamstring version: lying with the leg raised, drive the foot down into a yoga block with the quads "like you're trying to break the block." Moyer's description of the muscles is garbled, b
18:- **RAILs** (regressive angular isometric loading): the athlete then uses the *opposite* muscles to pull further into range. Hamstring version: actively lift the foot with the hamstrings to close the gap. "This is where the cramps come." Athletes "cheat like a son of a bitch."
21:- **Also used:** loaded stretches (single-leg standing and seated calf raises through full range; a seated cable-row "sit and reach" with heels driven in and feet actively dorsiflexed), a plantar-flexion stretch held for time, and PAILs/RAILs on it "if they're gluttons for punishment." Used for t

# Stretching to prevent or reduce muscle soreness after exercise
### Also available in
#### Related content
###### Search strategy
We searched the Cochrane Bone, Joint and Muscle Trauma Group Specialised Register (to 10 August 2009), the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (2010, Issue 1), MEDLINE (1966 to 8th February 2010), EMBASE (1988 to 8th February 2010), CINAHL (1982 to 23rd February 2010), SPORTDiscus (1949 to 8th February 2010), PEDro (to 15th February 2010) and reference lists of articles.

###### Selection criteria
Eligible studies were randomised or quasi-randomised studies of any pre-exercise or post-exercise stretching technique designed to prevent or treat delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS). For the studies to be included, the stretching had to be conducted soon before or soon after exercise and muscle soreness had to be assessed.

###### Data collection and analysis
Risk of bias was assessed using The Cochrane Collaboration's 'Risk of bias' tool and quality of evidence was assessed using GRADE. Estimates of effects of stretching were converted to a common 100-point scale. Outcomes were pooled in fixed-effect meta-analyses.

###### Main results
Twelve studies were included in the review. This update incorporated two new studies. One of the new trials was a large field-based trial that included 2377 participants, 1220 of whom were allocated stretching. All other 11 studies were small, with between 10 and 30 participants receiving the stretch condition. Ten studies were laboratory-based and other two were field-based. All studies were exposed to either a moderate or high risk of bias. The quality of evidence was low to moderate.

There was a high degree of consistency of results across studies. The pooled estimate showed that pre-exercise stretching reduced soreness at one day after exercise by, on average, half a point on a 100-point scale (mean difference -0.52, 95% CI -11.30 to 10.26; 3 studies). Post-exercise stretching reduced soreness at one day after exercise by, on average, one point on a 100-point scale (mean difference -1.04, 95% CI -6.88 to 4.79; 4 studies). Similar effects were evident between half a day and three days after exercise. One large study showed that stretching before and after exercise reduced peak soreness over a one week period by, on average, four points on a 100-point scale (mean difference -3.80, 95% CI -5.17 to -2.43). This effect, though statistically significant, is very small.

###### Citation
Herbert RD, de Noronha M, Kamper SJ. Stretching to prevent or reduce muscle soreness after exercise. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews 2022, Issue 4. Art. No.: CD004577. DOI: 10.1002/14651858. CD004577.pub3.

## Abstract
**Background:**

Many people stretch before or after (or both) engaging in athletic activity. Usually the purpose is to reduce risk of injury, reduce soreness after exercise, or enhance athletic performance.

**Objectives:**

The aim of this review was to determine effects of stretching before or after exercise on the development of post-exercise muscle soreness.

**Search strategy:**

**Selection criteria:**

Eligible studies were randomised or quasi-randomised studies of any pre-or post-exercise stretching technique designed to prevent or treat delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS), provided the stretching was conducted soon before or soon after exercise. Methodological quality of the studies was assessed using the Cochrane Bone, Joint and Muscle Trauma Group's methodological quality assessment tool. Estimates of effects of stretching were converted to a common 100-point scale. Outcomes were pooled in a fixed-effect meta-analysis.

**Main results:**

Of the 10 included studies, nine were carried out in laboratory settings using standardised exercise protocols and one involved post-exercise stretching in footballers. All participants were young healthy adults. Three studies examined the effects of stretching before exercise and seven studies investigated the effects of stretching after exercise. Two studies, both of stretching after exercise, involved repeated stretching sessions at intervals of greater than two hours. The duration of stretching applied in a single session ranged from 40 to 600 seconds. All studies were small (between 10 and 30 participants received the stretch condition) and of questionable quality. The effects of stretching reported in individual studies were very small and there was a high degree of consistency of results across studies. The pooled estimate showed that pre-exercise stretching reduced soreness one day after exercise by, on average, 0.5 points on a 100-point scale (95% CI -11.3 to 10.3; 3 studies). Post-exercise stretching reduced soreness one day after exercise by, on average, 1.0 points on a 100-point scale (95% CI -6.9 to 4.8; 4 studies). Similar effects were evident between half a day and three days after exercise.

**Authors' conclusions:**

The evidence derived from mainly laboratory-based studies of stretching indicate that muscle stretching does not reduce delayed-onset muscle soreness in young healthy adults.

**Search strategy:**

**Selection criteria:**

Eligible studies were randomised or quasi-randomised studies of any pre-or post-exercise stretching technique designed to prevent or treat delayed-onset muscle soreness (DOMS), provided the stretching was conducted soon before or soon after exercise. To be eligible studies must have assessed muscle soreness or tenderness.

**Data collection and analysis:**

Methodological quality of the studies was assessed using the Cochrane Bone, Joint and Muscle Trauma Group's methodological quality assessment tool. Estimates of effects of stretching were converted to a common 100-point scale. Outcomes were pooled in a fixed-effect meta-analysis.

**Main results:**

Of the 10 included studies, nine were carried out in laboratory settings using standardised exercise protocols and one involved post-exercise stretching in footballers. All participants were young healthy adults. Three studies examined the effects of stretching before exercise and seven studies investigated the effects of stretching after exercise. Two studies, both of stretching after exercise, involved repeated stretching sessions at intervals of greater than two hours. The duration of stretching applied in a single session ranged from 40 to 600 seconds. All studies were small (between 10 and 30 participants received the stretch condition) and of questionable quality. The effects of stretching reported in individual studies were very small and there was a high degree of consistency of results across studies. The pooled estimate showed that pre-exercise stretching reduced soreness one day after exercise by, on average, 0.5 points on a 100-point scale (95% CI -11.3 to 10.3; 3 studies). Post-exercise stretching reduced soreness one day after exercise by, on average, 1.0 points on a 100-point scale (95% CI -6.9 to 4.8; 4 studies). Similar effects were evident between half a day and three days after exercise.

**Authors' conclusions:**

The evidence derived from mainly laboratory-based studies of stretching indicate that muscle stretching does not reduce delayed-onset muscle soreness in young healthy adults.

10:- **Course slide decks (Week 1, Week 3, Class 4)**: co-branded to Ruf/Rash/Wenger on every title slide. Per `spring-2026-teaching.md`, Eric was the assigned instructor for the Feb. 5 and Feb. 12 sessions (Week 3 Lecture and Class 4 2026 respectively), so bullets from those two decks are marked **Explicit**. Week 1 (Jan. 22, "All") and Class 8/Lesson 8 (Mar. 19, Wenger's session) are marked **Inferred** — shared team material, not confirmed as Eric's individual position.
11:[Omitted long matching line]
26:- "Inconsistent data from a good test is still bad data" — a test's validity doesn't rescue it if it can't be collected consistently at scale. **Explicit** [2026-02-20-sportsmith-6otb-nordbord-er.md]
27:- Reject ownership language ("my team," "my athletes"): the athlete's development is shared across every department that touches them, not owned by any one coach. **Inferred (transcript, speaker unconfirmed)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.5, "we got to get away from like the me and my"]
28:- Injury risk can be reduced, not eliminated, through sound programming, progression, and collaboration with Athletic Medicine — an explicit refusal to promise injury prevention. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.4]
31:- "Knowledge from experience" as a stated operating value: safety first, keep things simple, teach basic movement skills and basic lifts before anything advanced, treat strength as the base, and require bodyweight competency before loaded work. **Inferred (transcript + Week 1 slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.4-5; week1-lecture.md p.12]
44:- Assessment is continuous, not a single test day: start with movement quality, injury history, and training background, then observe daily via warm-ups and practice. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.4-5]
48:- Preparedness (the athlete's underlying physical capability, built over a long period) is explicitly distinguished from readiness (day-to-day fluctuation) — both are tracked, but they answer different questions. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md p.7]
55:## Force plate and neuromuscular monitoring
58:- Modified reactive strength index (mRSI) from daily CMJ testing was deliberately chosen as the daily athlete-readiness marker in place of subjective wellness questionnaires, because it is "objective, consistent, and actionable in a way the wellness surveys never quite were." **Explicit** [2026-02-19-sportsmith-6otb-er.md]
76:- Split times are interpreted by physical quality, not just total time: 0-10m is read as an acceleration score (reflecting maximal strength/power/slow stretch-shortening-cycle development), 30-40m as a speed score (reflecting sprint-specific/fast stretch-shortening-cycle development), and 40m peak velocity is derived from the 30-40m split divided by 10. **Inferred (author uncertain)** [ap-assessment-manual-draft-v12.md]
83:- Exercise selection is organized on a spectrum from general preparation through specific preparation, specific development, to competitive exercises (Bondarchuk), replacing the loose and often-misapplied idea of "sport specific." **Inferred (transcript + slides)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.13-16; week1-lecture.md pp.32-36]
101:- "Everything we do is some form of conditioning": lifting, agility work, and skill drills each load a specific energy system (power vs. capacity, alactic/glycolytic/aerobic) and should be classified and counted as conditioning, not treated as separate from it. **Explicit** [class-4-2026.md p.31, tables pp.35-42]
129:- Performance Nutrition is explicitly a separate Health & Wellness unit from Applied Performance, owning individual nutrition consultations, supplement education, body composition and bone density assessment, and the training table/fueling stations. **Explicit** [baylor-applied-performance-playbook.md p.5]
139:- Basic movement skills and basic lifts are taught before anything advanced, on the observed premise that many incoming athletes have high sport-specific skill from early specialization but poor general movement competency. **Inferred (transcript)** [01192022-hp5355-class1-transcript.md pp.4-5]

# Review: Supertraining Chapter 3, 3.4.3 to end (36 entries)

Reviewer: Claude Opus (independent falsification pass), 2026-09-27.
Brief: `staging/review_book_prompt.md`. Standards: `docs/ATOMIZE_BRIEF.md` (including the Ch1 lessons).
Scope: the 36 files in `staging/_scope_supertraining_ch3b.txt`, folder `staging/library/strength-and-conditioning/supertraining--verkhoshansky/`, plus the `_book.md` Ch3 rows from 3.4.3 on.
Source: `staging/books/supertraining-6th-expanded.pdf`, printed pp. 166-200. Page convention: entry "PDF p. N" is the 0-based index; PDF idx = printed + 11; viewer page = idx + 1. Every page reference below gives both ("PDF 192 / printed 181").

## How the source was checked

- Full text of PDF idx 174-212 (printed 163-201) was extracted with PyMuPDF and read in full. Every entry was compared line by line with it.
- Page images opened with the Read tool (viewer pages): 181 (Tables 3.10-3.12, printed 169), 191 (3.5.3 end, 3.5.4, 3.5.5 start, printed 179), 199 (Fig 3.35, printed 187), 202-203 (Figs 3.37-3.39, printed 190-191), 205 (printed 193), 208-209 (Figs 3.43-3.45, printed 196-197).
- What the images settled: Table 3.10 rows are labelled "I-III" and "MS"; at 67.5 kg MS is 13.1 vs I-III 13.0 (MS higher). Table 3.12 caption reads "kcalories"; front squat elite is 12.7. Johns & Wright figures print as 41 / 35 / 11 / 10% (sum 97%). Fig 3.35: relaxation time about 0.40 s at level 1 falling to about 0.22 s at level 5; contraction time about 0.30 s to about 0.22 s. Fig 3.37 (stretch matrix, shoulder): biceps stretched by shoulder **extension + lateral rotation**; triceps by shoulder **flexion + abduction**. Fig 3.38: biceps stretched by elbow extension + pronation. Fig 3.39: iliopsoas stretched by hip extension + medial rotation. Fig 3.44 (movement matrix): triceps acts in shoulder extension + adduction.
- External checks (fetched, not from recall): Herbert, de Noronha & Kamper, Cochrane 2011 (CD004577.pub3; PMID 21735398), abstract via cochrane.org; Herzog & Leonard 2000, J Biomech 33:531-542, abstract via full-text PDF. Everything else external below is marked "(verify)".
- Vault (`SecondBrain/Knowledge/library`): no Herbert/Cochrane, Valsalva, blindfold, irradiation, stretch-tolerance or Johns & Wright material. Relevant stretching items found: `research-papers/dupuy-2018-...` (stretching did not improve DOMS or fatigue, p. 11), `research-papers/carvalho-2012-...` and `research-papers/chatzopoulos-2014-...` (acute stretching mode effects), Moyer `heuristic--passive-vs-active-rom-decision-rule-sprint` and `heuristic--pails-rails-close-active-passive-gap-sprint` (active-passive gap), `research-papers/collings-2026-...` (non-contact ACL mechanism).
- All `[[links]]` in the 36 files resolve. No inline em dashes (headers only). Nobody uses "Eric's baseline:" (no misuse; see G6).
- Rule 3: one `proven` (stretch-reflex framework), one `contested` (stretching benefits), five `untested` (no-unsafe-stretch, Olympic lifters, dedicated-stretching, spinal ligaments; plus none else), rest `supported`.

## Global findings (rows cite "G1" etc.)

- **G1. Locator errors, 3.5.3-3.5.9.** Several entries are one PDF page off, or cite a page the text is not on. 3.5.4 and 3.5.5 start on PDF 190 / printed 179 (not 189/178); the Magnusson bullet is PDF 192 / printed 181 (not 191); 3.5.9 is PDF 198-199 / printed 187-188 (not 199-201). Rows mark these "locator only" so they can be batched.
- **G2. Voice.** "The authors" is used throughout, which the brief allows. But 3.5-3.7 is clearly Siff's text: printed 180 (PDF 191) calls the section "this article", and printed 198 (PDF 209) says "a myotensiometer, which we used ... (Siff, 1986)". Where an entry rests on Siff (1986) or Siff (1987), say it is the author citing his own work. This matters for confidence in the Olympic-lifters, six-parameters and flexibility-definition entries.
- **G3. Missing mandatory section.** `claim--irradiation-...` and `claim--hypnosis-...` have no **When to apply** section (the skill schema requires it).
- **G4. "The book's own example" used for mixed content.** In several rows the Example adds the writer's material under that label (ligament "acute exposure", spurious tension "same tissue flexibility", movement matrix calf raise and leg curl, no-unsafe-stretch "paired example"). Only the source's words may sit under that label; the rest needs "Inference:".
- **G5. ## The three uncited claims on printed 181 (PDF 192)

The printed-181 bullet list has many uncited lines. Three became entries or parts of entries:

1. **Steroids disrupt the three-material bone-tendon transition** (`claim--tendon-insertion-...`). No citation in the book. The graded enthesis itself is well described in anatomy (fibrocartilaginous entheses with uncalcified and calcified fibrocartilage zones; e.g. Benjamin et al. 2006, J Anat 208:471, verify). I found no source for the steroid-disrupts-gradient mechanism; the steroid-tendon-rupture association rests mainly on case reports and animal studies (verify). Recommendation: set `confidence: untested` for the steroid clause (or split: `supported` for the graded transition, `untested` for the steroid effect), and keep the "uncited" flag the entry already has.
2. **"There is generally no such thing as an unsafe stretch or exercise"** (`heuristic--no-unsafe-stretch-...`). Uncited aphorism. `untested` is right.
3. **Russian/Eastern European scientists discourage cycling, push-ups and sit-ups for ROM** (absorbed into `framework--six-parameters-...`). Uncited ("they have discovered"). Treat as `untested` inside that entry. Note the book elsewhere lists cycling as an indirect warm-up that "can often enhance performance" (Franks list, printed 164 / PDF 175).

# Review: Supertraining Chapter 3, 3.4.3 to end (36 entries)

Reviewer: Claude Opus (independent falsification pass), 2026-09-27.
Brief: `staging/review_book_prompt.md`. Standards: `docs/ATOMIZE_BRIEF.md` (including the Ch1 lessons).
Scope: the 36 files in `staging/_scope_supertraining_ch3b.txt`, folder `staging/library/strength-and-conditioning/supertraining--verkhoshansky/`, plus the `_book.md` Ch3 rows from 3.4.3 on.
Source: `staging/books/supertraining-6th-expanded.pdf`, printed pp. 166-200. Page convention: entry "PDF p. N" is the 0-based index; PDF idx = printed + 11; viewer page = idx + 1. Every page reference below gives both ("PDF 192 / printed 181").

## How the source was checked

- Full text of PDF idx 174-212 (printed 163-201) was extracted with PyMuPDF and read in full. Every entry was compared line by line with it.
- Page images opened with the Read tool (viewer pages): 181 (Tables 3.10-3.12, printed 169), 191 (3.5.3 end, 3.5.4, 3.5.5 start, printed 179), 199 (Fig 3.35, printed 187), 202-203 (Figs 3.37-3.39, printed 190-191), 205 (printed 193), 208-209 (Figs 3.43-3.45, printed 196-197).
- What the images settled: Table 3.10 rows are labelled "I-III" and "MS"; at 67.5 kg MS is 13.1 vs I-III 13.0 (MS higher). Table 3.12 caption reads "kcalories"; front squat elite is 12.7. Johns & Wright figures print as 41 / 35 / 11 / 10% (sum 97%). Fig 3.35: relaxation time about 0.40 s at level 1 falling to about 0.22 s at level 5; contraction time about 0.30 s to about 0.22 s. Fig 3.37 (stretch matrix, shoulder): biceps stretched by shoulder **extension + lateral rotation**; triceps by shoulder **flexion + abduction**. Fig 3.38: biceps stretched by elbow extension + pronation. Fig 3.39: iliopsoas stretched by hip extension + medial rotation. Fig 3.44 (movement matrix): triceps acts in shoulder extension + adduction.
- External checks (fetched, not from recall): Herbert, de Noronha & Kamper, Cochrane 2011 (CD004577.pub3; PMID 21735398), abstract via cochrane.org; Herzog & Leonard 2000, J Biomech 33:531-542, abstract via full-text PDF. Everything else external below is marked "(verify)".
- Vault (`SecondBrain/Knowledge/library`): no Herbert/Cochrane, Valsalva, blindfold, irradiation, stretch-tolerance or Johns & Wright material. Relevant stretching items found: `research-papers/dupuy-2018-...` (stretching did not improve DOMS or fatigue, p. 11), `research-papers/carvalho-2012-...` and `research-papers/chatzopoulos-2014-...` (acute stretching mode effects), Moyer `heuristic--passive-vs-active-rom-decision-rule-sprint` and `heuristic--pails-rails-close-active-passive-gap-sprint` (active-passive gap), `research-papers/collings-2026-...` (non-contact ACL mechanism).
- All `[[links]]` in the 36 files resolve. No inline em dashes (headers only). Nobody uses "Eric's baseline:" (no misuse; see G6).
- Rule 3: one `proven` (stretch-reflex framework), one `contested` (stretching benefits), five `untested` (no-unsafe-stretch, Olympic lifters, dedicated-stretching, spinal ligaments; plus none else), rest `supported`.

## Global findings (rows cite "G1" etc.)

- **G1. Locator errors, 3.5.3-3.5.9.** Several entries are one PDF page off, or cite a page the text is not on. 3.5.4 and 3.5.5 start on PDF 190 / printed 179 (not 189/178); the Magnusson bullet is PDF 192 / printed 181 (not 191); 3.5.9 is PDF 198-199 / printed 187-188 (not 199-201). Rows mark these "locator only" so they can be batched.
- **G2. Voice.** "The authors" is used throughout, which the brief allows. But 3.5-3.7 is clearly Siff's text: printed 180 (PDF 191) calls the section "this article", and printed 198 (PDF 209) says "a myotensiometer, which we used ... (Siff, 1986)". Where an entry rests on Siff (1986) or Siff (1987), say it is the author citing his own work. This matters for confidence in the Olympic-lifters, six-parameters and flexibility-definition entries.
- **G3. Missing mandatory section.** `claim--irradiation-...` and `claim--hypnosis-...` have no **When to apply** section (the skill schema requires it).
- **G4. "The book's own example" used for mixed content.** In several rows the Example adds the writer's material under that label (ligament "acute exposure", spurious tension "same tissue flexibility", movement matrix calf raise and leg curl, no-unsafe-stretch "paired example"). Only the source's words may sit under that label; the rest needs "Inference:".
- **G5. ## The three uncited claims on printed 181 (PDF 192)

The printed-181 bullet list has many uncited lines. Three became entries or parts of entries:

1. **Steroids disrupt the three-material bone-tendon transition** (`claim--tendon-insertion-...`). No citation in the book. The graded enthesis itself is well described in anatomy (fibrocartilaginous entheses with uncalcified and calcified fibrocartilage zones; e.g. Benjamin et al. 2006, J Anat 208:471, verify). I found no source for the steroid-disrupts-gradient mechanism; the steroid-tendon-rupture association rests mainly on case reports and animal studies (verify). Recommendation: set `confidence: untested` for the steroid clause (or split: `supported` for the graded transition, `untested` for the steroid effect), and keep the "uncited" flag the entry already has.
2. **"There is generally no such thing as an unsafe stretch or exercise"** (`heuristic--no-unsafe-stretch-...`). Uncited aphorism. `untested` is right.
3. **Russian/Eastern European scientists discourage cycling, push-ups and sit-ups for ROM** (absorbed into `framework--six-parameters-...`). Uncited ("they have discovered"). Treat as `untested` inside that entry. Note the book elsewhere lists cycling as an indirect warm-up that "can often enhance performance" (Franks list, printed 164 / PDF 175).

# Review: Supertraining Chapter 3, 3.4.3 to end (36 entries)

Reviewer: Claude Opus (independent falsification pass), 2026-09-27.
Brief: `staging/review_book_prompt.md`. Standards: `docs/ATOMIZE_BRIEF.md` (including the Ch1 lessons).
Scope: the 36 files in `staging/_scope_supertraining_ch3b.txt`, folder `staging/library/strength-and-conditioning/supertraining--verkhoshansky/`, plus the `_book.md` Ch3 rows from 3.4.3 on.
Source: `staging/books/supertraining-6th-expanded.pdf`, printed pp. 166-200. Page convention: entry "PDF p. N" is the 0-based index; PDF idx = printed + 11; viewer page = idx + 1. Every page reference below gives both ("PDF 192 / printed 181").

## How the source was checked

- Full text of PDF idx 174-212 (printed 163-201) was extracted with PyMuPDF and read in full. Every entry was compared line by line with it.
- Page images opened with the Read tool (viewer pages): 181 (Tables 3.10-3.12, printed 169), 191 (3.5.3 end, 3.5.4, 3.5.5 start, printed 179), 199 (Fig 3.35, printed 187), 202-203 (Figs 3.37-3.39, printed 190-191), 205 (printed 193), 208-209 (Figs 3.43-3.45, printed 196-197).

Johns & Wright figures print as 41 / 35 / 11 / 10% (sum 97%). Fig 3.35: relaxation time about 0.40 s at level 1 falling to about 0.22 s at level 5; contraction time about 0.30 s to about 0.22 s. Fig 3.37 (stretch matrix, shoulder): biceps stretched by shoulder **extension + lateral rotation**; triceps by shoulder **flexion + abduction**. Fig 3.38: biceps stretched by elbow extension + pronation. Fig 3.39: iliopsoas stretched by hip extension + medial rotation. Fig 3.44 (movement matrix): triceps acts in shoulder extension + adduction.
- External checks (fetched, not from recall): Herbert, de Noronha & Kamper, Cochrane 2011 (CD004577.pub3; PMID 21735398), abstract via cochrane.org; Herzog & Leonard 2000, J Biomech 33:531-542, abstract via full-text PDF. Everything else external below is marked "(verify)".
- Vault (`SecondBrain/Knowledge/library`): no Herbert/Cochrane, Valsalva, blindfold, irradiation, stretch-tolerance or Johns & Wright material. - All `[[links]]` in the 36 files resolve. No inline em dashes (headers only). Nobody uses "Eric's baseline:" (no misuse; see G6).

Locator errors, 3.5.3-3.5.9.** Several entries are one PDF page off, or cite a page the text is not on. 3.5.4 and 3.5.5 start on PDF 190 / printed 179 (not 189/178); the Magnusson bullet is PDF 192 / printed 181 (not 191); 3.5.9 is PDF 198-199 / printed 187-188 (not 199-201). - **G3. Missing mandatory section.** `claim--irradiation-...` and `claim--hypnosis-...` have no **When to apply** section (the skill schema requires it).

"The book's own example" used for mixed content.** In several rows the Example adds the writer's material under that label (ligament "acute exposure", spurious tension "same tissue flexibility", movement matrix calf raise and leg curl, no-unsafe-stretch "paired example"). ## The three uncited claims on printed 181 (PDF 192)

The printed-181 bullet list has many uncited lines. Three became entries or parts of entries:

1. **Steroids disrupt the three-material bone-tendon transition** (`claim--tendon-insertion-...`). No citation in the book. The graded enthesis itself is well described in anatomy (fibrocartilaginous entheses with uncalcified and calcified fibrocartilage zones; e.g. Benjamin et al. 2006, J Anat 208:471, verify). I found no source for the steroid-disrupts-gradient mechanism; the steroid-tendon-rupture association rests mainly on case reports and animal studies (verify). Recommendation: set `confidence: untested` for the steroid clause (or split: `supported` for the graded transition, `untested` for the steroid effect), and keep the "uncited" flag the entry already has.
2. **"There is generally no such thing as an unsafe stretch or exercise"** (`heuristic--no-unsafe-stretch-...`). Uncited aphorism. `untested` is right.
3. **Russian/Eastern European scientists discourage cycling, push-ups and sit-ups for ROM** (absorbed into `framework--six-parameters-...`). Uncited ("they have discovered"). Treat as `untested` inside that entry. Note the book elsewhere lists cycling as an indirect warm-up that "can often enhance performance" (Franks list, printed 164 / PDF 175).

2011-07-01 Stretching to prevent or reduce muscle soreness after exercise. ffects were evident between half a day and three days after exercise. One large study showed that stretching before and after exercise reduced peak soreness over a one week period by, on average, four points on a 100-point scale (mean difference -3.80, 95% CI -5.17 to -2.43). This effect, though statistically significant, is very small.

Authors' conclusions

The evidence from randomised studies suggests that muscle stretching, whether conducted before, after, or before and after exercise, does not produce clinically important reductions in delayed-onset muscle soreness in healthy adults.
